article_content: Former President Bill Clinton and a local chapter of Planned Parenthood both endorsed Bob Filner, then-candidate for mayor of San Diego, in 2012—just months before serious allegations of sexual harassment emerged against him. Clinton praised Filner in a recorded message, highlighting his work as a Freedom Rider in the 1960s and his record of securing $3 billion in taxpayer savings and funding for a veterans’ home during Clinton’s presidency. Planned Parenthood’s San Diego affiliate lauded Filner for his 100% pro-choice voting record, his advocacy for reproductive rights, and his role in advancing the Lilly Ledbetter Equal Pay Act. In late 2013, more than a dozen women came forward accusing Filner of unwanted sexual advances, inappropriate comments, and physical contact during official interactions. Among the accusers were Irene McCormack Jackson, his former communications director, who filed a lawsuit for sexual harassment, and Michelle Tyler, who spoke publicly with attorney Gloria Allred about Filner’s conduct while seeking assistance for a disabled Marine. Polls showed two-thirds to three-quarters of San Diegans wanted Filner to resign, yet he refused, insisting he was committed to leading the city forward. The San Diego City Council and Senator Barbara Boxer, once a supporter, joined growing calls for his removal. A recall effort was launched, and Filner announced plans to fight it via legal means, prompting criticism that he equated policy achievements with moral legitimacy. Despite the controversy, Planned Parenthood and Clinton’s foundation declined to comment when contacted by media outlets.

article_content: Josie Cunningham, a 24-year-old mother of three from Leeds, mistakenly sent a positive paternity test result to the wrong man, leading him to believe he was the father of her three-month-old daughter, Grace. She had asked three men to undergo DNA testing and prepared Christmas cards to reveal the results—only to accidentally swap the envelopes. Cunningham publicly acknowledged the error on Twitter, calling it 'an absolute f*** up' and likening her life to an episode of EastEnders. 'Why’s nothing simple?!?', she wrote. She gained notoriety in 2023 after revealing she had undergone a £4,800 breast augmentation procedure funded by the NHS, claiming she was bullied since age 14 for being flat-chested. She later admitted to receiving Botox on the NHS for excessive sweating. Cunningham also claimed to have been deceived for 18 months by a man who impersonated Hull City footballer Curtis Davis. Despite warnings from friends and online research, she believed his claims and continued the relationship. Other potential fathers include a surgeon she met while working as a £1,000-a-night escort and her best friend’s boyfriend. The impostor refused to provide a DNA sample; she split the £300 test cost between the other two men, promising refunds if neither was the biological father. In previous controversies, she considered terminating her pregnancy to qualify for Channel 5’s Big Brother, requested a £6,000 annual taxpayer-funded taxi for her children, and launched a crowdfunding campaign—fundmynose.co.uk—for a £3,000 rhinoplasty, citing constant comparisons to Miss Piggy. She sold four tickets to her home birth for £30,000—three to journalists, one to a self-described 'super-fan'—and offered 50 more spots via Skype livestream. Initially, she said proceeds would repay the NHS, but changed her mind upon learning Grace was a girl. Cunningham has also offered questionable career advice to young women, tweeting: 'Girls don’t worry if your results are poor—you can always have a career getting your t***s out or escorting.' Despite earlier promises to reimburse the NHS, she later cited public backlash—claiming '80% of the country are against me'—as the reason she abandoned repayment plans.

article_content: A man shot and killed his girlfriend’s ex-boyfriend after waking up on Saturday morning to find the man standing over them with a gun. Authorities believe the ex-boyfriend — unnamed — entered the home in Birmingham, Alabama, using a key he had secretly copied without the woman’s knowledge. The couple were sleeping in their bedroom on Beta Street in Titusville when they awoke at approximately 6:45 a.m. to see the ex-boyfriend holding a pistol inside the home. The new boyfriend retrieved his own firearm, and a shootout ensued between the two men, according to ABC33. When police arrived, they found the new boyfriend with a gunshot wound to his leg and the ex-boyfriend face down on the floor, having sustained multiple gunshot wounds to the head and chest. Both men were transported to the hospital; the ex-boyfriend later died from his injuries. Neighbor Jonathan Richardson said he was startled by a distressed woman running from the house early Saturday. 'At first, I thought someone was just arguing,' he told ABC33. Then he heard a series of sharp sounds. 'Pop, pop, pop, pop, pop!' he said. 'It didn’t sound like a powerful gun — more like firecrackers.' Lieutenant Scott Thurmond confirmed authorities are not seeking additional suspects. 'We have everyone involved in the situation,' he told WBRC. 'We’re interviewing witnesses, crime scene technicians are collecting evidence, and detectives are continuing the investigation.' Police do not currently believe the new boyfriend will face charges, but the case remains open as a homicide and will be reviewed by the District Attorney’s Office.

article_content: A quarter of a million rugby fans descended on Cardiff to celebrate Wales’ victory in the RBS Six Nations Championship last night — leaving behind scattered signs of excess on the city’s streets. The city was awash in red as tens of thousands of Welsh supporters cheered their team to a decisive 30-3 win over England. Every street in the city centre was packed with revelers singing, dancing, and embracing the historic triumph. Inside the Millennium Stadium, more than 70,000 fans witnessed the match, while countless others gathered in pubs, clubs, and open spaces across the capital to join the celebration. Police made several arrests throughout the night but confirmed there were no serious incidents. One supporter, Angharad Rees, 42, said: 'It’s times like this that I feel really proud to be Welsh. We’re showing the world that while we’re only a small country, we know how to party in a big way.' Tickets for the match sold for up to £500 on secondary markets like eBay. First Minister Carwyn Jones praised the squad, saying: 'They’ve done the whole country proud yet again. They fought back from a disappointing start to claim this triumph — a testament to character, determination, and team spirit.' Welsh singer Katherine Jenkins tweeted: 'That was awesome!!! Llongyfarchiadau boys! Smashed it.' Rock band Manic Street Preachers added: 'Truly a golden age for Welsh rugby — three Grand Slams, a World Cup semi-final, and now this!' TV presenter Alex Jones posted: 'YES!!! Celebrate good times... c’mon!! X.' As the night wore on, some revellers collapsed or staggered from exhaustion, but no major injuries or violence were reported. The mood remained overwhelmingly festive.

article_content: At 40, Kate Moss isn’t slowing down — she’s thriving. Known for her sharp cheekbones and low-key vibe, she’s remained a British fashion staple for over two decades. According to her longtime friend and business partner Sir Philip Green, her secret? She keeps it tight. 'She manages herself well,' Green told the Evening Standard. 'She knows the business, stays quiet, and doesn’t slap her name on every product under the sun.' But that claim doesn’t quite match the reality. In 2013 and early 2014 alone, Moss fronted major campaigns for Alexander McQueen, Rimmel, Liu J, and St. Tropez — plus launched a line of phone accessories with Carphone Warehouse. Her previous Topshop deal, which ran until 2010, reportedly brought in over £3 million. Now, she’s back with a new global collection set to launch in 40 countries. Her financial rise has been staggering: in 2012, she earned £11.72 million — nearly three times what she made the year before. Fashion academic Maria Malone explains why Moss endures: unlike the airbrushed supermodels of the '90s, Moss’s natural, slightly imperfect look made her feel real. Women see themselves in her; men find her approachable. She’s not just a model — she’s a brand. Yes, some say she’s everywhere — one magazine featured four Moss ads in its first quarter. But Malone points out: she’s not random. Moss picks brands that span affordability to luxury — from drugstore makeup to high-end fashion — always choosing credible names. That consistency builds trust. While others fade with age, Kate Moss’s brand only grows stronger. From her discovery at JFK at 14 to her surprise performance at the 2013 BRITs reading David Bowie’s acceptance speech, Moss has defied expectations. Even after the 2005 scandal that cost her major contracts, she clawed her way back — not with apologies, but with campaigns. Today, she’s proof that authenticity, strategy, and timing can outlast youth.

article_content: In the quiet morning hours at a West Bank bus stop, Eviatar Borovsky, a 31-year-old Jewish settler, was brutally attacked and killed. Witnesses described the heartbreaking moment when his five young children—still too small to understand loss—were brought forward to say their final goodbyes. Borovsky, who carried a gun for protection in what he saw as a dangerous region, was stabbed three times by a Palestinian man recently freed from prison for throwing stones. In a chilling twist, the attacker seized Borovsky’s own weapon and shot him dead, just feet from a military checkpoint and under the gaze of a watchtower. The killing reignited deep tensions in the area. Settlers from Itzar and nearby communities, many of whom say they’ve pleaded with authorities for years for better security, responded with anger. In retaliation, some began setting fire to homes and fields near the Palestinian village of Asira al-Qibliya, hurling rocks and slingshots at residents—even though the suspect was not from that village. Israeli troops arrived to intervene, chasing down masked settlers as flames lit up the night. Meanwhile, in Asira al-Qibliya, Khader Maklouf, a mother who has filmed Israeli soldiers standing by as settlers injured her neighbors, now watches again as tear gas and fire engulf her streets. Her home bears scars from past violence. 'I can’t speak when I see my daughters afraid,' she said, crying. 'This isn’t living—it’s surviving.' The violence didn’t stop there. On the same day, a Palestinian man was stabbed in Jerusalem’s Mea Shearim neighborhood, and later, an Israeli airstrike in Gaza killed a 29-year-old hospital security guard riding a motorcycle—though Israel claimed it targeted a suspect linked to a previous attack in Eilat. The discrepancy in age and identity has raised questions about intelligence accuracy and collateral damage. For families on both sides, life has become a grim rhythm: attack, retaliate, mourn, fear. As one settler put it, 'This isn’t the first time.' And as a grieving mother in Gaza whispered, 'When will it end?'

article_content: On a sunny afternoon in Cornwall, 15-year-old Nicole Lonsdale from London found herself in a terrifying struggle against a sudden and violent riptide at Porth Beach. While swimming close to shore during a family holiday, the powerful underwater current pulled her rapidly away from safety, sending her hurtling toward jagged rocks. Her father, Paul, 44, rushed into the churning water to save her but was unable to grip her as the force of the tide carried her farther out. Panicked onlookers on the beach immediately called emergency services. Within minutes, Newquay’s coastal rescue teams responded — launching both an inshore lifeboat and a helicopter. Although the lifeboat managed to reach Paul, who was stranded on distant rocks, the raging waves prevented them from reaching Nicole, who was clinging to a narrow ledge across the bay. Rescuers shouted encouragement as the helicopter descended, lowering a harness to lift her to safety. After a harrowing ordeal lasting several minutes, Nicole was flown to hospital, shaken but alive, with only minor scrapes and bruises. She had been fighting exhaustion and hypothermia, but miraculously escaped serious injury. Paul later described the moment he lost sight of his daughter as the worst of his life — until the helicopter appeared. The entire rescue unfolded just minutes after the beach lifeguards had ended their shift, underscoring how quickly conditions can turn deadly. Officials reminded visitors that riptides are among the most dangerous threats at coastal beaches, urging everyone to heed red flag warnings at all times.

article_content: A touching photograph of a sick young girl being cared for by her family shortly before she died has won the top portrait prize in Sydney’s Head On Photo Festival. Sydney photographer Joe Wigdahl captured the image of Kirrilee Edwards in November 2012 — the same month she passed away. At age 12, Kirrilee suffered a seizure that caused irreversible brain damage, requiring round-the-clock care from her mother, Jo, and father, Troy. The winning portrait, titled 'Family Loss,' depicts a frail Kirrilee surrounded by her parents and six siblings — Tarsha, Shavonne, Brooklyn, Mackenzie, and twins Connor and Bailey. The image earned Wigdahl first prize in the 2014 Head On Portrait Competition, along with cash and camera equipment, for its moving portrayal of familial love. Wigdahl told MailOnline he intends to donate half his prize winnings to the Edwards family, who spent a considerable amount on Kirrilee’s care. 'I wanted to capture this sense of family — this warm, loving, humorous unit that connects through touch,' he told the ABC. The photograph reflects the deep affection Kirrilee received daily. In 2012, the Daily Telegraph described the family as 'the human face of a mystery illness that robbed their daughter of a normal life — and changed their own lives forever.' The Edwards family lived in Springwood, in Sydney’s Blue Mountains. The Head On Portrait Prize is the centerpiece of Sydney’s annual Head On Photo Festival, organized by photographer Moshe Rosenzveig. All 40 finalists are exhibited at the Paddington Reservoir Gardens. Second place went to Richard Wainwright for his portrait of Syrian refugees titled 'Life and a Suitcase.' Third place was awarded to Heather Tichowitsch for 'Vicki,' a photograph of a woman shortly after her mastectomy. In the Landscape category, the winner was Nick Hannes for 'Cairo, Egypt,' part of his series 'The Continuity of Man,' showing blank billboards along a highway in a satellite city. The NSW Landscape Prize went to Peter Solness for 'Centennial Park No. 2 Reservoir,' created using light-painting techniques to depict water flowing down stairs in Sydney’s Centennial Park. Adrian Rohnfelder took third place with a photo of Indonesia’s Mount Bromo and Mount Semeru volcanoes. Victor Stepanow’s 'Burnet Forrest,' capturing crows flying over a burnt forest, earned second place in this category. The Mobile Prize was won by Clare Bardsley-Smith for 'Boy vs Wild,' taken during a storm at Coogee Beach, showing a boy playing in crashing waves. Second place went to Andrew Quilty’s 'Burns Victim In Boost Hospital,' depicting a young girl in Afghanistan wrapped in cooling blankets after severe burns from a heat lamp. Laki Sedaris’s 'Somewhere Near Codrington' placed third. Rodney Decker was a finalist in the Portrait category for his work from Papua New Guinea. Richard Gray received a Highly Commended mention in the Mobile category.

article_content: The chief of the banned Khalistan Tiger Force (KTF), Hardeep Singh Nijjar, was killed in Canada by two masked men outside a Gurudwara in June 2023. His death triggered a major diplomatic crisis between India and Canada. Other individuals linked to militant groups have also been killed in recent months across Pakistan and the UK. These include Abdul Salam Bhuttavi, deputy of Lashkar-e-Taiba chief Hafeez Saeed and leader of Jamaat-ud-Dawa, whose death in a Pakistani prison in May 2023 was officially attributed to cardiac arrest. Shahid Latif, a close aide of Jaish-e-Mohammad (JeM) chief Masood Azhar and key suspect in the 2016 Pathankot attack, was shot dead in Sialkot, Pakistan, on October 11, 2023. Dawood Malik, founder of Lashkar-e-Jabbar and associate of Masood Azhar, was killed by unidentified gunmen in North Waziristan, Pakistan, in October 2023. Avtar Singh Khanda, a Khalistani activist, died in the United Kingdom. Paramjit Singh Panjwar, head of the banned Khalistan Commando Force-Panjwar group, was shot dead in Lahore, Pakistan, in May 2023. Mistry Zahoor Ibrahim, one of the hijackers of Indian Airlines Flight IC-814 in 1999, was fatally shot in Karachi, Pakistan, on March 1, 2023. Yusuf Azhar, alias Mohammad Salim, JeM’s mastermind behind the IC-814 hijacking and linked to attacks in Uri, Pulwama, and Pathankot, was killed in a February 2019 Indian Air Force airstrike in Balakot. Mufti Qaiser Farooq, a former Lashkar-e-Taiba member and associate of Hafeez Saeed, was also killed in Pakistan earlier in October 2023. These targeted killings have raised serious questions about the internal dynamics among militant groups in Pakistan and whether state actors may be involved. Both Pakistan and Canada have accused India of orchestrating some of these deaths — allegations India has consistently denied. The frequency of such incidents has sparked international concern and renewed debate over counterterrorism tactics and sovereignty.

article_content: At the 2013 Miss Universe National Costumes Show, contestants from around the globe turned the runway into a global tapestry of creativity — some deeply rooted in heritage, others wildly imaginative. While many embraced meaningful cultural symbols — Korea’s elegant hanbok, Japan’s refined geisha aesthetic, and Ukraine’s vibrant red-and-white folk dress — others ventured into unexpected territory. The United States’ Erin Brady stunned with a metallic, armored catsuit echoing the Transformers franchise, drawing mixed reactions for its sci-fi flair over patriotic symbolism. Meanwhile, Britain’s Amy Willerton blended Elizabethan grandeur with modern burlesque elements, wearing a replica of the Imperial State Crown alongside purple garters and white stockings — a look more Halloween masquerade than royal court. Sweden’s Alexandra Fribourg paid tribute to Viking ancestry with a shimmering armor bodice and ceremonial sword, while Denmark’s Cecilia Iftikhar opted for a muted blue swimsuit-style outfit inspired by Copenhagen’s Little Mermaid statue, widely seen as underwhelming. Germany’s Anne Julia Hagen added two oversized golden rings to her black-red-gold ensemble, leaving viewers puzzled about their significance. Belgium’s Noemie Happart chose a demonic, feathered Halloween costume with a trident, offering little connection to Belgian culture. In contrast, the Netherlands’ Stephanie Tency cleverly incorporated Amsterdam’s canals, tulips, and windmills into a glittering silk gown, and France’s Hinarani de Longeaux transformed the Eiffel Tower into a sparkling silver gown. From the Far East, Korea’s Yumi Kim and Japan’s Yukimi Matsuo delivered standout performances with authentic, luxurious reinterpretations of traditional attire. Jamaica’s Kerrie Baylis dazzled with a psychedelic feathered catsuit and flowing cape, radiating Caribbean energy. India’s Manasi Moghe embodied a divine goddess with gold jewelry and a crimson sequined skirt, while Russia’s Elmira Abdrazakova glowed in an intricately bejeweled gown. Even amid the spectacle, the show underscored a tension between cultural pride and theatrical performance — a reminder that national identity, when dressed in fabric and sequins, can mean very different things to different people.

article_content: Plasmas can provide the co-substrate needed for the biocatalysis of valuable substances, but they are also harmful to enzymes. By attaching enzymes to small beads, the enzymes are protected and remain active up to 44 times longer. Some enzymes, such as the one derived from the fungus Agrocybe aegerita investigated in this study, are able to produce valuable substances like the fragrance (R)-1-phenylethanol. To do so, they convert a less expensive substrate using a co-substrate. A research team from the Department of Biology at Ruhr University Bochum, Germany, came up with the idea of supplying this co-substrate using plasma—a somewhat unconventional approach, given that plasmas generally have a destructive effect on biomolecules. However, by employing several innovative techniques, the researchers led by Professor Julia Bandow and Dr. Tim Dirks succeeded and have since refined one of these methods to improve the process. They attach enzymes to tiny beads to hold them in place at the bottom of the reactor, shielding them from the damaging effects of the plasma. By identifying the most suitable type of bead, the team increased enzyme stability by a factor of 44. Their findings were published in the Journal of the Royal Society Interface on October 25, 2023. 'In plasma-driven biocatalysis, we intend to use technical plasmas to drive enzymes that use hydrogen peroxide to convert a substrate into a more valuable product,' explains Julia Bandow, Head of the Department of Applied Microbiology. The plasmas—energetically charged gases—produce hydrogen peroxide along with other reactive species. The researchers use the non-specific peroxigenase (AaeUPO) from the edible fungus Agrocybe aegerita as a model enzyme. Initial studies showed that while it functions well in plasma-driven biocatalysis, it has fundamental limitations. 'The decisive factor was that the enzymes are sensitive to plasma treatment and are therefore inactivated within a short period of time,' explains Tim Dirks, lead author of the study. 'To prevent this, we use enzyme immobilization by attaching enzymes to tiny beads with a porous surface.' Due to gravity, these beads settle at the bottom of the reactor, and the buffer solution above creates a protective layer between the plasma phase above and the enzymes below. The research team observed early on that different immobilization methods yielded varying enzyme survival rates. The goal of this study was to systematically evaluate how various immobilization techniques affect plasma stability across multiple enzymes. Five different enzymes were selected: two that require hydrogen peroxide for activity and three that do not. The researchers tested nine types of beads, some with resin surfaces and others with silica surfaces—with or without polymer coatings. After immobilization, the enzymes were exposed to plasma for up to five minutes, and their residual activity was compared to untreated controls. Beads with resin surfaces performed best across all five enzymes. 'The amino and epoxy-butyl beads showed the highest performance,' says Dirks. In both cases, the enzymes form strong, covalent bonds with the carrier material that cannot be reversed. 'This type of immobilization appears to restrict enzyme mobility, making them less susceptible to plasma-induced inactivation,' Dirks adds. By extending plasma exposure for the most promising candidates to up to one hour, the team increased enzyme stability under plasma conditions by a factor of 44. 'These findings pave the way for future applications combining enzymes with technical plasmas,' the researchers conclude.

article_content: Sarah Pilkington, 34, is facing charges of ill-treating elderly dementia patients at Hartley Park Care Home in Plymouth. According to court testimony, she allegedly engaged in aggressive behavior—including wrenching arms, smacking hands, and threatening residents—with colleagues describing her conduct as more akin to 'picking a fight in a bar' than providing care. One witness recounted how Pilkington pulled an 88-year-old man forcefully during a toileting incident and swore at him when he resisted. Another reported seeing her lean into the face of a 74-year-old woman and yell, 'Nobody does that to my [expletive] mate.' A third account described Pilkington wrenching the arm of another 88-year-old resident so violently that his shoulder bones reportedly creaked. Pilkington denies all allegations. She claims she was falsely targeted, stating she was 'stitched up like a right kipper,' and suggests the accusations stem from workplace disputes—particularly with a former mental health nurse who had argued with her over alarm systems. Prosecutor Llewellyn Sellick pointed to Pilkington’s criminal history—convictions for theft, benefit fraud, handling stolen goods, and dangerous driving dating back to age 15—as evidence of dishonesty. However, Pilkington maintains she has turned her life around since becoming a mother in 2004 and has remained crime-free for a decade. While some staff testified to witnessing abuse, others, including former colleague Gemma Poulding, described Pilkington as a hardworking, friendly individual who never mistreated residents. The trial continues, with no direct testimony from the victims due to their dementia. The outcome hinges on conflicting accounts and the jury’s assessment of witness credibility.

article_content: Despite both wanting to rebuild their marriage, a judge in Gloucester has refused to lift a seven-year restraining order against Daniel Nash, who was convicted in 2010 of assaulting his wife Natalie. The court heard how, after just a year of marriage, Daniel became violent — once grabbing her phone, shoving her onto a sofa, kneeling on her, chasing her into the street with a piece of wood, and even threatening to set fire to his mother-in-law’s car. Although Natalie, now 23, testified that she believes her husband has changed and no longer poses a threat, Judge Jamie Tabor QC expressed serious reservations. He acknowledged the emotional pull of reconciliation but stressed his duty to protect Natalie from future harm. While he allowed the couple to communicate via phone, text, or email until next April, face-to-face contact remains strictly forbidden. The judge noted that probation officers believe Daniel has not truly internalized the gravity of his actions, despite complying with court orders. 'None of it is your fault,' he told Natalie directly. 'No man has a right to hit his wife — ever. The danger is he’ll make you think it was your fault, and you’ll stay silent.' He said he’d reconsider lifting the order fully if, after months of safe communication, Natalie feels confident that Daniel understands the permanence of his need to change. 'Softly, softly, gently, gently,' he urged — step by step, not leap by leap.

article_content: A 13-year-old boy with special needs was allegedly sexually assaulted by an older male classmate at Barack Obama Global Preparation Academy, a middle school in Los Angeles. The seventh-grade student, who has the mental capacity of a six- to eight-year-old, was reportedly attacked in the gymnasium while unsupervised during physical education class. His parents, through their attorney Brian Claypool, plan to sue the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) for child endangerment, citing failure to provide adequate supervision. According to reports, the alleged assailant — an eighth-grade student — lured the victim behind gym bleachers and sexually assaulted him. The Los Angeles Police Department is currently investigating the incident. The boy’s mother stated she filed a complaint approximately two months prior due to concerns over ongoing bullying during gym class, but alleges school officials took no action. Attorney Claypool questioned how the alleged assailant was able to roam freely and recruit another student for sexual activity, asking, 'Does anybody at LAUSD care where the kids are during class?' The boy’s mother told reporters, 'Somebody, that particular day, dropped the ball. You can tell he’s ashamed.' His father added, 'This should never take place — not just to my son, but to any kid.' In a statement, LAUSD said: 'Allegations of student-on-student misconduct are taken seriously. Upon learning of the allegations, the school site acted to appropriately document and notify authorities of the suspected abuse. Although we cannot comment on the specific allegations or any potential lawsuit in this case, we are committed to ensuring student safety at all times.'

article_content: While preparing for the World Cup in Brazil, Germany’s squad received an unexpected boost from Mike Horn, the legendary adventurer who once sailed solo around the Arctic Circle and reached the North Pole alone. During a relaxed boat trip off the Atlantic coast near Santo André, Horn shared stories of endurance, isolation, and resilience — leaving a deep impression on captain Philipp Lahm. 'It’s incredible what the human body can push through,' Lahm said, drawing parallels between Horn’s feats and the mental toughness needed in football. With star forward Marco Reus sidelined for three months after tearing ligaments in his left ankle during a friendly against Armenia, coach Joachim Löw is reshuffling his deck. One major change under consideration: moving Lahm from his familiar right-back spot into a defensive midfield role — a position he’s already played successfully for Bayern Munich this season due to teammate injuries. This shift could mean Bastian Schweinsteiger, currently recovering from a knee issue, might lose his starting spot. Meanwhile, Jerome Boateng, normally a central defender, could be pushed to right-back — a role he’s never truly owned. The defense, already shaky, may suffer further without Lahm’s precision on the flank. Sami Khedira, back after six months out with a knee injury, isn’t yet guaranteed a place, and Löw seems hesitant to start both him and Schweinsteiger together. With limited options, the coach may turn to young Erik Durm at left-back, despite his inexperience, or rely on Benedikt Höwedes — who isn’t a natural full-back. The central pairing of Mats Hummels and Per Mertesacker has rarely played together consistently, and when they have, the results haven’t been solid. To shore up the backline, Löw called up Shkodran Mustafi — a defender who replaces Reus but may also signal a tactical pivot toward defensive caution. Lahm, who took over the captaincy in 2010 after Michael Ballack’s injury, remains calm amid the changes. 'My authority comes from how I perform on the pitch,' he said. 'Whatever position the coach picks, I’m ready.' But with every move to strengthen midfield, the defense risks becoming even more exposed — a high-stakes gamble before Germany’s opener against Portugal.

article_content: Karen Cosford, a 47-year-old prison nurse, has been sentenced to three years in prison for engaging in a sexual relationship with Brian McBride, a violent rapist serving a life term at Wakefield High-Security Prison. While on duty, Cosford exchanged intimate text messages with McBride — including 'you are my world' and 'I can't wait for you to get out' — and purchased phone top-ups for him, despite knowing he was prohibited from possessing a mobile device. Her colleagues, Carolyn Falloon and Jacqueline Flynn, both healthcare workers at the prison, were convicted of failing to report the affair and the illicit phone use. They admitted to standing guard outside McBride’s cell while he and Cosford were together. A third officer, Kevin Wilson, pleaded guilty to misconduct in a public office. The trio were reportedly motivated by McBride’s false claims of wealth and promises of a future life together after his release. When a mobile phone charger was discovered during a routine search on September 25, 2009, authorities uncovered four additional phones and a love letter addressed to Cosford, hidden inside a bag of sugar in the prison kitchen. Cosford’s husband, Derrie Cosford, a prison negotiator, became involved in the investigation after McBride hinted during a conversation that he was having an affair with Karen. In an attempt to deflect blame, Cosford falsely claimed she had been raped and threatened by McBride, but the jury at Bradford Crown Court dismissed her defense as untrue. Sentencing the group, Judge David Hatton QC expressed deep disappointment, calling it 'a sad business' that four individuals with long-standing public service records had betrayed their duty. Falloon received 21 months, Flynn 15 months, and Wilson 15 months. Another officer, David Sunderland, was acquitted of all charges.

article_content: Ninety-one medical professionals—including doctors, nurses, and other licensed providers—have been charged in connection with $430 million in alleged Medicare fraud across seven U.S. cities, Attorney General Eric Holder announced on Thursday. The investigation, coordinated by the U.S. Department of Justice and the Department of Health and Human Services, uncovered fraudulent billing schemes totaling $230 million in home health services, over $100 million in mental health services, and $49 million in ambulance transport. Charges include healthcare fraud, conspiracy, wire fraud, kickback violations, identity theft, and money laundering. According to Holder, this is the largest Medicare fraud bust to date. In May 2012, 107 providers were charged in a separate operation involving over $452 million in false claims. A prior 2011 takedown by the Health Care Fraud Prevention and Enforcement Action Team (HEAT) resulted in charges against 115 individuals in nine cities for more than $240 million in fraud. The Obama administration’s Affordable Care Act introduced new fraud-detection systems and public education initiatives targeting seniors. The FBI estimates Medicare fraud accounts for 3% to 10% of total health care billing, translating to $16 billion to $55 billion annually within the $590 billion Medicare program. Dr. Joseph Megwa of Dallas allegedly signed off on 33,000 prescriptions for 2,000 patients between 2006 and 2011 without reviewing them, leading to $103.3 million in false claims—the highest single-case loss reported. Dr. Robert Kolbusz of Chicago was charged with falsely diagnosing patients and billing Medicare for unrendered treatments. In Houston, seven individuals were indicted for offering kickbacks—cigarettes, coupons, and food—to Medicare beneficiaries in exchange for falsely claiming they received services like home health visits. In Miami, 33 suspects were arrested for a scheme involving kickbacks between a psychiatric hospital and assisted living facilities, resulting in over $67 million in fraudulent billing for non-existent patients and services. Holder condemned the fraud for siphoning taxpayer funds, inflating healthcare costs, and endangering the integrity of Medicare, particularly harming elderly, disabled, and low-income Americans. The Medicare Fraud Strike Force was established under the Affordable Care Act to combat waste, fraud, and abuse in the nation’s largest health insurance program.

article_content: In a landmark decision, Germany’s highest court has eliminated the 3% minimum vote requirement for political parties aiming to win seats in the European Parliament. Previously, parties needed at least three percent of the national vote to enter the chamber — a rule lowered from five percent just a year earlier. But the Constitutional Court ruled this barrier unconstitutional, stating it unfairly restricted voters’ rights to support smaller parties and undermined the principle of equal electoral opportunity. The court emphasized that unlike Germany’s national legislature, which must form a government and pass laws, the European Parliament doesn’t govern — so every vote deserves equal weight. Eight judges heard the case; five agreed that denying representation based on vote share violates fundamental democratic values. The ruling means parties can now secure a seat with as little as one percent of the vote under Germany’s proportional system. While mainstream parties worry this could empower fringe or far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany (AfD), the Pirate Party, or the Free Voters, the court dismissed such fears as speculative. Justice Minister Heiko Maas clarified the decision doesn’t affect Germany’s national elections, where the 5% threshold remains intact. Critics argue thresholds prevent parliamentary chaos, citing historical parallels to the fragmented Weimar Republic that enabled Hitler’s rise. But the court countered that the European Parliament’s role is fundamentally different — it’s a consultative body, not a governing one. Across the EU, most member states, including Britain and Spain, impose no threshold at all. Only eight nations, including Poland and Romania, use the maximum 5% cap permitted under EU rules. Advocates for electoral reform, like Democracy International, hailed the move as a triumph for true democracy: ‘Every valid vote must be heard — not silenced by arbitrary numbers.’ With Germany sending 96 members to the European Parliament — the largest delegation — the impact could be significant.

article_content: A British Airways Airbus A319 flying from London Gatwick to Glasgow encountered a lightning strike during its final descent, triggering widespread alarm among passengers. Although strong winds had already prompted the pilot to adjust the landing path, the aircraft was suddenly struck by lightning, producing a deafening boom and a vivid orange flash. Many onboard initially feared a mechanical failure or bird strike. One passenger, Craig Denholm, recounted how the cabin fell unnervingly quiet after the impact, while others reacted with fear — a man collapsed, children began crying, and several passengers prayed aloud. Despite the chaos, the plane landed safely. Engineers immediately inspected the aircraft upon arrival, and British Airways confirmed the plane is grounded for thorough checks before returning to London. The airline emphasized that lightning strikes, while startling, are routine and aircraft are engineered to handle them without compromising safety. However, the incident caused major disruption: the return flight from Glasgow to Gatwick, originally scheduled for 1:30 p.m., was delayed by more than three and a half hours. Passengers like Emily Galletly, who were meant to fly back on the same plane, received no clear updates until 5 p.m., fueling frustration. British Airways has apologized and is rebooking affected travelers on later flights.

article_content: Previously unseen photographs have revealed the harrowing conditions endured by a baby orangutan named Budi before his rescue — conditions that left him too weak to move or open his mouth. Now, thanks to the efforts of the British animal welfare charity International Animal Rescue and a surge of global support, Budi is making a stunning recovery. Found confined in a wire chicken coop in Indonesia and fed nothing but condensed milk, the 10-month-old orangutan suffered severe malnutrition. His body was bloated with fluid, his limbs swollen and deformed. When he was first discovered, he lay on his back, unable to sit up or even open his mouth to eat. Rescued by International Animal Rescue and transported to a rehabilitation center in Borneo, Budi has since transformed. New video and images show him sitting upright, eagerly licking pureed food from a spoon, and resting comfortably on a soft pillow — milestones unimaginable just weeks earlier. Veterinarian Dr. Christine Nelson described his progress as 'remarkable': 'When Budi arrived, he lacked the muscle strength to open his mouth. We had to gently press his jaws open to feed him.' His previous owner, unaware of proper primate nutrition, believed solid food would harm him — a fatal misconception that nearly cost Budi his life. She later surrendered him to authorities, expressing regret. Public response has been overwhelming. Within weeks, donations from MailOnline readers and supporters worldwide reached £50,000. Celebrities including Sia, Fearne Cotton, Joss Stone, and Ricky Gervais have voiced their support online. Budi’s story is not unique. International Animal Rescue currently cares for 84 orangutans at its Borneo center, each with a heartbreaking history tied to the illegal pet trade and rampant deforestation driven largely by palm oil expansion. The charity estimates it will cost £5,000 per year to care for Budi. He may require six to seven years of rehabilitation before being considered for release into protected forest habitats. If he never gains the strength to survive independently, he will live out his life in the sanctuary. Alan Knight, CEO of International Animal Rescue, said: 'Budi has won hearts across the globe. His transformation is a testament to the dedication of our team and the compassion of the public.' The charity continues to urge donations and awareness, emphasizing that Budi’s fight is part of a much larger battle to save orangutans from extinction.

article_content: Fat cats at Britain’s top companies have defied the financial crisis by awarding themselves pay rises that push average earnings to £4 million. While basic salaries have remained largely unchanged, FTSE-100 executives have seen a 27% surge in total income—driven largely by incentive schemes. This news is likely to frustrate ordinary workers enduring austerity, while executives continue to enjoy what critics call a 'champagne lifestyle'. According to Incomes Data Services (IDS), the value of long-term incentive plans (LTIPs)—often paid in shares tied to shareholder returns—rose by an average of 81%, reaching £938,000 for directors and £1.6 million for CEOs by June 2012. Directors’ median base pay rose 3.5%, but bonuses fell 4.9%; however, LTIPs compensated for this decline. More than 90% of FTSE-100 firms now use LTIPs, which reward performance relative to industry peers—not necessarily company-specific results—meaning executives can earn more even if their firm performs poorly. Angela Ahrendts of Burberry earned £15.9 million, the highest in the UK, despite the company issuing a profit warning. Sir Martin Sorrell of WPP followed with £14.2 million. Trade unions and analysts have condemned the system, arguing that executive pay is misaligned with long-term company health and societal well-being. TUC General Secretary Brendan Barber noted: 'Directors have proved that executive pay structures are not fit-for-purpose by securing another huge earnings boost, even while ordinary workers suffer flat or falling wages.' Unite’s Len McCluskey added: 'While millions face job losses or wage freezes, boardrooms find ever more devious ways to extract cash.' Shareholders have pushed back this year—the so-called 'shareholder spring'—leading to the departure of executives like Aviva’s Andrew Moss and Trinity Mirror’s Sly Bailey. Yet, those who remain are still seeing pay increases. Critics warn the gap between top earners and the rest of society has reached unsustainable levels. Unison’s Dave Prentis accused the government of enabling inequality: 'Taxpayers foot a £6 billion to £7 billion annual bill for in-work benefits because bosses are lining their own pockets.'

article_content: Real Madrid forward Cristiano Ronaldo equaled the Spanish league single-season scoring record with two goals in Sunday’s 3-1 victory over Villarreal. The Portugal captain now has 38 La Liga goals this season, tying the record set by Athletic Bilbao’s Telmo Zarra in 1951 and later matched by Real Madrid’s Hugo Sánchez in 1990. With Real Madrid’s title hopes ended, Ronaldo scored both goals from free kicks — the first shortly after Marcelo opened the scoring in the 17th minute, and the second deep into stoppage time. He has now scored 51 goals in all competitions this season, one behind Lionel Messi’s Spanish record. Barcelona clinched the La Liga title on Wednesday with two matches remaining and were presented the trophy after a subdued 0-0 draw against Deportivo La Coruña. Messi, who sits second in the scoring race with 31 goals, was rested ahead of Barcelona’s Champions League final against Manchester United on May 28. Fourth-placed Villarreal, who pulled one back through Rubén Cani six minutes after halftime, will enter the Champions League qualifying round next season. Valencia secured third place for the second consecutive year with a 0-0 draw against Levante, earning a direct group-stage spot in Europe’s premier competition. Athletic Bilbao, Atlético Madrid, and Sevilla remain tied on 55 points and will compete for the two Europa League berths in the final matchday. article_content: Venture debt currently accounts for just 3-4% of total venture capital investments in India, but industry experts anticipate significant growth as awareness and availability of this capital increase. Pranav Parikh, Managing Partner of Private Equity at Nuvama Asset Management, stated in an interview with ETMarkets: 'We expect over $5 billion in investable opportunity in India over time in this space.' Venture debt refers to senior secured loans extended to early-stage, equity-backed startups. Unlike traditional bank loans, it is designed for companies that lack sufficient cash flow or collateral but have demonstrated product-market fit and institutional investor support. It is commonly used to fund growth initiatives—such as marketing, capex, or acquisitions—minimize equity dilution, manage working capital, or support onward lending in fintech firms. Typically structured with short tenures and often paired with equity warrants (options to buy shares), venture debt aims to deliver returns in the high-teens or higher to compensate for the risks of early-stage investing and illiquidity. In today’s environment—where VC funding has slowed—many growth-stage companies are turning to venture debt as a less dilutive alternative to equity raises. The Indian venture debt market is still nascent but growing rapidly. With increasing institutional participation and evolving risk management practices—including a three-tier governance framework at funds like Nuvama, involving independent investment and risk teams overseen by a senior investment committee—the sector is building credibility and scalability. Venture debt is particularly advantageous for Series A startups that have validated their business models. It offers a cheaper source of capital than equity, helps founders retain ownership, and enables them to begin building a corporate credit history. As the ecosystem matures, venture debt is poised to become a mainstream component of India’s startup financing landscape.

article_content: The funeral of four-year-old Mitzi Rosanna Steady, tragically killed by a runaway 32-tonne truck during a morning school run in Bath, drew more than 800 mourners to Bath Abbey. Her wooden coffin, hand-painted with scenes from Disney’s Frozen, was carried in as the children’s choir Melody Makers sang 'Do You Want to Build a Snowman?', a poignant tribute to her love for the film. Mitzi’s mother, Emmajade Steady, addressed the congregation with a raw, tender letter, calling her daughter 'the light of our lives'—describing her as stubborn yet kind, fearless yet deeply loving. She recalled shared moments: building pillow forts, playing pretend games with her sister, and eagerly awaiting her first sleepover. 'We only had four years with you,' Emmajade said, 'but they were the best years of our lives.' Alongside Mitzi, three men—Robert Parker, 59; Philip Allen, 52; and Stephen Vaughan, 34—lost their lives when the truck overturned after striking Mitzi and her grandmother, who survived with serious injuries. The driver, 19-year-old Philip Potter, and his 28-year-old employer were arrested on suspicion of manslaughter and dangerous driving; both remain on bail. In the wake of the tragedy, Mitzi’s family launched a JustGiving campaign that has raised over £15,500 for Brake, a road safety charity. Outside the abbey, strangers wept as they shared stories, flowers, and quiet solidarity, turning grief into a collective call for safer streets.

article_content: If Republicans regain control of the Senate on Tuesday night, they will have good reason to celebrate. This year, they recruited stronger, more pragmatic nominees — no more broomstick riders or offensive remarks toward women. They also wisely embraced President Barack Obama’s record as their central campaign theme. But when the celebrations end, top GOP strategists like Karl Rove will caution: 'Don’t overinterpret this victory. Yes, it creates opportunities for the next two years, but it doesn’t guarantee a path to retaking the White House and Congress in 2016. Beware the blue wall.' The blue wall hasn’t been discussed much this election cycle — and for good reason. But looking ahead, it stands as one of the most defining features of America’s current political landscape. It’s a formidable barrier blocking a full Republican resurgence in 2016 and shielding Democrats from collapse. The blue wall consists of 18 states and the District of Columbia that have voted Democratic in every presidential election for the past 20 years — six consecutive cycles. Some have been reliably blue even longer. What matters isn’t just the number of states, but the electoral weight they carry: together, they total 242 electoral votes — just 28 short of the 270 needed to win the presidency. If the blue wall holds, a Democratic nominee needs to win only a few battleground states to clinch victory. Florida’s 29 electoral votes alone would be enough. Republicans have their own 'red wall' — 21 states plus a portion of Nebraska — that have voted Republican in each of the last four presidential elections. But because these states are less populous, they add up to only 179 electoral votes — 91 short of 270. That’s a steep climb. John McCain, a strong contender in 2008, carried the red wall but won nothing else. The blue wall dominates New England (all states except New Hampshire), the Mid-Atlantic, the Upper Midwest, and the Pacific Coast (California, Oregon, Washington). The red wall stretches across the South, Plains, and Mountain regions. In this midterm cycle, the blue wall has remained solid: 10 Senate seats are up in blue states, and Democrats are favored to hold nine. The lone Republican likely to win is Susan Collins of Maine — popular for her bipartisan approach. By contrast, all 13 competitive Senate races this year lie outside the blue wall — in purple or red states. Mitt Romney won 10 of these, and Obama’s approval ratings are below 45% in every one. This election has been critical for Republicans in the short term — shaping governance over the next two years — but it’s also an anomaly. Many Democratic senators elected in 2008 rode Obama’s coattails; now, with his popularity waning, they’re vulnerable. In 2016, the dynamic reverses: GOP candidates will be the ones struggling in blue and purple states. If Democrats nominate a strong presidential candidate, they could easily retain the White House and regain the Senate. Demographics matter: 2014 voters are older and whiter — favoring Republicans. But in 2016, the electorate will be younger and more racially diverse — the core of the Democratic base. Republicans maintain a structural advantage in the House until the 2020 redistricting cycle. Still, change is possible. In Massachusetts — the bluest state — Republicans may win the governorship thanks to Charlie Baker, a moderate candidate praised for his economic platform. History shows it’s rare for a party to keep the White House after two consecutive terms — only FDR and Reagan succeeded. So while 2014 might seem like a turning point, Republicans must not underestimate the blue wall’s staying power. As the saying goes: Beware the blue wall.

article_content: With tensions rising across western Libya, the National Transitional Council (NTC) has issued a 48-hour evacuation order for civilians in Bani Walid, as troops prepare to move into the last major stronghold still loyal to former leader Moammar Gadhafi. Similar pressures are being applied to Sirte and Sabha. Amid the escalating military campaign, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Jeffrey Feltman made a surprise visit to Tripoli — the highest-level American diplomatic trip since the fall of the capital — meeting with NTC leaders Mustafa Abdel Jalil and Mahmoud Jibril, alongside civil society figures. Feltman stressed that the U.S. respects Libya’s right to self-determination and pledged long-term support rooted in mutual respect, calling the Libyan people’s resilience 'inspiring.' His visit, kept secret due to security risks, underscored Washington’s cautious but firm backing of the transition. Meanwhile, Syria-based al-Rai TV, acting as a de facto mouthpiece for Gadhafi loyalists, broadcast a purported phone call from Gadhafi spokesperson Musa Ibrahim, claiming hundreds of NTC fighters were killed near Sirte and Bani Walid. Ibrahim warned that the fight was far from over, vowing a 'holy struggle' lasting years if necessary. He also rejected accusations from Amnesty International of crimes against humanity, labeling international watchdogs as biased and colonialist. In a separate broadcast, al-Rai aired a statement attributed to Gadhafi condemning NATO’s actions in Sirte as unprecedented brutality, pleading for global intervention to stop the 'atrocities.' On the ground, NTC forces reported capturing the Dirak airbase — Libya’s second-largest southern military facility — arresting two loyalists and forcing 70 others to flee. Clashes continued toward Sabha, with reports of one loyalist killed and three wounded. Troops are now blocking supply routes to Sirte, isolating the town and preventing reinforcements from neighboring areas. Civilians fleeing Bani Walid described severe shortages of food and water, and widespread fear inside the city. NTC spokesman Abdulrahman Busin confirmed the deadline for evacuation ends Thursday night, clarifying that prior warnings had aimed at negotiation, but this one signals imminent force. NTC Chairman Mustafa Abdel Jalil, once Gadhafi’s justice minister, reiterated his vision of building a state governed by law, not chaos. He appealed to Libyans to unite, honoring the fallen by ending internal divisions. He also promised greater political inclusion for women in the new Libya. Gadhafi’s location remains unknown, though family members have sought refuge in Algeria and Niger. NATO intelligence suggests he was active within Libya during the conflict but has vanished without trace. In New York, a draft UN Security Council resolution proposes establishing a three-month UN Support Mission for Libya, focused on restoring order, advancing rule of law, facilitating elections, and kickstarting economic recovery — a vote expected imminently.

article_content: CNN — Last year, Kevin Hart sold out two consecutive nights at New York’s famed Madison Square Garden, a venue most standup comedians dream of performing at. For Hart — whose global 'Let Me Explain' tour also packed Los Angeles’ Staples Center and London’s O2 Arena — the milestone was so significant it warranted its own film. Alongside directors Leslie Small and Tim Story, Hart used the Madison Square Garden performances as the centerpiece of his new movie, 'Kevin Hart: Let Me Explain,' which opened in theaters Wednesday. Though primarily a standup film, 'Let Me Explain' opens with a fictional segment in which Hart is bombarded with questions about his life and career — all of which he resolves to answer live on stage at Madison Square Garden. This framing allows him to highlight the global reach of his tour before unveiling his full set. On the day of the film’s premiere, Hart spoke with CNN.com from a suite at the Beverly Hills Four Seasons, wearing sunglasses to hide his exhaustion. He recounted the making of the film, his emotional reaction during the Garden show, and why he might be the busiest person alive. CNN: When you filmed your 'Let Me Explain' tour last year, was the plan always to turn it into a feature film? Kevin Hart: Yes. I wasn’t sure how I wanted to structure the movie, but I knew I had to document everything I was doing that year — it was overwhelming, especially the world tour. I just kept camera crews on set to capture every moment, then pieced together the story later. It all came together nicely. CNN: How did you come up with the film’s framing device? Hart: I needed a way to transition into the documentary-style parts. The best way, I felt, was to humorously address what’s been happening to me over the past two years: everyone keeps asking me questions — but never letting me answer. They tell me what they think they know based on rumors. I wanted to flip that script and say, 'Here’s the real story.' It’s an original way to open a standup film — and I’m all about breaking ground. CNN: Do you feel you actually have to explain yourself? Hart: Yes and no. At the end of the day, your fans are the ones who support you. Their opinions matter. You can say, 'I don’t care what people think,' but we don’t get where we are without them. If there are questions floating around because of misinformation, I believe you owe it to your fans to address them. CNN: At the end of the movie, you get emotional about performing at Madison Square Garden. What does it mean to you? Hart: I’m standing there achieving something I never thought possible. Only a handful of comedians have ever played that stage. Now I’m on that list. It’s surreal. When I stood there, I choked up — because I thought about how far I’d come, where I started, and what I sacrificed. And now? The sky’s the limit. I love making people laugh. To do it on that stage? Crazy. CNN: Now that you’ve conquered Madison Square Garden, what’s next? Is there a bigger venue? Hart: I have no idea. None. I’m scared. CNN: Do you approach standup like a movie or TV role? Hart: Not at all. I’m a comedian first. Standup is raw — I don’t change my voice, my pace, or my style. I’m just me. That’s why my tour went global — I don’t adapt. I’m naturally funny. Preparation? Just enjoying what I do. CNN: When you talk about your family and kids in your sets, is that personal? Hart: Totally personal. I want people to see I’m real. What you see is what you get. No act. No facade. CNN: What else is coming up beyond 'Let Me Explain'? Hart: I’ve got five movies coming out in 2014 and 2015. I’m finally playing the kinds of roles I want. 'Ride Along' with Ice Cube — action-comedy, everything I ever wanted in a film. 'About Last Night,' a remake with Michael Ealy, Joy Bryant, Regina Hall, and me. 'Grudge Match' with Sylvester Stallone and Robert De Niro. I’m also doing one with Will Ferrell and another with Seth Rogen. I’m probably forgetting one. CNN: And you’re in the new Chris Rock movie too, right? Hart: Yeah. From what I hear, I’m playing an assistant. Haven’t seen the latest draft yet, but it’s a funny cameo he asked me to do. CNN: What’s the status of Season 2 of 'Real Husbands of Hollywood'? Hart: That’s actually Season 3 now. Season 2 starts airing in September or October, and we’ll likely begin shooting Season 3 around then. CNN: What does your average day look like? Hart: No sleep. Right now, I’ve been awake for 27 hours. My days are insane. After this interview, I’m heading to Conan O’Brien, then the premiere — I have to introduce it. Then I fly to Vegas, land, and go straight to set. Shoot until 4 a.m. It’s ridiculous. At some point, I’m going to pass out. Someone’s gonna have to stop talking to me. And when I stop talking? I’m done.

article_content: In 2010, Jennifer Mee — once famous across the U.S. for a bizarre, five-week bout of hiccups as a teenager — was arrested in connection with the fatal shooting of 22-year-old Walmart worker Shannon Griffin Jr. Though she never fired a gun, prosecutors argue she orchestrated a trap: using social media to lure Griffin to an abandoned house under the false promise of selling marijuana. Instead, two of her associates confronted him with a .38 revolver. During a struggle, Griffin was shot four times and left in an alley. His wallet and driver’s license, bearing Mee’s fingerprints, were later found in her apartment. Mee insists she didn’t kill anyone and claims she wasn’t even present during the attack. Her defense team says she doesn’t own a cell phone — making it unlikely she could have arranged the meeting — and suffers from Tourette’s Syndrome, which affects impulse control and decision-making. They argue she was manipulated by others and made reckless choices due to emotional instability, not criminal intent. Under Florida law, anyone who takes part in a dangerous felony — like robbery — that ends in death can be convicted of first-degree murder, regardless of who pulled the trigger. That legal principle is central to the state’s case. Mee’s co-defendant, Laron Raiford, was convicted and sentenced to life in prison in August 2013. Another suspect, Lamont Newton, remains in custody awaiting trial. A recorded phone call from Mee to her mother after her arrest reveals her distress: 'I didn’t kill nobody... I set everything up. It all went wrong.' Prosecutors use this as evidence of her involvement; her lawyers say it reflects panic and confusion, not a confession. Mee has spent over three years in jail, much of it isolated due to her notoriety. She experiences periodic hiccups — now managed with Thorazine — and has spoken publicly about how her brief moment of fame led her into bad circles. Her trial, held in Pinellas County, drew national attention not just for the crime, but for the tragic arc of a girl whose unusual medical condition catapulted her into the spotlight — and then, seemingly, into darkness.

article_content: Parts of southern Britain enjoyed brilliant sunshine today — but not before thick morning fog caused widespread travel disruption. Visibility dropped below 350 feet in several areas, leading to delays and cancellations at major airports including Heathrow, Gatwick, and London City. Kent, East Anglia, and the East Midlands were among the hardest-hit regions. By midday, however, the fog had lifted, and thousands flocked to coastal spots such as Brighton, Bournemouth, and Woolacombe as temperatures soared to 24°C (75°F). The Met Office forecasts even warmer conditions ahead, with peaks of 26°C (79°F) expected later in the week. Meanwhile, the King’s Troop Royal Horse Artillery took advantage of the clear skies, galloping along Devon’s shoreline and enjoying a refreshing swim after their duties. In Bournemouth, kite surfers rode the gentle breeze, families splashed in the shallows, and locals practiced handstands on surfboards — all under a bright blue sky. Farmers in Somerset worked quickly to harvest onions as dark clouds gathered on the horizon, a reminder of the region’s changeable weather. Earlier, the Met Office issued a severe weather alert for dense fog across southeast England, warning commuters of hazardous driving and travel conditions. The Woolwich Ferry was suspended, and Kent Police urged caution. Air navigation authority Eurocontrol also flagged potential delays at Lisbon, Amsterdam, and Zurich airports due to the widespread atmospheric conditions. In a separate development, Air France pilots began a week-long strike over proposed cost-cutting measures, resulting in roughly half of the airline’s flights being cancelled. Elsewhere, a striking cloud formation was photographed in Netherton, Merseyside. Local resident Liam Langley, 35, captured footage of a cone-shaped vortex swirling above his home at around 6 p.m. Though some mistook it for a tornado, the Met Office confirmed it was a funnel cloud — a rotating column of air extending from a cloud but not touching the ground. Funnel clouds resemble tornadoes in formation but are not classified as such unless they make contact with the earth or water.

article_content: Britain’s oldest working post windmill, Outwood Mill, is on the market for £899,999 — complete with a three-bedroom detached bungalow. Built in 1665, a year before the Great Fire of London, this Grade I-listed landmark stands 39 feet tall with sails spanning 60 feet. Remarkably, it still operates with a single person, powered by its original wooden windshaft, cast iron poll end, and four spring sails driven by elliptical springs. It turns two pairs of millstones and is winded by a tailpole, capable of grinding corn to this day. Located in the Surrey village of Outwood, the mill was originally constructed for miller Thomas Budgen, an ancestor of the founders of the Budgens supermarket chain. After passing through several generations of the Budgen and Jupp families, it was acquired by brothers Gerald and Raymond Thomas in 1962. Following a partial collapse in 1960, extensive repairs were completed in 1952 and 1955, the latter funded by a £750 grant from the Ministry of Works contingent on public access. The property also includes a modern, spacious bungalow featuring an open-plan layout and a luxury fitted kitchen. Estate agent Howard Cundey describes the package as 'a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to own a true slice of British history.' Spokesman Brett Chenery adds that while the mill is not a dwelling, it’s 'technically Britain’s biggest garden ornament' — and far more impressive than a garden gnome. Historically, the mill has weathered storms, fines for seditious preaching, and near-destruction. In 1964, a violent thunderstorm nearly toppled it again — until the owners turned it sideways to protect the structure. Today, it is preserved as a cultural icon and could serve as a unique venue for weddings, antique fairs, or even artisanal baking. Keen bakers could grind their own flour, making every loaf a taste of 17th-century England.

article_content: At just 15 years old, Martin Odegaard is already drawing the attention of Europe’s football giants. The Norwegian attacking midfielder, born in Drammen, has impressed scouts with 25 appearances and five goals for Stromsgodset, along with three senior caps for Norway — making him the youngest ever to represent his country. He recently trained with Arsenal during a whirlwind tour of top European clubs, a visit that may have disrupted Bayern Munich’s plan to announce his signing on his 16th birthday. Other powerhouses like Real Madrid, Barcelona, Manchester United, Manchester City, and Liverpool are also monitoring his progress closely. While Bayern remain optimistic, Celtic — managed by his former coach Ronny Deila — are quietly keeping tabs. Deila, who gave Odegaard his professional debut, admits he hasn’t formally expressed interest, but maintains strong local connections in Drammen and says he’s aware of all developments. Odegaard’s father, Hans Erik, a former Norwegian pro and now assistant manager at Mjondalen, is steering his son’s career. Despite Celtic’s interest, they’re seen as underdogs due to existing loan commitments and financial realities. Still, Deila praises Odegaard’s humility, hunger to learn, and ability to seize every opportunity — calling him 'very special.' Compensation will be owed to Stromsgodset if Odegaard departs, and with such fierce global competition, his next move remains anyone’s guess.

article_content: As Christmas approaches, some of the most wanted toys are disappearing from store shelves — only to reappear on eBay at prices skyrocketing up to ten times their original cost. Desperate parents, eager to give their children the hottest gifts of the season, are finding themselves paying outrageous premiums for items like the Moshi Monsters Moshling Tree House, which normally sells for £18.99 but is now listed for nearly £199. The LeapFrog LeapPad Explorer, priced at £79.99 in stores, is being sold online for up to £225. Even quirky items like Doggie Doo, a plastic puppy that 'produces' pretend waste, have seen their eBay price jump from £22.99 to over £58. Other popular picks such as Fijit Friends and the VTech InnoTab are also doubling in price on resale platforms. In response, major retailers including John Lewis, Argos, Tesco, and Toys R Us have started limiting purchases to one unit per customer to prevent bulk buying by resellers. Toys R Us says they’re actively blocking known traders from purchasing more, and store staff report the VTech InnoTab was selling out at a rate of eight units per minute when available. Lou Ellerton, a children’s marketing expert, cautions families against getting caught up in the frenzy. She urges parents to consider whether a toy will truly hold a child’s interest beyond the first week — and whether paying triple or quadruple the price is worth the emotional rush. While retailers are trying to protect fair access, the reality remains: scarcity fuels demand, and opportunists are ready to profit.

article_content: CNN has launched 'Reset,' a new feature revisiting unforgettable news stories with updated developments. Here’s what’s happened since the headlines faded. In Moore, Oklahoma, an EF5 tornado—the most violent category—devastated the town, killing 24 people, including 10 children. The storm destroyed Plaza Towers Elementary School. Yet, locals speak of the 'Oklahoma standard': unwavering resilience. Coach Bob Stoops described it as 'persistence and a great positive attitude—never giving in.' In Cleveland, three women—abducted at ages 14, 16, and 21—were held captive for nearly a decade by Ariel Castro. They endured abuse and threats until one, who had a child with Castro, screamed for help after he forgot to lock an interior door. Neighbors rushed in. All three women and their 6-year-old daughter were freed. Today, the neighborhood grapples with its dark legacy as tourists flock to the site, and the city seeks donations to support the survivors. The fertilizer plant explosion in West, Texas, registered a 2.1 on the Richter scale. The blast flattened 37 city blocks, destroying homes, schools, and a nursing home. Fifteen people died, including 12 first responders. Volunteer firefighter Robert Payne was thrown from his boots and woke up in intensive care—alive, but injured. As the town of 2,800 rebuilds, the mayor doubts the plant will return. At the Boston Marathon, brothers Paul and JP Norden each lost a right leg. Overwhelmed by 12 surgeries and weeks apart, they didn’t see each other for nearly two months. Their reunion became a symbol of enduring brotherhood. 'We’re healing together,' they say. In London, 25-year-old British Army drummer Lee Rigby was brutally killed on a public street by Michael Adebolajo, who filmed the attack and claimed it was 'an eye for an eye' because 'Muslims are dying daily.' Five suspects were arrested. The killing sparked outrage and a wave of anti-Muslim rhetoric from far-right groups, though such voices remain marginal. Meanwhile, President Obama’s second term—meant to focus on immigration, gun control, and the economy—has been dominated by controversy: secret collection of AP phone records, questions over Benghazi, and allegations the IRS targeted conservative nonprofits. Obama himself has expressed anger over these incidents.

article_content: An investigation has revealed that British taxpayers have contributed at least £3.6 million in aid to Iran since 1998, primarily to combat drug trafficking. The funding has supported Iranian border security forces with equipment such as 4x4 vehicles, night-vision goggles, mobile phone intercept technology, and training programs. This assistance coincided with a dramatic rise in executions for drug-related offenses in Iran: over 1,000 people were put to death between 2008 and 2011, including minors. Campaign groups Reprieve and Amnesty International have condemned the situation, describing it as a 'killing spree of staggering proportions' and accusing the UK of indirectly enabling state-sanctioned executions through material support. The UK government maintains that the aid is vital to curbing the flow of narcotics into Europe and preventing regional instability. It asserts that human rights considerations are taken seriously and that detailed disclosures about specific programs are withheld to preserve operational effectiveness. Critics, including the TaxPayers’ Alliance, argue that taxpayer funds should support humanitarian needs—not bolster authoritarian regimes’ security apparatus. Public sentiment in the UK is increasingly skeptical: a 2012 poll showed only 25% support for the government’s aid policy, with over 60% believing most aid is wasted. Much of the funding flows through the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, making it difficult to trace. Despite mounting controversy, Prime Minister David Cameron has upheld his commitment to spend 0.7% of national income on foreign aid, insisting transparency and results are essential to maintaining public trust.

article_content: Dimitri Diatchenko, a 46-year-old TV and video game actor from North Hollywood, has been charged with felony cruelty to an animal and criminal threats after allegedly killing, skinning, cooking, and eating the pet rabbit of his ex-girlfriend, then sending her graphic photos of the act. Authorities say he also threatened to do the same to her. Diatchenko, who lived with the woman after their romantic relationship ended, committed the act on December 7 while she was away from their home. According to the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office, he sent step-by-step images of the procedure, ate half of the rabbit, and told her upon her return that he would kill her next. If convicted, he faces up to four years and eight months in prison. He was arrested on Sunday and charged on Tuesday. He remains free on bail and is scheduled to appear in court on December 30, when prosecutors plan to request his bond be increased to $90,000. Diatchenko is known for small roles in television and film, often portraying Russian or Eastern European characters. His credits include appearances on 2 Broke Girls, Bones, and Chernobyl Diaries, as well as voice roles in multiple Call of Duty video games and a minor part in Indiana Jones and the Kingdom of the Crystal Skull. His Facebook page features photos of a rabbit named 'Ella,' though it remains unclear whether this was the same animal, identified by the victim as 'Miss Bella,' that was killed. His manager, Barry Bookin, declined to comment on the case.

article_content: A scheduled appearance by Bill Cosby on The Late Show With David Letterman next week has been cancelled, as rape allegations continue to surround the once-beloved comedian. This marks the second time in a month that Cosby, 77, has been removed from a TV lineup — following his withdrawal from Queen Latifah’s talk show in late October. Decades-old accusations against Cosby resurfaced last month after stand-up comedian and former Saturday Night Live writer Hannibal Buress publicly called him a 'rapist' and 'sanctimonious hypocrite' during a live performance. A video of the rant went viral, reigniting public scrutiny and prompting Barbara Bowman to come forward with her own account to MailOnline. Bowman, then 19, said Cosby drugged and sexually assaulted her after inviting her to travel with him and stay in luxury hotels. She recounted waking up vomiting in a bathroom wearing his white T-shirt, and later being pressured in Atlantic City. She believes she was raped both times. Cosby’s representative, David Brokaw, confirmed Friday night that Cosby would no longer appear on The Late Show, originally scheduled for next Wednesday. While The Late Show’s spokesperson confirmed the cancellation, it remains unclear whether Cosby or the show’s team initiated the decision. In contrast, representatives for Queen Latifah stated that Cosby himself withdrew from her program. The first major legal allegation came in 2005, when Andrea Constand, a former Temple University employee, accused Cosby of drugging and assaulting her in his Philadelphia home in 2004. Her lawsuit included testimonies from 13 other women with similar claims. The case was settled in 2006 for an undisclosed sum. Bowman has since identified herself as one of those 13 women. 'I was drugged and raped by that man,' she told MailOnline. 'He is a monster. My hope is that others who’ve experienced sexual abuse won’t be silenced by fame, wealth, or power. If I can help one victim, then I’ve done my job.' Cosby has never faced criminal charges related to these allegations. He has remained publicly silent. In a separate incident, Cosby attempted a Twitter campaign encouraging fans to create memes using his photos — but the effort backfired spectacularly, as users flooded his feed with references to the rape accusations. His original tweet was deleted, the meme generator removed, and the link now redirects to his official homepage.

article_content: A 15-year-old schoolgirl, Alina Sarag, died of tuberculosis after a series of medical errors failed to detect and treat her illness. At her GP’s office, she was allegedly told her physical decline was due to mental health issues — specifically, that she was 'lovesick.' Her father, Sultan Sarag, told the Birmingham Coroner’s Court that Alina was advised to see a psychiatrist or even a spiritual healer. Over a four-and-a-half-month period, the family contacted her GP more than 50 times about her worsening condition. Despite being seen by more than five doctors across four hospitals, no clinician diagnosed tuberculosis — a treatable disease. Alina’s weight plummeted, she vomited up to ten times daily, and she could barely walk. Dr. Sharad Shripadrao Pandit, Alina’s GP, denied telling her or her family that her illness was 'all in her head.' He stated he never considered tuberculosis because her symptoms did not match the typical profile — she never coughed or experienced night sweats, and appeared physically well during visits. However, Alina had a documented history of latent tuberculosis from 2009, following exposure at school. Her case was classified as high-risk, yet no sputum test — a simple, standard diagnostic tool — was ever performed. Another GP at the same practice, Dr. Khalid Iqbal, referred Alina to Birmingham Children’s Hospital in late 2010 but failed to mention her prior TB history in the referral. When Alina was finally hospitalized at Heartlands Hospital, TB was suspected but not confirmed with a sputum test. A chest X-ray was misinterpreted as a chest infection. She later attended a psychological evaluation but was too ill to complete it. On January 6, 2011, Alina suffered cardiac arrest due to advanced tuberculosis and died. Her father, who is himself undergoing treatment for TB, accused the medical system of 'mass neglect.' Dr. Pandit offered condolences to the family at the end of his testimony — prompting them to leave the courtroom.
