article_content: The United States are tied 1-1 with France after the first day of the Davis Cup World Group quarterfinal at the Monte Carlo Country Club in Roquebrune, France. France's Jo-Wilfried Tsonga gave the hosts the initiative with a four-set victory of 7-5, 6-2, 2-6, 6-2 over Ryan Harrison in the opening rubber. But the United States hit back to level the tie as big-serving John Isner fired nine aces in a straight-set win of 6-3, 6-2, 7-5 over Gilles Simon. "I took the court very confident," Isner said, according to DavisCup.com. "No matter who I was going to play today, I felt confident. That was the case today," he added. "I went out there and played very well—simple as that. I'm happy with how I played and glad I could help the team." The U.S., without Andy Roddick or Mardy Fish, will look to the Bryan brothers (Bob and Mike) to take the lead tomorrow as they face Michael Llodra and Julien Benneteau. Meanwhile, in Castellón, Spain took a firm grip on their tie against Austria as Nicolas Almagro and David Ferrer recorded straight-set wins over Jurgen Melzer and Andreas Haider-Maurer, respectively. The five-time champions, without injured Rafael Nadal, can now clinch the tie on Saturday with a doubles victory. Almagro was on court for just under two hours in his 6-2, 6-2, 6-4 win over Melzer, while world No. 5 Ferrer demolished Haider-Maurer 6-1, 6-3, 6-1 to extend his unbeaten streak in Davis Cup singles matches. "I won relatively easily and am happy with my game," Ferrer said, per DavisCup.com. "Maybe my opponent played a bit poorly and made many mistakes, but I stayed solid and consistent." In Prague, Serbia, without World No. 1 Novak Djokovic, got off to a rough start against the Czech Republic as Tomas Berdych cruised to a straight-set win over Victor Troicki, 6-2, 6-1, 6-2. But Janko Tipsarevic overcame Radek Stepanek in a five-set thriller: 5-7, 6-4, 6-4, 4-6, 9-7, leveling the tie. The winners will face either Argentina or Croatia, who are locked in a tight battle in Buenos Aires. That tie is evenly poised after Croatian No. 1 Marin Cilic defeated David Nalbandian 5-7, 6-4, 4-6, 7-6, 6-3, before Juan Martín del Potro leveled the match with a straight-set victory over Ivo Karlovic, 6-2, 7-6, 6-1.

article_content: On August 29, 2012, Australia endured its deadliest day of combat since the Vietnam War, losing five soldiers in two separate incidents in Afghanistan. Three members of the 3RAR task group were shot and killed by an Afghan soldier named Hekmat, who was on duty at a patrol base near Tirin Kot in Uruzgan province. He reportedly mistook the Australian troops for Taliban fighters and opened fire at close range during their evening downtime before fleeing. In a separate event, two Australian special forces soldiers died when their helicopter crashed in Helmand province. These losses brought Australia’s total military deaths in Afghanistan to 38. Prime Minister Julia Gillard abruptly ended her attendance at the Pacific Islands Forum to return home and oversee the national response. Defense officials confirmed this marked the third 'green-on-blue' attack involving Australian forces — a disturbing trend that had already claimed 45 coalition lives in 2012, accounting for approximately 14% of all coalition fatalities that year. Although Afghan officials described the shooting as a tragic misidentification, NATO continues to face serious challenges in fostering trust between local troops and international partners. Despite the profound grief and eroding morale, Gillard maintained that Australia’s mission was yielding tangible progress and remained essential to stabilizing Afghanistan. Australia, a long-standing U.S. ally, first deployed in 2001, re-engaged in 2005, and now plans to begin withdrawing its troops in 2013 — a move hastened by improved security conditions and increasing public demand to end the prolonged conflict.

article_content: CNN — There are many ways to lose or ruin your smartphone: forgetfulness, crime, gravity, anger, intoxication, or acts of God. These devices are deeply woven into our daily lives, and being without one can feel like a major loss. They’re also expensive, especially if you’re not eligible for a carrier-subsidized upgrade. Between theft, water damage, and our own clumsiness, accidents happen. Here are some real stories of smartphone disasters. Share your own in the comments. Thievery: Smartphones are easy to spot, steal, and resell, making them prime targets for thieves. Mobile tracking apps now help locate lost or stolen devices, and law enforcement is improving its response. But in 2008 — before Find My iPhone existed — Jessica Jenkins, a 5-foot-1 grad student in New York City, lost her brand-new iPhone 3G on the 6 train. Late at night, she’d taken it out to play a maze game. A teenager twice her size snatched it and bolted through the train doors. Jenkins chased him, grabbed his shoulder, but couldn’t stop him. When she called the NYPD, officers were more worried about her safety than her phone. Unhurt but angry, she took the subway home with her old Nokia. She reactivated it, spent $5 on Tetris, and became an expert at cell phone Tetris. She stuck with feature phones until 2011, after her heart and wallet had healed — and now, as an immigration lawyer in the Bay Area, she refuses to use her iPhone on San Francisco public transit — except on Caltrain, which she says 'somehow feels safer, like an Apple commercial during rush hour.' Drowning: Smartphones and water don’t mix — but 70% of Earth’s surface is water, so collisions are inevitable. Photo producer Amber lost two iPhones to liquid: one when she was playfully pushed into a pool in Bordeaux, France, while the phone was in her pocket. She took it to Apple in Paris, but they couldn’t revive it. She borrowed an iPhone 3G for the rest of the trip. Two years later, her 1-year-old daughter tossed her iPhone 4 into the toilet. It jammed tightly in the drain. 'I was frantically trying every tool I could find to pull it out,' Amber recalled. 'My toddler was jumping around, screaming because she wanted to play with me in the toilet.' It didn’t work. The phone remained stuck until her husband came home eight hours later. All photos from her daughter’s first birthday were lost. Since she wasn’t eligible for a replacement, she paid full price for a new phone and bought AppleCare plus a $90 waterproof case. Breaking: We’ve all seen people with cracked screens who keep using their phones. Often, the damage is cosmetic — but not always. CNN iReporter Terry Balmer, a 20-year-old college student, was hanging out on his roof with friends when he placed his phone down. He forgot about vibration. Moments later, he watched it slide off and crash onto the pavement below. 'Hearing it hit the concrete was one of the most gut-wrenching sounds I’ve ever heard,' he said. 'No one’s ever climbed down a roof that fast.' The phone still worked — but the screen was shattered, with only one small section still displaying. He learned to read texts by taking screenshots and examining them in his photo roll. He typed messages from memory. To call someone, he had to memorize numbers. For music, he navigated his library by instinct. He even used it as a camera — guessing what he was pointing at, trusting that the images would look normal once synced to his laptop. Seven months later, he’s still using it. At first, he couldn’t afford a replacement. Now, he’s emotionally attached. 'This phone has become almost a part of me,' he said. 'I just can’t bring myself to let it go.' Repairing: Balmer’s story isn’t rare. Sometimes, smartphones are 'only mostly dead.' You can endure the damage, pay a pro to fix it, or try DIY. Brian Buizer dropped his month-old Evo 4G, shattering the screen. (Spoiler: Kids are terrible for phone longevity.) The manufacturer quoted him $150 to replace the screen on a $200 phone. He opted to fix it himself using online tutorials, a $20 screen, and basic tools. The repair took over an hour — but left a tiny crack in the frame. Over the past year and a half, fine white dust crept in through that gap, settling in the center of the screen where he scrolls most. 'I think it’s static buildup,' he said. 'Now I’ve got a hazy white spot right where I need to see the clearest.' He’s waiting for his new iPhone. Tinkering: Then there are the tinkerers — the geeks, the dreamers, the ones who bring on the damage themselves. Designer Eliza Wee loves modifying her devices, even when she’s not sure what she’s doing. She rooted her Evo phone successfully, installed a custom Android ROM, and got it working on a different carrier. Thrilled, she moved on to a Motorola Triumph on Virgin Mobile. She rooted it again — but when she flashed a new ROM, the phone bricked. 'Genius that I am, I did this two days before a work trip,' she said. She rushed to Sprint, signed a two-year contract, and gave up her freedom after years without one. Bonus: iPhone 5 users have reported strange purple tinting in their photos.

article_content: While Australia is renowned for its breathtaking natural landscapes, many of its man-made structures have drawn sharp criticism for their aesthetics. One notable example is the Brisbane Transit Centre at Roma Street, set to be demolished to make way for a redesigned Bus and Train tunnel. Transport Minister Scott Emerson has welcomed the move, calling the aging structure one of Brisbane’s most disliked buildings—and stating that its removal presents an opportunity to create an iconic city gateway. This redevelopment is part of a broader conversation about urban renewal across Australia. Other cities have their own controversial landmarks. In Melbourne, The Pixel Building—famously listed among the world’s top 10 eyesores by Trippy.com and Reuters in 2012—draws stares with its colorful, fragmented glass façade. Federation Square, similarly criticized by Virtual Tourist in 2009, has been described as frenzied and cluttered, with dangling wires and overwhelming visual noise. In Adelaide, Parliament House has been called awkward and inelegant by some architects, while Perth’s urban sprawl has been ranked among the worst globally for prioritizing low-density expansion over vertical growth. Local landmarks like the Perth Arena, Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre, and Telstra Exchange have all faced heavy public backlash. A recent PerthNow poll showed the Arena leading as the city’s most disliked building, receiving over 28% of more than 10,000 votes. Sydney isn’t spared either. Stockland House on Pitt Street draws ire for its pink marble exterior, obstructive car park entrance, and unattractive pedestrian bridges. The Meriton Tower, designed by Harry Seidler, has been labeled his least successful work, with poorly integrated balconies and a clunky canopy. Even in Canberra, the Edmund Barton Building divides opinion: praised by modernists for its bold concrete forms, reviled by others as a cold, imposing eyesore. The Australia War Memorial Annex and The Star in Pyrmont have also faced similar critiques, with the latter accused of blocking harbor views and alienating pedestrians. As Brisbane prepares to remove one of its most despised structures, the question arises: if we can replace one eyesore, why not others? This moment offers a chance to rethink how Australian cities balance innovation, functionality, and public taste in architecture.

article_content: An amateur astronomer has described the discovery of Ireland’s second supernova in less than two years as the shock of his life. Dave Grennan, a 41-year-old software developer from Raheny, north Dublin, spotted the celestial event while stargazing from his backyard. The supernova, now officially designated 2012ej, occurred 120 million years ago in the distant galaxy IC2166 — its light has only just reached Earth. 'I had the shock of my life,' Grennan said. 'I was about to pack up and go to bed, but when I downloaded the last photo I took, I nearly fell off my chair. I couldn’t believe it.' He immediately recognized it as a supernova, not camera dust. This marks his second such discovery; his first, found in September 2010, was also made using the same telescope. Grennan dedicated his latest find to Neil Armstrong, who passed away days earlier. He spent hours analyzing his data and verifying no one else had reported the event before notifying the International Astronomical Union. Experts confirmed the exploded star was roughly 100 times more massive than the Sun, and its collapse triggered a cataclysmic explosion. 'It’s about 120 million light-years away,' Grennan explained. 'That means we’re seeing history — the light left that star long before dinosaurs walked the Earth.' Grennan, a member of Astronomy Ireland, calls his passion for the night sky a vocation. His wife, Carol, has been his steadfast supporter. Four years ago, he discovered a small asteroid, three meters wide, and named it after his late mother, Catherine Griffin, who first sparked his interest in the stars as a child. Next month, Grennan and fellow enthusiasts including BBC’s Pete Lawrence will present at Astronomy Ireland’s star party in Roundwood, County Wicklow. David Moore, editor of Astronomy Ireland magazine, noted that supernovae are the universe’s most powerful explosions since the Big Bang. 'If one occurred near our Sun, it would obliterate all life on Earth. To detect even one from Irish soil is extraordinary — to find two? That’s truly remarkable.'

article_content: A Colombian mayor is demanding the removal of a plaque unveiled by Prince Charles just one week earlier, following strong local backlash. The memorial, installed in Cartagena, honors British soldiers who died attempting to seize the city from Spanish forces in 1741. Mayor Dionisio Vélez has called for its removal, citing 'very negative reactions' from residents. Colombian police have already arrested one individual for attempting to damage the plaque. The British attack, led by Vice-Admiral Edward Vernon, was one of the largest naval assaults in Royal Navy history. It ended in catastrophic failure: approximately 18,000 British troops died—11,000 in combat and 7,000 from disease—while Spanish losses totaled roughly 2,000, including those who succumbed to illness. The Spanish commander, Don Blas de Lezo, became a national hero, and a statue of him stands near the plaque’s location at the Castillo San Felipe de Barajas. The conflict originated from the War of Jenkins’ Ear, sparked in 1739 after Spanish coast guards cut off the ear of British captain Robert Jenkins, who later displayed it in Parliament. The war was fought over colonial trade dominance in the Caribbean, where Cartagena was one of four major Spanish ports handling vast shipments of South American gold and silver. Governor Juan Carlos Gossain questioned the logic of the plaque, asking why there isn’t a similar tribute in London for Nazi pilots who bombed British cities during World War II. Mayor Vélez stated, 'A mayor must avoid mistakes—but when it’s clear one has been made, he is obligated to correct it.' Prince Charles departed Colombia for Mexico on Sunday, concluding a South American royal tour. Meanwhile, the Duchess of Cornwall drew unintended attention in Monterrey, Mexico, when her cream-colored outfit closely matched that of First Lady Gretta Salinas de Medina.

Yedlin, 21, made three substitute appearances for the USA during the World Cup and appears likely to join Spurs, though Pochettino may have to wait longer for Morgan Schneiderlin, as Southampton insist the French midfielder will not be sold. In a pre-season friendly, Tottenham defeated Schalke 2-1, with Emmanuel Adebayor opening the scoring in the 29th minute and Roberto Soldado doubling the lead with a header after a cross from Andros Townsend. Despite the win, Spurs were nearly undone in the final 15 minutes, conceding a goal to Kevin-Prince Boateng after a cross from Dennis Aogo. Eric Dier, a new signing from Sporting CP, impressed at centre-back, while Ben Davies returned to action at left-back after injury. Erik Lamela, who struggled last season following his £30 million move from Roma, showed signs of improvement, contributing to the first goal and looking sharp in the first half. Pochettino praised the team's progress, noting Adebayor’s recovery from malaria and Dier’s adaptability, while acknowledging there’s still work to do to fully implement his philosophy.

article_content: At first glance, the cemetery on the grounds of the former Dozier School for Boys in Florida appears ordinary — 31 simple metal crosses mark the graves of students who died during influenza outbreaks and a 1914 fire. But investigators now suspect there may be many more unmarked graves nearby, potentially holding the remains of up to 50 additional boys whose deaths were never properly recorded. Though the school closed in 2011 and a 2009 state investigation found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing related to the 31 identified graves, former students — now in their 60s, 70s, and 80s — have come forward with harrowing accounts of physical and sexual abuse, torture, and even murder. They describe a whitewashed cinder block building on campus known as the 'White House,' where boys were brutally beaten. One such case involves Owen Smith, a 14-year-old sent to Dozier in 1940 after running away from home and stealing a car. His sister, Ovell Smith Krell, says the family received conflicting stories after his disappearance: first, that he escaped; then, that he was recaptured and returned to the school; finally, that his decomposed body was found under a house — allegedly from pneumonia. But the homeowners living there at the time say they never heard or smelled anything unusual. Dr. Erin Kimmerle, an anthropologist from the University of South Florida, leads a team searching the site. Of the 100 boys known to have died at the school, burial records exist for only 78. Her team has uncovered signs of possible human remains — including fragments of red soil consistent with disturbed earth — in areas beyond the marked graves. Krell hopes to finally lay her brother to rest beside their parents. 'I would take him and put him down with my mom and dad in their cemetery,' she said. 'I hope I get the chance.'

article_content: A former staffer of Republican Representative Blake Farenthold has filed a lawsuit alleging wrongful termination and sexual harassment. Lauren Greene, who served as Farenthold’s communications director, claims she was subjected to a hostile work environment by both the congressman and his chief of staff, Bob Haueter. According to court documents filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, Greene alleges that Farenthold made repeated inappropriate comments, including suggesting she had semen on her skirt, commenting on her clothing in sexually suggestive ways, and disclosing intimate details about his marriage. She also claims he shared stories of sexual fantasies about her, conveyed through his executive assistant, Emily Wilkes. Greene further alleges that Haueter created a hostile atmosphere by publicly humiliating her, blaming her for mistakes made by others, and undermining her authority. After reporting these issues to Farenthold, she says he offered only superficial support and subsequently marginalized her, leading to her termination in July without warning. The lawsuit accuses Farenthold’s office of violating the Congressional Accountability Act. Greene began working for Farenthold in February 2013 and was promoted to communications director in January 2014, despite being asked to re-interview for the role — a request she viewed as a tactic to diminish her credibility. Farenthold’s office has denied all allegations, stating that neither the congressman nor his staff discriminated against Greene based on gender or any other protected status. Spokesperson Kurt Bardella emphasized that the office has a different perspective on the events and intends to respond through the legal system. Separately, renewed public attention has focused on Farenthold’s ownership of the domain name 'blowe-me.org', registered in 1999 during his time as a private entrepreneur. His office confirmed the domain exists but stated it has never been active and will not be renewed.

article_content: At 68, Carol Highsmith set out on a personal mission fueled by three 'fifties': she wanted to shed 50 pounds, wear a 50-year-old high school dress, and reconnect with her past at Minnehaha Academy’s 50th reunion. Once weighing 175 pounds and feeling trapped by her own body image, she refused to let nostalgia become a source of shame. Instead, she turned it into fuel. Highsmith didn’t start with a crash diet. She remembered how she’d once survived on hot dogs just to squeeze into dresses — a pattern that stuck with her into adulthood. Traveling for her photography work with the Library of Congress meant constant exposure to roadside junk food, including memorable encounters with Krispy Kreme donuts — one time, she devoured five in a single sitting. Over time, those habits led to physical discomfort and emotional unease. She avoided mirrors, hid behind polyester pants, and never tucked in her shirt. When the reunion invitation arrived, she created the WWW Plan: Watch what you eat, Walk every day, and Water always. She cut her daily intake to 1,300 calories from whole, unprocessed foods. She walked between 10,000 and 25,000 steps daily — even pacing hotel hallways after dark. And she drank five to six bottles of water each day, making hydration non-negotiable. On the road, she stocked up on portable, healthy snacks: unsalted nuts, canned baked beans, plain Greek yogurt, and apples. Breakfasts were protein-rich — eggs, ham, fruit, and black coffee. Lunches came only when hunger struck, never because the clock said so. Dinners were simple: grilled fish, sweet potatoes, steamed veggies, sometimes with a tiny pat of butter as a treat. She never called it a 'diet.' To her, this was a lifelong shift. 'I eat only when I’m hungry,' she said. 'And if I’m hungry, I eat — but only what’s good for me.' Every time temptation crept in — skipping steps, reaching for extra nuts — she pictured herself walking into that reunion looking radiant. And she did. At 130 pounds, her classmates were stunned. One friend noted, 'She always gives 115%.' But Carol’s journey didn’t end there. Still aiming for 105 pounds by her next birthday, she remains committed: no sugar, daily movement, mindful eating. 'I didn’t gain this weight fast — so why rush to lose it?' she says. 'We are what we eat. And now, everything that goes into my mouth has to earn its place.'

article_content: On Saturday, the Palestinian news agency WAFA reported that an Israeli military strike targeted the Maghazi refugee camp in central Gaza, killing 51 people, predominantly women and children. The Israeli military has not yet responded to requests for comment, and Reuters could not independently verify the claim. As the death toll in Gaza surpassed 9,488 since Hamas’ October 7 attack on southern Israel—which killed 1,400 Israelis and took over 240 hostages—pro-Palestinian demonstrations erupted worldwide, from London and Berlin to Jakarta and Washington, D.C., demanding an immediate ceasefire. Foreign ministers from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan, and the United Arab Emirates met U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken in Amman, urging Washington to pressure Israel into halting hostilities. Jordan’s Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi warned the conflict risks deepening regional hatred and dehumanization. Blinken, however, dismissed ceasefire calls, arguing they would only allow Hamas to regroup. Israel has proposed no formal ceasefire but has accepted temporary humanitarian pauses to deliver aid and evacuate civilians—a proposal rejected by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a meeting with Blinken in Tel Aviv. In the occupied West Bank, violence has surged, with 121 Palestinians killed since the Gaza war began, according to U.N. data. Daily settler attacks have more than doubled, even as most fatalities stem from clashes with Israeli forces. Gaza’s humanitarian crisis has reached catastrophic levels. Nearly 1.5 million of its 2.3 million residents are displaced. Food, clean water, and medical care are scarce. Residents report drinking saltwater, while hospitals operate without power or supplies. Iran’s First Vice President Mohammad Mokhber condemned Israeli actions as 'war crimes' and called for immediate humanitarian relief. Israel maintains its operations target Hamas militants, not civilians, and alleges the group uses civilians as human shields. Meanwhile, the U.S. special envoy David Satterfield estimated that between 800,000 and one million people have fled northern Gaza for the south, while 350,000–400,000 remain trapped in and around Gaza City.

article_content: Joe McGinniss, the fearless journalist whose immersive reporting reshaped political and true crime writing, passed away at 71 in Worcester, Massachusetts. Diagnosed with advanced prostate cancer the previous year, his death resulted from complications tied to the illness, confirmed by his attorney and close friend Dennis Holahan. McGinniss rose to fame with 'The Selling of the President 1968,' a searing exposé that revealed how Nixon’s team crafted a polished public image—despite his ruthless political tactics. The book, published in 1969, became a bestseller and turned McGinniss into a media sensation, prompting him to leave his column at The Philadelphia Inquirer. His most controversial work, 'Fatal Vision' (1983), documented his evolving relationship with Dr. Jeffrey MacDonald, a Green Beret convicted of stabbing his pregnant wife and two young daughters to death in 1970. Initially charmed by MacDonald’s demeanor, McGinniss eventually concluded the doctor was a manipulative sociopath who staged the crime scene. This shift sparked outrage: MacDonald sued, claiming betrayal, and won a $325,000 settlement. Critics like Janet Malcolm labeled McGinniss a 'confidence man,' but he defended himself, asserting that MacDonald had deceived him first. Beyond politics and crime, McGinniss wrote about soccer, horse racing, and travel. He also penned memoirs detailing his marital breakdowns, alcoholism, and financial woes. One book, 'The Last Brother' (1993), about Ted Kennedy, was mocked for inventing dialogue—a rare misstep in an otherwise relentless pursuit of truth. Even in decline, McGinniss remained active. He returned to journalism with 'The Rogue,' a book on Sarah Palin that didn’t sell well—but drew attention when he rented a house right next to hers in Wasilla, Alaska, to observe her life firsthand. He later used Facebook to share candid updates about his health and opinions, refusing to disappear from public view. Though never again matched the success of 'Fatal Vision,' McGinniss stood by his convictions. In 2012, he wrote in his e-book 'Final Vision': 'Every court, including the U.S. Supreme Court, has affirmed MacDonald’s guilt. No amount of rumor or sympathy changes that.' He died with his voice still loud—and his questions still unanswered.

article_content: Whether it’s Manolo Blahnik, Kurt Geiger, or even New Look, few can deny that women adore buying new pairs of heels. In the UK, this passion comes at a steep price: British women spent a staggering £3.5 billion on footwear last year. Yet, despite this massive spending, two-thirds of those shoes are never worn—they sit unused at the back of wardrobes. According to a survey commissioned by Diamond Insurance, the average British woman owns 19 pairs of shoes but regularly wears only seven. While this may seem modest, one in 20 women admit to owning more than 50 pairs, and 7% purchase at least 10 new pairs annually. For some, this obsession extends beyond personal habit—it strains relationships. One in eight women reported arguing with their partners over either the cost or volume of their shoe collections. Designer labels like Christian Louboutin and Nicholas Kirkwood remain highly coveted, especially among women inspired by celebrities like Jennifer Lopez and Victoria Beckham. Still, the average woman spends just £41 per pair. Research also reveals a strong preference for quantity over quality: 69% said they’d rather buy several inexpensive shoes than one luxury pair if given a £300 budget. Style remains king—over a third of women admitted they wear uncomfortable stilettos purely because they like how they look.

article_content: Jawbone’s popular UP fitness trackers are facing serious reliability problems, with hundreds of users reporting devices that suddenly stop working — often referred to as 'bricked.' During independent testing, three separate units failed within days of use, exhibiting symptoms like unexplained vibrations, data loss, and complete power failure. User forums and Amazon reviews reflect a pattern of discontent, with many customers giving the product just two out of five stars. According to Jawbone CEO Hosain Rahman, the root cause lies in two specific capacitors within the power circuit, which prevent the bands from holding a charge reliably. A separate hardware flaw is also disrupting the syncing process between the device and its companion app. These issues typically appear within the first week of use but do not present any safety hazards. Despite the setbacks, Jawbone has taken decisive action: production of the UP bands has been halted indefinitely, and the company is now offering a full, no-questions-asked refund to any buyer — even allowing customers to keep their broken devices. Refunds are available through December 31, 2012, for purchases made through authorized retailers. Additionally, users eligible under warranty can still receive replacement units. Jawbone’s VP of Product, Travis Bogard, confirmed the company is working urgently to resolve the technical flaws and plans to resume sales as soon as possible. When functioning correctly, the UP band tracks daily steps, sleep cycles, and sends subtle vibration alerts to encourage movement, all synced through a clean iOS interface — but for too many users, those features remain out of reach.

article_content: These striking pumpkins truly stand out as the highlight of the season, illuminating the night across New York and Rhode Island this autumn. A total of 10,000 carved pumpkins are on display in two major exhibitions: Pumpkinville at Roger Williams Park Zoo in Rhode Island, and The Great Jack O'Lantern Blaze at Van Cortlandt Manor in New York. Pumpkinville, created by the team Passion for Pumpkins, features 5,000 pumpkins depicting American heroes and cultural icons—from Audrey Hepburn and Bruce Springsteen to John F. Kennedy and Rosa Parks—alongside a moving tribute to the victims of the Sandy Hook shooting. Each design is meticulously drawn with a permanent marker before artisans carefully shave away the pumpkin skin—rather than cutting through it—to leave a thin, translucent layer that glows beautifully under LED lights. The centerpiece of Pumpkinville is the ‘Laughing Tree,’ a breathtaking installation of half a ton of glowing pumpkins arranged among tree branches. The Great Jack O'Lantern Blaze, running from October 5 to November 11, showcases 5,000 additional pumpkins in themed displays including a functioning doomsday clock, lifelike dinosaurs inspired by Jurassic Park, a spooky spider, and a riverside scene with swamp monsters. A companion exhibit, 'The Art of the Pumpkin: Contemporary Sculpture Inspired by the Hudson Valley’s Legendary Squash,' features 25 locally selected artists. All artworks are handcrafted over eight weeks and continuously refined throughout the 30-day run. The team estimates using approximately 20,000 pumpkins total, all of which are composted after the event. Music specially composed by Richard Kristy enhances the atmosphere. According to Roger Williams Park Zoo owner Paul Cadieux, planning begins a year in advance to ensure artistic precision and avoid frustration. 'We start with an image and a black Sharpie,' he said. 'Then we shave the skin, clean the inside, and let the light bring it to life.'

article_content: Zeng Yushan, born in June 1994 in rural Sichuan, China, appears to be a child despite being 19 years old. At age seven, she was diagnosed with a benign tumor on her pituitary gland — a tiny organ near the base of the brain responsible for releasing vital hormones including growth and puberty regulators. The tumor disrupted her body’s ability to produce growth hormone, halting her physical development permanently. She never reached puberty, lost body hair, and remained the size of a young child. Because of her youthful appearance, Zeng was exploited by her family, forced to beg on city streets instead of attending school. After her parents divorced amid financial strain and emotional conflict, she lived with her father until he passed away from stomach cancer in 2013. Left alone and destitute, she continued begging across several cities until a kind couple, Guo Liu and his wife, took her in. The couple, who raised two adult daughters themselves, initially struggled to determine Zeng’s gender due to her lack of hair and childlike frame. Now, they provide her with daily care, emotional support, and medical attention. Their goal is to bring her to a specialist in Beijing after the Lunar New Year to assess whether synthetic growth hormone therapy could still benefit her — though doctors warn her bones may have already fused, making further growth unlikely. Professor Ashley Grossman of Oxford University explained that while pituitary tumors in children are extremely rare, early detection in developed nations typically leads to immediate hormonal treatment. In China, however, such therapies are inaccessible without private payment, leaving many families powerless. Although modern medicine can now replace missing hormones via daily injections, timing is critical. If the growth plates in her bones have closed — likely, given her age — intervention may only improve other hormone imbalances, not height. Zeng has expressed a deep desire to attend school, but no institution accepts her due to her legal age, not her appearance. She is emotionally bonded to her adoptive parents and relies on them entirely. Experts stress that even if she cannot grow taller, treating her remaining hormonal deficiencies could improve her long-term health, energy, and quality of life. Her story underscores the devastating consequences of economic barriers to basic medical care.

article_content: CNN — President Obama’s Ambien finally wore off, and he entered the second presidential debate against Mitt Romney with renewed energy. His performance Tuesday night was stellar — though not perfect — thanks to two debate techniques I emphasize relentlessly to my students: the primacy effect and using your opponent’s language against them. To win a debate, you must master both. The primacy effect refers to the psychological phenomenon where the first things a speaker says are more memorable and persuasive than later points — whether in casual conversation, a 90-minute debate, or a series of speeches. Obama came out swinging. After a lackluster first debate, he delivered a fiery response to the first audience question, immediately setting the tone. He criticized Romney’s economic plan not as a five-point strategy, but as a 'one-point plan': that folks at the top play by a different set of rules. Right then, we saw a different Obama. Yes, many are fixated on that line as a sound bite — and rightly so. But for me, it’s the primacy effect in action. I teach my debaters: lead with your strongest arguments. If you save them for later, you risk losing the judge’s attention — and the weight of your message — before you even deliver it. The second principle I insist on? Use your opponent’s language against them. If a team I coached failed to turn their opponent’s own words into a rebuttal, I’d make them run laps. (Yes, that’s absurd — imagine a debate team jogging around a gym.) Obama did this repeatedly. He quoted Romney saying, 'This plant kills' — referencing Romney’s reversal on coal. He cited Romney’s claim that lowering taxes for the wealthy 'grows the economy.' He referenced Romney’s spokesperson’s initial response — 'I’ll get back to you on that' — regarding the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, which empowers women to sue over wage discrimination. When you trap someone with their own words, they can’t easily escape. It’s a timeless, winning tactic. Romney tried to mirror this strategy during the sixth question — when asked what Obama had accomplished to deserve another term. Romney repeatedly used the phrase 'He said...' to highlight Obama’s perceived failures on unemployment, Medicare, Social Security, and immigration. It was Romney’s strongest moment — but it came nearly an hour into the debate. Too late. Because of the primacy effect, undecided voters are far more likely to remember the opening than the middle. Romney’s late surge helped, but it couldn’t fully undo the damage of Obama’s commanding start. Fortunately for Romney, this wasn’t the first debate — Obama’s earlier performance was weak. The primacy effect across both debates may have actually saved Romney’s campaign. I expect Obama to gain ground in the polls after this debate — but it could have been far worse for Romney. Imagine if the debates were reversed: Romney’s strong moment would’ve opened the cycle, and Obama’s shaky start would’ve closed it. The race would look completely different today. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Todd Graham.

article_content: In preparation for the 2014 FIFA World Cup, Brazilian federal forces launched a major security operation in Complexo da Maré, one of Rio de Janeiro’s largest and most densely populated favelas. Armed troops, supported by navy tanks and helicopters, entered the sprawling network of 16 communities to dismantle gang control and reduce crime. The operation, occurring six weeks before the World Cup’s kickoff on June 14, disrupted daily life for the estimated 130,000 residents. Police in bulletproof vests and camouflage uniforms moved through narrow streets, setting up checkpoints and conducting searches, while residents watched from doorways and balconies. Although no gunfire was reported during the incursion, the militarized presence sparked unease. The area, located just minutes from Rio’s international airport, is highly visible to arriving tourists — a factor many believe motivated the timing of the operation. This effort is part of the broader Pacification Program (UPP), initiated in 2008, which aims to permanently replace armed gangs with community police units. After federal forces withdraw, UPP officers are expected to maintain order and build trust with residents. Yet, the operation has drawn criticism. Human rights advocates point to past abuses, including the 2013 torture and disappearance of bricklayer Amarildo de Souza in the nearby Rocinha favela — a case that ignited national outrage and exposed deep mistrust in police practices. Despite government claims that the goal is to improve living conditions, many residents remain skeptical. Daily hardships persist: families rely on a single water pipe, rubbish piles up in alleyways, and graffiti bearing slogans like 'Politicians and the UPP will die' mark walls. Protests have erupted across Rio, including the burning of a police station last week, reflecting growing anger over perceived state overreach. While authorities insist the mission is humanitarian, the images of tanks rolling past homes and children playing amid armed patrols raise urgent questions about whose safety is truly being prioritized.

article_content: It has been a turbulent few years for the people of Egypt. Since the 2011 revolution, the economy has collapsed, street protests have become nearly daily, and the political climate remains unstable. Yet, a small group of young Egyptians has found a powerful way to respond—not with violence, but with laughter. 'We’re like a little beam of sunlight breaking through,' says Rami Borai, a member of Hezb El Comedy, one of Egypt’s first homegrown comedy troupes. 'We remind people: Don’t worry. When this cloud passes, it will be brighter. Happier.' Founded in 2009 by Hashim Al Gahry with zero initial funding, Hezb El Comedy—whose name means 'The Comedy Party'—began as a passion project. Al Gahry and his friends pooled their savings and promoted their shows through social media. Beyond performing, they mentor aspiring comedians, teaching them timing, delivery, and stage presence. 'We’re not the funniest people in the world,' Al Gahry admits. 'But our experience lets us guide others. These are our mistakes—learn from them.' Similar grassroots movements are emerging across the Arab world. In Qatar, young performers formed SUCQ (Stand Up Comedy Qatar). 'It’s an American art form,' says 24-year-old Hamad Al Amri, who works as a banker by day. 'But we’ve reshaped it to fit our culture, our people.' Mohamed Kamal, another SUCQ member, notes the limits imposed by Qatar’s political environment: 'We can’t joke about politics, sex, or religion.' For comedians who push too far, the consequences can be severe. Earlier this month, Egyptian satirist Bassem Youssef gained international attention after being charged for mocking Islam and former President Mohamed Morsy. Others haven’t been so lucky: Tunisian puppeteer Sami Fehri was imprisoned on corruption charges linked to his political satire, and Saudi blogger Raif Badawi was jailed for criticizing religious figures. Al Gahry acknowledges the tightrope comedians walk: 'You have to push the limit—but be very careful.' Borai, however, finds dark humor in the possibility of arrest. 'If I ever saw a headline saying, “Ramy was indicted,” I’d call my mom and say, “Yo, this is it!” I’d fly out of here… but I’d be proud. I got kicked out of my country for being too damn funny!'

article_content: Andy Murray, known for describing himself as 'boring,' maintains a highly structured and simple diet during Wimbledon. Each evening, he eats one of three meals — salmon with rice, roast chicken with vegetables and potatoes, or steak with salad — all prepared by his long-term girlfriend, Kim Sears, at their £5 million home in Oxshott, Surrey. Kim also handles household tasks such as laundry and grocery shopping at Tesco. For breakfast, Murray enjoys a nutrient-rich smoothie and a bagel topped with mashed banana. His smoothie typically includes strawberry yoghurt, raspberries, apple juice, orange juice, and blueberries. On Tuesdays, he adds an apple and a peach. He acknowledges that while he once claimed to dislike bananas, he now enjoys them when mashed on a bagel — likely due to the texture. Before matches, Murray drinks a full litre of a sports drink to pre-hydrate. Afterward, he consumes a chocolate-flavoured protein shake, which he admits doesn't taste great. In the past, Murray's diet was far more elaborate — including up to 50 portions of sushi in one sitting to support his 6ft 3in, 13½ stone frame. He even kept sushi chilled in an ice cooler for post-match consumption during late Wimbledon matches. His grandmother recently sent him homemade shortbread as a treat. Meanwhile, Murray has been enjoying the World Cup but finds 11 p.m. kick-offs too late. When asked in April to describe himself in one word, he replied 'boring.' His mother, Judy, supports this lifestyle, saying it helps him relax — staying home, sleeping in his own bed, and spending time with his dogs provides essential calm amid the tournament’s intensity.

article_content: Alex Snelson, a 33-year-old inmate in Nevada, has filed a federal lawsuit alleging that jail officials violated his First Amendment rights by denying him meals consistent with his religious dietary beliefs. Snelson, who identifies as a practicing Satanist, claims his faith prohibits him from consuming processed foods containing additives or byproducts—but permits ice cream as a 'whole food.' He submitted a handwritten complaint to the U.S. District Court in Reno, stating that being forced to eat non-compliant meals causes him profound spiritual distress. Snelson says he is a member of the Church of Light in Chino Hills, California, though no public record confirms the existence of this organization. Prosecutors argue that Snelson has not clearly linked his dietary preferences to a recognized religious doctrine. In prior filings, the court noted that religious claims must be 'rooted in sincerely held religious belief,' not personal philosophy. The Church of Satan, founded in 1966 by Anton Szandor LaVey, stated through its high priest, Magus Peter H. Gilmore, that its members are free to choose any diet—making Snelson’s claim of religious restriction inconsistent with official doctrine. Snelson is currently serving a two- to six-year sentence for possession of a stolen vehicle, following prior convictions for methamphetamine and brass knuckles possession. Washoe County officials maintain their policy is to accommodate all inmates’ religious practices and assert that Snelson’s allegations remain unproven.

article_content: A 40-meter water tower dating back to the Victorian era and nicknamed 'Jumbo' is going up for sale after its former owner failed in his bid to convert it into a block of flats. The Grade II*-listed building, constructed in 1883, dominates the town of Colchester in Essex and is England’s tallest 19th-century water tower. It has stood unused for more than 25 years, following repeated failures to secure planning permission for redevelopment. The tower was built to store Colchester’s water supply, using 1.2 million bricks and 400 tonnes of cement. It features a viewing platform accessible via a central spiral staircase with 157 steps. It ceased operations in 1987, sparking decades of debate over its future. An evangelical Christian group once converted it into a 'prayer tower' and installed a banner reading 'Jesus is Lord' on its exterior. In 2006, businessman George Braithwaite purchased the tower at auction for £330,000 with initial permission to convert it into a single residence. He later proposed a more ambitious plan — including a museum, restaurant, offices, and flats — but was denied planning permission last year. Braithwaite has now relisted the tower for sale, though the asking price remains undisclosed. David Ross of Britain Express called Jumbo 'a wonderful example of Victorian civic architecture,' noting its 131-foot height and capacity to hold 221,000 gallons of water. He described it as a 'marvellous feat of Victorian engineering' that deserves preservation as a heritage treasure. Despite numerous proposals — from luxury flats to cultural venues — none have succeeded. The new owner may be permitted to build a penthouse but must guarantee public access to the 40-meter viewing platform. Campaigners, including the Balkerne Tower Trust, are seeking donations to purchase and restore the tower as a public monument celebrating Victorian water infrastructure.

article_content: As diplomats at the United Nations condemned the Syrian government, violence intensified across the country, leaving residents fearing the worst. 'Everyone we’ve spoken to believes Syria is either already in a full-blown war or hurtling toward it — and recovery will be devastating,' said CNN’s Arwa Damon, reporting from an opposition safe house inside Syria. For safety reasons, CNN is withholding her exact location. Damon described a relentless flow of people and information, noting that many now accept the grim reality: 'This is going to be a bloody battle — more lives will be lost.' Her report followed remarks by UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Navi Pillay, who called the regime’s actions an 'ongoing onslaught' and warned that crimes against humanity may have been committed since the uprising began in March 2011. Pillay told the UN General Assembly that abuses by Syrian forces appear systematic and widespread, targeting homes, hospitals, and schools, suggesting high-level authorization. Syria’s UN ambassador, Bashar Jaafari, angrily rejected the accusations, calling them an 'unprecedented' media and political campaign aimed at destabilizing his country. Meanwhile, ground reports from activists and residents described soldiers conducting door-to-door raids, tank rollouts, and relentless shelling. Last week alone, more than 680 people were killed, mostly in Homs, according to the Local Coordination Committees of Syria (LCC). On Monday, 30 civilians — including two children — died in Homs and Idlib. The state-run Syrian Arab News Agency reported the funeral of 19 soldiers killed by 'terrorists,' but CNN cannot independently verify claims due to severe restrictions on foreign journalists. A draft UN General Assembly resolution condemning Syria’s human rights violations had not yet been formally introduced. Though non-binding, it would represent the strongest collective UN statement to date. Previous attempts at the Security Council were blocked by Russia and China. Jaafari dismissed an Arab League proposal for a joint UN-Arab peacekeeping mission as 'incitement to terrorism,' arguing that foreign troops would support armed rebels and violate Syrian sovereignty. 'We could never send soldiers to protect Occupy Wall Street,' he said. 'No government would send troops to protect demonstrators in London or Paris.' Russia expressed caution, with Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stating peacekeepers require host-nation consent — and there is no peace to keep. China supported mediation but did not commit to backing the plan. The humanitarian situation in besieged cities like Homs is dire: no food, water, or electricity. The UN and Red Crescent teams have delivered aid during brief cease-fires, but many areas remain inaccessible. Wounded civilians avoid public hospitals fearing arrest or torture, instead relying on makeshift underground clinics with poor sanitation and scarce supplies. US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, speaking in Washington alongside Turkey’s foreign minister, pledged increased funding to the Red Crescent, ICRC, and local Syrian groups to deliver life-saving aid. Pillay estimates over 5,400 people have died since the uprising began; the LCC puts the death toll above 7,000.

article_content: Princes William and Harry have publicly endorsed the Terrence Higgins Trust on its 30th anniversary, honoring the legacy of their late mother, Princess Diana, a pioneering advocate for people living with HIV/AIDS. In a heartfelt letter, the princes urged their generation to 'pick up the sword and continue the fight' against HIV, acknowledging that while the virus is now treatable and manageable, harmful stigma still affects those living with it. Princess Diana broke barriers in 1987 when she opened England’s first dedicated AIDS ward at Middlesex Hospital, helping to humanize the epidemic during a time of widespread fear and misinformation. The Terrence Higgins Trust was established in 1982 by three friends following the death of Terry Higgins, a British man who died of an AIDS-related illness at age 37. Today, it stands as the United Kingdom’s largest HIV and sexual health charity. To mark the milestone, a rare photograph of William and Harry with their mother, taken by John Swannell, will be auctioned at Christie’s on March 21 to benefit the trust. Sir Nick Partridge, CEO of the Terrence Higgins Trust, expressed deep gratitude, saying the princes’ support echoes how Diana once inspired her generation — and now inspires theirs.

Dani Osvaldo, meanwhile, joined Inter Milan on loan from Southampton for the 2013–14 season and was actively preparing for the match. In a recent interview with MUTV, Vidic reflected: 'I received offers from several countries, including England. But I decided to retire. I still admire Inter’s project — the club is in transition, striving to improve. I’m confident Inter will grow bigger, and I wish them well.' The training session at Appiano Gentile featured Vidic engaging in light strength work and interacting with teammates, including Osvaldo, but he did not feature in the 3-1 defeat to Eintracht Frankfurt. Footage of the match was released afterward, showing Osvaldo in action for Inter.

article_content: Paul 'Gazza' Gascoigne, once celebrated as England’s most gifted footballer of his generation, has faced a long and painful battle with alcohol addiction and mental health struggles since retiring in 2004. His emotional collapse during a recent charity event in Northampton — where he appeared barely coherent and broke down in tears — has sparked renewed concern among fans and former teammates. In a statement released to CNN, his management agency, GamePlan Solutions, confirmed that Gascoigne has voluntarily entered a specialized treatment center in Phoenix, Arizona, seeking help for his complex addictions. He has been overwhelmed by the outpouring of support from the public and those close to him. Gascoigne’s descent has mirrored that of George Best, another football icon whose brilliance was eclipsed by addiction. Over the years, he has been sectioned three times under the UK Mental Health Act and repeatedly entered rehabilitation programs, only to relapse. Gary Lineker, his former England and Tottenham teammate, expressed deep concern, recalling the iconic moment in 1990 when Gascoigne wept after receiving a yellow card — a moment that meant he would miss the World Cup final *if* England reached it. 'I can only hope he finds peace,' Lineker tweeted, 'but fear those hopes may be forlorn.' Piers Morgan and Ronnie Irani, a former England cricketer, played key roles in arranging Gascoigne’s transport to the U.S. clinic. Irani recounted contacting British Airways to secure a flight, saying, 'We just had to get him on the plane — he needs help, and if not, who knows what’s going to happen?' Gascoigne’s career was marked by extraordinary talent — including his legendary solo goal against Scotland and his iconic 1990 World Cup performance — but also by off-field chaos: the infamous 'Dentist’s Chair' incident in Hong Kong, a very public divorce, admissions of domestic violence in his autobiographies, and multiple legal troubles. Gordon Taylor of the Professional Footballers Association warned that Gascoigne’s situation risks becoming another George Best tragedy. 'He’s got support,' Taylor said, 'but it’s heartbreaking when progress unravels.'

article_content: Adam Mayes, 35, is accused of murdering Jo Ann Bain and her 14-year-old daughter Adrienne in Whiteville, Tennessee, in April 2012 — not in a fit of anger, but to kidnap the two younger girls, Alexandria, 12, and Kyliyah, 8. His wife, Teresa Mayes, told police she was present during the killings and helped transport the bodies and the children to their trailer in Guntown, Mississippi. She has been charged with two counts of first-degree murder and especially aggravated kidnapping. Mary Mayes, Adam’s 65-year-old mother, faces four counts of conspiracy after admitting she heard digging in the yard — believed to be the burial of the victims — but failed to report it. The bodies of Jo Ann and Adrienne were discovered buried in the backyard of the Mayes home a week after the girls disappeared. Despite nationwide efforts and multiple credible sightings, including one at the County Line One Market in Guntown where Mayes was recognized despite a new haircut, Alexandria and Kyliyah remain missing. The FBI believes Mayes may have altered their appearances by cutting or dyeing their hair to evade capture. He is now on the run across several states — including Arizona, Texas, North Carolina, and Florida — and may be using aliases such as Christopher Zachery Wylde or Paco Rodrigass. Though acquaintances describe him as friendly and helpful, even likening him to an uncle, authorities warn he is armed and extremely dangerous. Teresa’s sister, Bobbi Booth, publicly appealed to Mayes through CNN to release the girls, revealing that her sister had confided in her about the murders but was too afraid to contact police until it was too late. Vigils have been held in Bolivar, Tennessee, and the FBI continues to urge the public to stay vigilant, holding onto hope that the two young girls are still alive.

article_content: Felix Baumgartner’s daring leap from the edge of space wasn’t just a test of nerves—it was a triumph of engineering. Behind the spectacle lay a suite of custom-built technologies designed to keep him alive in conditions no human had ever survived in freefall. The capsule, weighing nearly as much as a VW Beetle, was a sealed pressure sphere built from aerospace-grade materials, shielding him from temperatures colder than Antarctica. His suit, pressurized to prevent bodily fluids from boiling at extreme altitudes, featured mirrored visors and flexible joints to let him move like a skydiver, not an astronaut. A chest pack carried vital data—his speed, position, and oxygen levels—and streamed live video to mission control. Nine high-res cameras, armored in nitrogen-filled casings and solar filters, captured every moment. The parachute, five years in development, was the first ever built to open safely after breaking the sound barrier, with dual safeguards: a manual trigger and an automatic system activated by abnormal spin or pressure. Landing was precision work: teams timed the launch to avoid high-altitude winds, and after deploying his chute at 10,000 feet, Baumgartner steered himself 23 miles across the New Mexico desert, guided by a beacon in his suit to waiting rescuers. The tech developed here isn’t just for show—it could reshape how we design emergency systems for high-altitude pilots and future space travelers.

article_content: Can a small candy store in Missouri have a little fun? Apparently not — at least not without backlash. The Route 66 Candy Shoppe in Waynesville, Missouri, drew national attention after posting a Facebook offer: free fudge for anyone weighing over 300 pounds on Fat Tuesday. 'Walk, run, waddle, or ride your motorized wheelchair down to the Route 66 Candy Shoppe! See you Tuesday!' the post read. While the promotion was meant as a playful nod to Fat Tuesday’s tradition of indulgence, it ignited strong reactions. Former customer Deb Czuprynski told CNN affiliate KSPR, 'It made my blood boil. It might be a joke to them, but for others, obesity isn’t a punchline — some people die because of it.' Shop owner Charley Dill, who bears a resemblance to the late comedian Dom DeLuise and is known for his own love of sweets, insisted the offer was never meant to offend. 'We’re not trying to make a statement,' he said. 'We just thought it’d be a fun way to invite people in and share a laugh.' Despite the criticism, Dill reports receiving support from ‘fellow fatties’ — including customers traveling nearly 100 miles from Columbia, Missouri — who plan to show up for the free treats. He even mused about future promotions, such as free candy for pregnant women on Labor Day.

article_content: It was one of the most highly anticipated births of the year — but Britain will have to wait longer for its first captive-born panda cub. Edinburgh Zoo announced that Tian Tian, the country’s only female giant panda, has lost her cub late in pregnancy. After weeks of optimism following successful artificial insemination in April, signs of pregnancy — including rising hormone levels and milk production — led staff and the public to believe a cub was imminent. However, in recent days, Tian Tian returned to non-pregnant behavior, prompting experts to conclude the fetus had been reabsorbed by her body. The cub, if born, would have been smaller than half a block of butter. Professor Chris West, Chief Executive of the Royal Zoological Society of Scotland, expressed deep sadness at the outcome but emphasized the significance of what has been achieved in under two years of hosting pandas. He noted that most global institutions require three to four years before achieving successful panda reproduction. New research suggests lost pregnancies may be more common than previously understood, though the exact causes remain unknown. Tian Tian and her mate, Yang Guang, arrived in Scotland in December 2011 on a 10-year loan from China. Giant pandas face extreme biological challenges: females are fertile for only 36 hours annually, mating attempts often fail, and implanted embryos may remain dormant until triggered by unknown factors. Phantom pregnancies — like the one Tian Tian experienced in 2012 — further complicate detection. Despite the setback, the zoo remains committed to its breeding program. Iain Valentine, Director of the Panda Project, stated that pandas exist on a delicate biological balance between nutrition and reproduction, and disruptions can lead to pregnancy loss. 'We are determined to learn from this,' he said. The zoo plans to continue monitoring and research, with hopes of trying again in the next breeding season.

article_content: On a recent afternoon in Los Angeles’s Boyle Heights neighborhood, researchers Christian Benitez and Eric M. Wood stood outside a corner liquor store, binoculars in hand, scanning the shrubbery for birds. They quickly spotted a house sparrow — one of the most widespread and adaptable songbirds on Earth. 'They’re everywhere in Boyle Heights,' said Wood, an associate professor of ecology at Cal State Los Angeles. These birds thrive in dense urban settings, scavenging crumbs and nesting in roof tiles. But just ten miles northeast, in the affluent city of San Marino, house sparrows were absent. Instead, the manicured lawns and towering trees hosted a strikingly different avian community: band-tailed pigeons, acorn woodpeckers, California towhees, turkey vultures, dark-eyed juncos, mockingbirds, Anna’s hummingbirds, and even a Cooper’s hawk. 'There goes a band-tailed pigeon right over there,' Wood exclaimed, shifting focus from a red-tailed hawk. This dramatic contrast illustrates what scientists call the 'luxury effect' — the phenomenon where wealthier, often whiter neighborhoods support richer and more diverse bird populations. 'The sheer difference in wealth, separated by just a few miles, really surprised me when I first moved here,' said Wood, originally from Santa Rosa. A new study led by Wood and colleagues reveals that this divide isn’t accidental. It’s the lingering legacy of racially discriminatory lending practices from the 1930s. The federal Home Owners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC) created 'security risk maps' that labeled non-white neighborhoods — like Boyle Heights — as 'hazardous,' denying them investment. Meanwhile, white neighborhoods were marked in green as 'best' for lending. Decades later, these maps still shape the landscape: redlined areas have less tree cover, more pavement, and higher housing density. As a result, they host fewer bird species — mostly those adapted to human-dominated environments. Greenlined areas, by contrast, boast abundant vegetation and attract forest-dependent birds. 'The legacy of our discriminatory practices is still written into the city itself,' said study co-author Travis Longcore of UCLA. 'Even though those policies are illegal now, the city is an accretion of its history — and history doesn’t vanish with time.' Data collected between 2016 and 2018 across 132 sites in 33 L.A. communities confirmed a direct link between historical redlining, current income inequality, and bird biodiversity. San Marino’s tree canopy reaches 26%; Boyle Heights’ is just 12.6%. Median incomes reflect the same gap: $174,722 versus $69,778. Experts like historian Laura Redford and ecologist Danielle Shanahan stress that this pattern isn’t unique to L.A. — it’s global. Affluent areas consistently have more trees, more green space, and more wildlife — including in backyards. Beyond ecology, these disparities affect human health. Redlined neighborhoods face higher rates of asthma, heart disease, heat exposure, and pollution — all tied to lack of vegetation. Marcos Trinidad, a senior forestry director with TreePeople and former Audubon Center director, sees birds as silent messengers. 'When we see abundance of birds, we’re seeing the health of the ecosystem — and the health of the people,' he said. 'What birds need — food, shelter, habitat — mirrors what humans need to thrive.' Benitez, who grew up in South Gate, recalls never questioning why wealthier neighborhoods felt greener. 'I never looked at birds and trees the way I do now,' he said. 'Understanding how racism and poverty shape nature — that turned the light on for me.' The researchers conclude: if cities want to promote true urban biodiversity, they must confront their racist pasts. Without deliberate, equitable intervention, nature — like society — will remain segregated. 'Residential urban biodiversity,' they warn, 'will continue to be primarily for the affluent in the City of Angels.'

article_content: Amanda Knox’s retrial for the 2007 murder of her British roommate, Meredith Kercher, began in Florence, Italy, on September 29, 2013. Neither Knox nor her former partner, Raffaele Sollecito, attended the proceedings. Instead, photos emerged showing Knox walking in Seattle—over 5,000 miles away—shopping at a pet store and chatting on her phone. Knox, now 26, has publicly stated she will not return to Italy, calling her decision 'common sense.' She told NBC that being imprisoned as an innocent person made it impossible for her to relive that trauma. Knox and Sollecito were originally convicted in 2009 and served four years in prison before being acquitted on appeal in 2011. However, in March 2013, Italy’s Supreme Court overturned the acquittal, ordering a retrial. Judges cited 'deficiencies, contradictions, and illogical conclusions' in the appeal court’s ruling. In a memoir released earlier that year, titled 'Waiting to Be Heard,' Knox portrayed herself as a naive young woman misled by a foreign legal system—not the 'callous sexual deviant' depicted in some media reports after her initial conviction. While Knox is not legally required to attend the retrial, she may be represented by her attorneys. Should she be found guilty again, she retains the right to appeal. However, if that appeal fails, Italy could pursue extradition.

article_content: The release of confidential U.S. diplomatic cables by WikiLeaks exposed more than geopolitical tensions — it revealed how football, the world’s most popular sport, has become a magnet for authoritarian power, criminal networks, and political manipulation. Among the thousands of documents, a lesser-known but deeply revealing pattern emerged: dictators, generals, and industrialists have repeatedly sought to co-opt football to legitimize their rule, distract populations, or launder their reputations — while fans, in turn, have turned stadiums into rare spaces of resistance. In Myanmar, then-leader General Than Shwe was nearly persuaded by his grandson, Nay Shwe Thway Aung, to spend $1 billion on Manchester United — a move deemed politically toxic after Cyclone Nargis killed nearly 150,000. Instead, the regime launched a national league, handpicking wealthy cronies like Zaw Zaw — a powerful businessman and head of the Myanmar Football Association — to own clubs. One cable noted the league may serve as a distraction from economic hardship. Attendance surged from 2,000 to 13,000 per game, yet the move also included a curious detail: Zaw Zaw enlisted Than Shwe’s grandson as a player on Delta United — a clear act of flattery. In Bulgaria, football has long been entangled with organized crime. A U.S. diplomatic cable described the sport as 'a symbol of organized crime’s corrupt influence on important institutions.' Mafia-linked figures control top clubs, using them to launder money — and public image. Three former presidents of Lokomotiv Plovdiv, linked to the crime group VIS, were assassinated. Fan attendance collapsed as trust evaporated. In Sierra Leone, the national team’s coach, Mohamed Sesay, was arrested in connection with a major cocaine bust at Lungi Airport. Rumors suggest his political connections secured his coaching post — and his uncle’s appointment as transportation minister — to facilitate drug trafficking. Mohamed Sesay now serves a five-year prison sentence. Iran’s President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, a self-proclaimed football fanatic, intervened directly in national team affairs. He fired legendary coach Ali Daei and forced the return of star player Ali Karimi ahead of a crucial 2010 World Cup qualifier. He reportedly believed Iran’s victory over the UAE — secured by a Karimi goal — was essential to his electoral prospects. Days later, Iran’s disputed election sparked nationwide unrest. Karimi, wearing a green armband in solidarity with the Green Movement, defied presidential expectations by drawing 1-1 with South Korea — ending Iran’s World Cup hopes. In Eritrea, 11 of the 12 players on the national team — known as the Red Sea Boys — vanished after a humiliating 4-0 defeat to Tanzania. They eventually surfaced in Australia, seeking asylum. Only the coach and an escorting colonel returned. President Isaias Afewerki denied the defections, but Human Rights Watch confirmed the players’ safety. With Eritrea enforcing lifelong conscription and imprisoning dissenters, the team’s flight offered a chilling glimpse into life under his regime. In Jordan, a fierce derby between Al Faisaly (representing ethnic Hashemites) and Al Wihdat (representing Palestinians, who comprise up to 70% of the population) erupted into violent riots. Fans chanted against Queen Rania and the monarchy, exposing deep societal fractures. Police responded harshly; 250 fans were injured, some fatally. The king remained silent. The incident underscored how football mirrors — and magnifies — the nation’s unresolved ethnic and political tensions.

The family is staying in a rented oceanfront home in Kailua, Oahu, continuing a six-year tradition since Obama’s election. While they cover the $3,500 daily rent, local and federal taxpayers foot the bill for security and transport, totaling roughly $1 million. Security measures—including Navy SEAL patrols, Coast Guard cutters in the bay, vehicle searches, and roadblocks—have become routine but increasingly disruptive for neighbors on Kailuana Place. Some residents, like longtime local Madeline, admit the initial excitement has worn off. 'It used to feel special,' she said, 'now it’s just maddening.' Others, like Lanette Hayashi, appreciate the safety boost: 'When he’s here, the whole neighborhood feels secure.' Despite the inconveniences, the Obamas still make time for local favorites—like shave ice from Island Snow—and beach outings with their kids. Obama, born in Hawaii, took a moment with reporters to reflect: 'The end of the year is a good time to think about how to do better next year. I’m sure I’ll have better ideas after a few days of sun and sleep.' This year, the family’s focus is simple: rest, reconnect, and recharge—without a single official event on the calendar.

article_content: Fears have grown over a new online challenge called 'Wetnominate', which mirrors the deadly 'Neknominate' drinking trend. The latest incident involved a 20-year-old man, believed to be participating in the challenge, leaping backward off a bridge into a river. Videos show him running toward the bridge’s edge in his underwear, climbing over the railing, performing a backflip, and plunging into the water below. Wetnominate requires participants to soak themselves in extreme ways—often by jumping into bodies of water—before nominating others to do the same or escalate the stunt. The activity bears strong resemblance to Neknominate, a viral social media trend that began in Australia and led to the deaths of at least three young people who consumed large quantities of alcohol on camera. Public officials have reacted strongly. Cynon Valley MP Ann Clwyd warned: 'You cannot jump from those heights into water—you don’t know what’s below or how deep it is. He could have been killed. I'm glad he's not hurt, but this should be a warning to everyone.' South Wales Police echoed the concern, calling the behavior 'reckless' and stressing it could lead to 'tragic consequences.' Despite the backlash, Mr. Price told ITV he doesn’t regret the act. 'I’ve grown up jumping off that bridge,' he said. 'I only did it because I’ve done it before. People shouldn’t be so stupid as to copy me.' He later posted photos of scratches on his torso, suggesting minor injuries. Neknominate, which surged in early 2014, involved participants drinking large volumes of alcohol—sometimes exceeding safe limits—and posting videos of themselves doing so. Three confirmed deaths followed: Bradley Eames, 20, died after consuming nearly two pints of gin; Isaac Richardson, 20, collapsed after mixing whiskey, wine, vodka, and lager; and Stephen Brookes, 29, died after drinking nearly a full bottle of vodka, reaching a blood alcohol level more than six times the legal driving limit. In a separate case, nine-year-old Rhiannon Scully was hospitalized after drinking whiskey and vodka after seeing Neknominate videos online. She required stomach pumping and overnight monitoring but recovered fully.

article_content: After undergoing wisdom teeth removal, 23-year-old Jayci Underwood from Corona, California, emerged from sedation visibly shaken — not from pain, but from a profound sense of disappointment. Filmed by her husband Matt in the dental office waiting room, Jayci wept uncontrollably, insisting the surgery had failed because she hadn’t magically transformed into pop star Nicki Minaj. 'I paid so much money,' she sobbed, dabbing her bleeding tongue, 'and I still look like me.' She elaborated, pleading for Minaj’s curves and facial structure as if they were surgical options she’d selected. Her distress didn’t end there. In a moment that stunned even her husband, Jayci turned to Matt and declared, 'I also wanted to be friends with Ellen DeGeneres.' When Matt asked if she meant she wanted to look like Ellen too, she shot him a sharp look. 'No! I want to be her friend. Ellen’s generous — that’s literally her name!' she cried, clinging to the idea that celebrity status equaled personal connection. As the six-minute clip continued, Jayci mused aloud about what her life might be like if she resembled Jay-Z or Beyoncé — imagining herself invited into their inner circles, accepted, and loved. Matt, visibly bewildered, tried to reassure her that maybe someday she’d meet Ellen. 'Doubt it!' Jayci snapped back. When the nurse returned to check on her, Matt chuckled and said, 'She’s great!' — a jarring contrast to Jayci’s raw emotion. The video, posted on YouTube and Facebook with the comment 'you’re welcome,' quickly went viral. Yet many viewers dismissed it as an elaborate hoax designed to land Jayci on The Ellen DeGeneres Show. Others pointed out similarities to another viral video of a teen crying after surgery, wishing Beyoncé had been there. Whether real or staged, the footage laid bare the surreal lengths to which celebrity worship can warp perception — especially under the influence of anesthesia.

article_content: According to the Office for National Statistics, around 23.9 million people in Britain are now employed in the private sector — the highest number on record. This represents a gain of 627,000 jobs over the past year, while public sector employment declined by 128,000 to 5.7 million, its lowest level in a decade. Total employment across both sectors, including the self-employed, reached 29.6 million — the largest workforce since records began in 1971. Unemployment fell by 82,000 between August and October 2012 to 2.51 million, marking the steepest drop since the financial crisis and the largest decline since 2001. The unemployment rate stood at 7.8%, down half a percentage point from a year earlier. However, long-term unemployment remains a critical issue: over 904,000 of the unemployed — more than a third — have been out of work for more than a year. Regional disparities persist: unemployment in the North East was 9.5%, while the South West recorded the lowest rate at 5.7%. London and other urban centers saw modest increases, while areas like Yorkshire/Humber and Scotland experienced notable declines. Economists noted the figures are impressive given the UK’s sluggish economic performance. Andrew Goodwin of Ernst & Young’s Item Club called the job growth a 'phenomenal achievement' despite the economy flat-lining. Employment Minister Mark Hoban credited British businesses for stepping up where the state was retrenching. Yet, the data excludes the recent reclassification of 196,000 education workers from public to private roles — a factor that may have artificially boosted private sector numbers. Meanwhile, real wages continue to fall as earnings growth lags behind inflation. The employment rate for those aged 16–64 stands at 71.2%, below its 2005 peak of 73.1%. Neil Carberry of the CBI warned that persistent long-term unemployment is 'deeply troubling,' and the Prime Minister acknowledged it remains 'stubbornly high.'

article_content: In November 2013, 49-year-old Gary Jones was sentenced to two years in prison after destroying his sister’s holiday home in Torquay, Devon. His actions followed months of escalating anger over what he saw as lifelong favoritism by his mother toward his sister, Gail — a resentment that reached its peak when no birthday card arrived that year. Jones didn’t just vent; he broke into the property by smashing a window, scribbled his name and offensive graffiti across the walls, turned on the gas cooker and faucets to flood the house and inflate utility bills, and left behind food and alcohol he’d taken from inside. Prior to the break-in, he had called his mother’s voicemail three times, demanding £5,000 and accusing the family of cheating the state. He threatened to report them to authorities and warned he didn’t care if he was arrested. Neighbors called police after hearing glass shatter; officers found Jones outside the home with stolen items. At court, prosecutors highlighted how terrified his mother and sister had become, with his mother admitting she now felt unsafe even in her own house. Jones’ defense lawyer explained that a childhood fall from a tree had caused lasting brain trauma, leading to memory loss that ended his career as a truck driver. Though he had been making progress through treatment at a Torbay clinic, recent cuts to his support services triggered a relapse into alcohol abuse. Judge Phillip Wassall acknowledged the depth of Jones’ pain but condemned his violent response as ‘a twisted interpretation’ of distress. The case underscores not just personal grievance, but the consequences of untreated mental illness and fractured family dynamics.
