article_content: The American infant mortality rate dropped slightly to 6.14 deaths per 1,000 live births, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The figure, released by the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, is based on data from 2010 and reflects a modest decline from 6.39 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2009 — a 4% reduction. Infant mortality rates are widely used as indicators of a nation’s public health and socioeconomic well-being. Although preliminary estimates suggest the rate may fall further to 6.05 in 2011, the 2010 rate of 6.14 remains significantly higher than the OECD average of 4.0 deaths per 1,000 live births. The U.S. ranks 26th out of 34 wealthy nations in infant mortality, placing it behind countries like Iceland (1.6), Japan (2.0), Sweden (2.0), and Finland (2.0), according to OECD data. The report notes that life expectancy in the U.S., once above the OECD average in 1970, now falls below it. Premature births, low birth weight, and birth defects are the leading causes of infant death in the U.S., often linked to socioeconomic factors such as teenage pregnancy, lack of prenatal care, poverty, and lack of insurance. A Save the Children report emphasized that mothers with one risk factor — such as being a teenager — are more likely to face multiple disadvantages simultaneously. Multiple births also contribute significantly: the infant mortality rate for triplets is roughly ten times higher than for singletons. Promising progress is emerging from research by the Royal Women's Hospital in Melbourne, where a daily probiotic supplement containing three strains from Danish company Chr Hansen reduced the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) — a deadly intestinal disease in preterm infants — by more than half in a trial involving 1,100 babies. Chr Hansen is currently in discussions with potential partners to commercialize this probiotic solution targeting NEC, though it has not disclosed the names of the companies involved. Chr Hansen, a supplier of cultures, colors, and enzymes to major food producers including Danone and Nestlé, is advancing innovations aimed at improving neonatal health outcomes.

article_content: Marnie, a Shih-Tzu once known as 'Stinky,' endured a brutal life on the streets of Connecticut before her fortunes changed. Found by Animal Control in August 2012 with matted, foul-smelling fur and severe dental decay, she was taken to a shelter and given the unflattering name 'Stinky.' After a Petfinder.com post caught the attention of Shirley Braha, an MTV producer and director, Marnie was adopted and brought to New York City. The transition wasn't easy — Marnie famously stank up the entire train ride to her new home. Soon after, she underwent surgery to remove 14 decaying teeth and was diagnosed with blindness in her left eye due to a clouded, gray cornea. Her owner renamed her Marnie after musician Marnie Stern, and slowly, her health improved. Miraculously, her left eye regained vision. Her long tongue, a quirky anatomical trait, became a signature feature — often licked to stay moist, even in snow. Marnie’s unique appearance — including a persistent head tilt attributed to past Vestibular Syndrome — captivated online audiences. With over 134,000 Instagram followers, she’s appeared in photos alongside celebrities like Jonah Hill and Miley Cyrus. Her owner documents her journey on Tumblr, celebrating Marnie’s resilience and zest for life: long walks, chicken, broccoli, Greek yogurt, watermelon, eggs, and parties. The only thing she hates? Being left alone. Shirley Braha says Marnie embodies the profound gratitude often seen in senior rescue dogs. 'She lives every day exemplifying this joy and gratitude,' Braha writes. Marnie’s story isn’t just about beauty or fame — it’s about redemption, second chances, and the quiet power of love to heal.

Speaking on Saturday, Raut said the tweet—now deleted from his X account—was made months ago and reflected a broader critique of wartime inhumanity, not a direct attack on Israel. He emphasized that he has consistently condemned Hamas’s violent assault on Israel, including attacks on civilian infrastructure like hospitals in Gaza, where children were killed. 'I called it inhuman,' Raut stated. 'You can't claim morality when you're killing kids.' He added that the Israeli High Commission recently sent him a formal letter about the post, which he believes may have been prompted by individuals seeking to discredit him. Raut stressed he has no animosity toward Israel and regrets any unintended offense caused by his choice of words.

article_content: In a groundbreaking experiment conducted in 2014, scientists from the University of Southampton successfully charged a Nokia 925 mobile phone using a simulated lightning bolt. By passing 200,000 volts across an 11-inch gap, they replicated the intense heat, light, and electrical charge of natural lightning. This high-voltage pulse was directed through a secondary transformer to stabilize the current before it reached the phone’s battery. Remarkably, a single bolt was enough to fully charge the device. The team, led by researcher Neil Palmer, explained that the Nokia phone’s internal circuitry unexpectedly stabilized the erratic electrical signal — a discovery that could inform future efforts to harness natural electrical phenomena. 'We were amazed to see that the Nokia circuitry somehow stabilised the noisy signal, allowing the battery to be charged,' Palmer said. Phil B from the Nokia Conversations blog described the feat as a 'world’s first' and noted, 'For most of us, lightning can be a truly terrifying, powerful and awe-inspiring force of nature. But boffins from Nokia and the University of Southampton put their heads together to try and tame the beast — and they succeeded.' However, Nokia sales boss Chris Weber cautioned, 'We aren’t recommending people try this experiment at home.' Lightning forms when electrical imbalances between clouds and the ground discharge during storms. While this experiment shows promise for alternative energy in remote areas, it remains a laboratory demonstration — not a viable consumer technology.

article_content: Nathan Cirillo was more than a soldier — he was a man whose laughter echoed through hallways and whose heart extended to stray dogs and strangers alike. Though his muscular frame and ceremonial uniform made him look every bit the disciplined warrior, those who knew him remembered a different side: a guitarist strumming tunes, a man patiently waiting for a friend on a freezing night with coffee in hand, and a devoted dad to his young son. On Wednesday morning, while standing guard at Ottawa’s National War Memorial — a duty reserved for the most trusted soldiers — Cirillo was shot in the back by an attacker. Witnesses described the scene as sudden and brutal. Peter Henderson saw the fallen soldier lying beneath the memorial’s granite arch, his body riddled with catastrophic wounds. Within hours, Canadian leaders called it a terrorist act, condemning the killing as a cowardly ambush. Cirillo, a proud member of the Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders, came from Hamilton, Ontario — a city that honors its military legacy. His unit, known for its fierce combat history, trains to close with and destroy enemies on the battlefield — yet Cirillo never imagined his end would come in peace, under the watchful gaze of a national monument. Online, photos surfaced showing him in full kilt and gloves, grinning beside his dog, cuddling a kitten in his backpack, or lifting weights with joy. Friends recalled how he’d always have a joke ready, how he once rescued a puppy and found it a home, and how he never missed a chance to make someone smile. His Facebook and Instagram pages, filled with pets, music, and workouts, painted a picture of a man who loved deeply and lived fully. His final act of service, performed in quiet dignity, cost him his life — but left behind a legacy of warmth, humor, and unwavering kindness.

article_content: Writer and parenting guru Lenore Skenazy is on a mission to reclaim the simple joys of childhood from overprotective parents. Skenazy, a 55-year-old mother of two from Queens and founder of the Free Range Kids movement, made headlines in 2008 when she allowed her then-9-year-old son to ride the New York City subway unsupervised, earning her the nickname 'World’s Worst Mom.' Seven years—and one book deal—later, Skenazy is tackling helicopter parenting head-on as the host of Discovery Life’s new show, World’s Worst Mom, premiering January 22. According to the show’s description, the 13-part series is dedicated to diffusing parental paranoia by helping high-strung, fearful parents relax and grant their children the freedom they deserve. In each episode, Skenazy conducts interventions with families, challenges boundaries, and debunks myths about perceived dangers lurking around every corner. Skenazy’s core belief is that while parents must remain vigilant, they should not wrap their children in metaphorical bubble wrap. She argues that shielding children from all risk deprives them of essential opportunities to develop independence. 'Some kids are losing their childhood because their parents are so overprotective,' Skenazy told The New York Post. 'Fear is being shoved down their throats at every turn.' One of the anxious parents featured is Cayle White, a mother of three from Manhattan’s Upper West Side who describes her family as 'paralyzed' by her fears. To ease her anxiety about her 11-year-old son Amadeo’s walk home from school, he is required to call her repeatedly, narrating each step from the bus stop to their front door. A self-described germophobe, White overcooks food and microwaves it again to eliminate any lingering bacteria. Skenazy, acting like a modern-day Mary Poppins, intervenes by hosting a barbecue in the park—where White is barred from approaching the grill—to demonstrate that eating medium-rare steak won’t endanger her family. She then sends Amadeo out alone to walk the family dog in Central Park, asking him to leave his phone behind so his mother can’t monitor him. When he returns safely and proudly, White acknowledges his accomplishment. In another episode, Skenazy visits the Almonte family in Rockland County, New York, to help mother Phyllis overcome her fear of letting her children out of her sight. Ten-year-old Brianna says, 'Sometimes I feel like I’m in a box and nobody can come into it, and I’m not allowed out.' Phyllis bans sleepovers, insists on accompanying Brianna into public restrooms, and forbids 12-year-old Zach from riding his bike beyond the driveway, fearing a car accident. Even in their backyard, the children must stay in constant contact via walkie-talkies. 'I constantly fear that they’ll get abducted or hurt,' admits 47-year-old Phyllis. 'I know what I’m doing isn’t good, but I can’t help it.' To challenge these fears, Skenazy organizes a pool party for Brianna and sends Zach on a two-mile bike ride in the park. Two years later, Phyllis told The Post: 'Instead of thinking of all the things that could go wrong, I’m thinking about all the things that could go right.'

article_content: In a rare address to a joint session of the U.S. Congress, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared his willingness to negotiate a peace deal with the Palestinians — but only on terms that preserve Israel’s strategic control over key territories. He emphasized that while Israel might relinquish some settlements beyond its current borders, it would never revert to the pre-1967 ceasefire lines, calling them militarily indefensible. Netanyahu insisted that any future Palestinian state must be demilitarized and that Israel must retain a permanent military presence along the Jordan River to safeguard against threats from the east. He firmly rejected the longstanding Palestinian demand for the 'right of return' for descendants of those displaced during Israel’s creation in 1948, arguing instead that Palestinian refugees should be resettled in a future Palestinian state, not within Israel’s current borders. 'Jews have a right to come home to their ancestral land,' he said. 'So too should Palestinians have the right to build a homeland elsewhere — but not at the expense of Israel’s existence.' Netanyahu blamed Palestinian leadership for refusing to recognize Israel as a Jewish state, and he reiterated his stance that Jerusalem must remain undivided as Israel’s eternal capital. His speech came as a direct counterpoint to President Obama’s recent call for peace talks anchored in the 1967 borders, with mutually agreed land swaps to accommodate Israeli settlements. While Netanyahu received warm applause from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers, Palestinian officials responded with sharp criticism. Sabri Saidam of Fatah accused him of speaking not to negotiate, but to dictate — describing the proposed Palestinian state as fragmented, like 'Swiss cheese,' carved up by Israeli settlements and military zones. Nabil Shaath condemned the dismissal of the right of return as hypocritical, noting that while Jews claim ties to ancient lands, Palestinians were forcibly removed from their homes just decades ago. Netanyahu also used the platform to warn of an imminent nuclear threat from Iran, invoking the memory of the Holocaust to justify Israel’s right to act preemptively in its own defense. He praised the U.S. for killing Osama bin Laden, drawing a contrast between what he portrayed as American strength and Palestinian intransigence. Meanwhile, protests erupted both inside and outside Congress. A woman shouting 'Equal rights for Palestine' was removed by Capitol Police, and activists from Code Pink disrupted Netanyahu’s earlier appearance at AIPAC, condemning Israel’s occupation of Palestinian land and the blockade of Gaza. Despite the applause on Capitol Hill, critics questioned whether U.S. political support for Israel remains truly balanced when the lives and rights of millions of Palestinians hang in the balance. With direct negotiations stalled, Palestinian leaders signaled they will pursue formal recognition of statehood through the United Nations in September — a move Netanyahu dismissed as irrelevant without prior bilateral talks. He also ruled out engaging with Hamas, labeling it a terrorist group, even though it governs Gaza and holds popular support among many Palestinians. The path forward, he insisted, can only be paved through direct negotiation — not international pressure or unilateral declarations.

article_content: More than eight decades after Sir Arthur Conan Doyle passed away, the legendary detective Sherlock Holmes has returned—not as a reboot or parody, but in the first-ever officially sanctioned new novel: 'The House of Silk' by British author Anthony Horowitz. Written with full approval from the Conan Doyle estate and zero editorial interference, the book transports readers back to fog-drenched 1890s London, where Watson, now retired, finally unearths a case so harrowing it was locked away for a century. The story begins with a terrified art dealer, a ruthless American gang, and a chilling calling card: a strip of white silk. Soon, Holmes and Watson are pulled into a conspiracy threatening the heart of British society, with familiar faces like Mycroft, Lestrade, Mrs. Hudson, and even Moriarty returning to the stage. Horowitz, famed for the 'Alex Rider' series and TV hits like 'Midsomer Murders,' didn’t try to reinvent Holmes—he honored him. He preserved the voice, rhythm, and moral clarity of Doyle’s originals, while tightening the pacing for modern readers. In interviews, Horowitz revealed he fell in love with Holmes at 16 after reading 'The Sign of Four,' and considers Holmes and Watson’s bond the most profound friendship in all of literature. He also confirmed that 'The House of Silk' picks up just days after 'The Dying Detective,' one of his personal favorites. With blockbuster films and TV series reviving Holmes for new generations, Horowitz’s novel isn’t just a tribute—it’s a continuation, proving that some legends aren’t meant to die, only to be quietly passed on.

article_content: Looking for authentic travel experiences that celebrate cultural diversity and support sustainable tourism? The United Nations World Tourism Organization (UNWTO) has unveiled its 2023 list of the Best Tourism Villages — a curated selection of 54 lesser-known communities worldwide that exemplify responsible travel. These villages, spread across five continents, have been recognized for their outstanding efforts in preserving cultural heritage, protecting natural environments, and fostering inclusive economic growth through tourism. This year’s list builds upon previous editions: 44 villages were honored in 2021 and 32 in 2022. Among the standout nations, Peru leads with five入选 villages, followed by Portugal, Japan, and China, each with four. The UNWTO emphasizes that these destinations are not ranked — they’re listed alphabetically and grouped by region for easier exploration. In Europe, Ordino in Andorra stands out as a Biosphere Reserve where rural traditions harmonize with modern life. Austria’s Schladming combines alpine adventure with historic churches and a centuries-old skiing legacy. Croatia’s Slunj preserves ancient songs and dances alongside eco-friendly trails. Hungary’s Tokaj, a UNESCO site since 2002, invites wine lovers into its ancient cellars. Italy’s Lerici enchants with coastal beauty and a deep commitment to sustainable development. Across Asia, China’s Huangling dazzles with autumnal chili-drying landscapes, while Japan’s Shirakawa captivates with snow-laden thatched roofs. Indonesia’s Penglipuran and India’s Dhordo showcase resilient communities rebuilding through cultural tourism. South Korea’s Mosan offers a window into Bronze Age dolmen culture, and Türkiye’s Şirince blends vineyards with ancient Ephesus. In Latin America, Peru’s Taquile Island shines for its handwoven textiles and community-led stewardship. Chile’s Caleta Tortel reveals wooden walkways built from native cypress, and Mexico’s Jalpa de Cánovas celebrates tequila, tradition, and gastronomy. Colombia’s Filandia dazzles with colorful buildings and coffee plantations, while Ecuador’s Oyacachi — dubbed the ‘Land of Water’ — brims with waterfalls and thermal springs. Africa and the Middle East feature equally compelling stories: Egypt’s Dashour and Siwa preserve ancient desert heritage; Iran’s Kandovan is home to rock-carved homes still inhabited today; Jordan’s Al Sela boasts rare flora and sweeping valleys; and Uzbekistan’s Sentob revives Silk Road traditions through community-driven storytelling. According to UNWTO Secretary-General Zurab Pololikashvili, 'This initiative acknowledges villages that have harnessed tourism as a catalyst for their development and well-being.' These 54 destinations aren’t just places to visit — they’re models of how tourism, when rooted in respect and responsibility, can uplift entire communities. Note: In Chain [2], Morcote was incorrectly linked to Neanderthal relics. Correction: While the broader Swiss Prealps region contains significant paleontological sites, Morcote itself is recognized for its medieval architecture, lakeside setting, and blend of Alpine and Mediterranean influences — not direct fossil discoveries. This detail has been removed for accuracy.

article_content: Bronwyn Gray, an 18-year-old social sciences student from Paisley, was hospitalized after being bitten by a spider during her first week at Edinburgh Napier University. Initially, she believed her symptoms — including a small spot on her right arm and a developing cough — were signs of 'Freshers' Flu'. The spot grew larger, and angry red lines began spreading from it. After visiting a chemist who prescribed antiseptic, her condition worsened. She returned home to recover, but her symptoms intensified, leading to an emergency hospital visit. Gray spent one night in the hospital and was advised to return for multiple follow-up appointments to ensure the venom had not spread. Medical staff could not identify the type of spider responsible. Speaking to The Tab student website, Gray said: 'I had a wee spot on my arm and then it started growing, and lines started coming out of it. I went to the chemist and they gave me an antiseptic, but I ended up in hospital after a week. Then they told me it was a spider bite. I was really freaked out — I thought it was just Freshers’ Flu. I had a cough, but otherwise I was fine.' She added with dark humor: 'It’s getting better now, but I’m gutted I don’t have super spidey powers. My mates were really freaked out too — they’d never seen anything like it.'

article_content: On Wednesday morning, Chandigarh narrowly avoided a major disaster when 1,600 students from Sharda Sarvhitkari School in Sector 40 were urgently evacuated following a gas pipeline rupture. The leak, triggered by a JCB excavation that disrupted underground sewer lines, released dangerous levels of natural gas into the area. Acting swiftly, school staff shut down all electrical systems—including CCTV cameras—to eliminate ignition risks, then moved all students to a nearby park before arranging their safe return home. Principal Archana Nagrath told The Indian Express that parents were immediately notified by phone, and local authorities including the police and councillor were alerted amid rising panic. Local Councillor Gurbax Rawat confirmed all children were unharmed and praised the school’s decisive actions. He blamed the incident on improper pipeline installation following sewer line work, warning that such negligence could lead to catastrophic outcomes if left unchecked. Chandigarh Mayor Anup Gupta has ordered a full report from the Executive Engineer, while Commissioner Anindita Mitra confirmed that an FIR has been registered against the contractor for criminal negligence. IOC-Adani, the sole provider of piped natural gas in the region, is not directly implicated but faces renewed scrutiny over oversight protocols.

article_content: A lightning strike on Fort Myers Beach in southwest Florida killed one person and injured two teenagers on Tuesday afternoon. According to the Lee County Sheriff’s Office, 41-year-old Scott Wilcox of Lehigh Acres was fatally struck while walking near the water. Two others — teens Chelsea Gill and Zachary Latawiec, also from Lehigh Acres — were seriously injured and transported to the hospital. Witnesses reported hearing a loud crack as the lightning hit around 2:10 p.m. near the Lani Kai resort. Emergency crews were delayed due to the severity of the storm, forcing responders to remain in their vehicles until conditions improved. Zachary Latawiec is in critical condition and has been placed in an induced coma, according to family sources. Chelsea Gill, though burned and in pain, was conscious upon arrival at the hospital and is expected to make a full recovery after several days of observation. Matt Rector, a local wave runner rental operator who knows CPR, attempted to assist the victims. He said Latawiec had no pulse, so he performed chest compressions and rescue breathing — observing slight chest movement but no improvement. Gill was breathing but suffered burns. Witness Robert Gustafson described the scene as devastating: 'The blood was rolling, just floating down to the water’s edge, and the water was turning red right there.' Alice Lynch, another witness, said, 'Three people hit by lightning... at the same time... that’s terrible.'

article_content: Nearly two decades after revolutionizing late-night TV as the first Black host of a nationally syndicated talk show, Arsenio Hall is making a bold return with his new program, 'Arsenio.' His original 1989–1994 show wasn’t just entertainment—it was a cultural phenomenon, known for its energetic crowd chants and unpredictable celebrity cameos, from Bill Clinton picking up a saxophone during his presidential campaign to Magic Johnson sharing his HIV diagnosis live on air. Even the night the 1992 LA riots erupted, Hall turned his studio into a space for raw, honest dialogue. Now 57, Hall isn’t just returning—he’s redefining what late-night can mean today. In a crowded field dominated by Leno, Fallon, Kimmel, and Stewart, he’s not chasing trends. Instead, he’s bringing back the soul: unscripted moments, deep conversations, and music that moves people. His debut episode? Pure celebration—no clips, no agenda, just friends, laughter, and good vibes. Behind the scenes, Hall’s journey has been deeply personal. He stepped away from Hollywood not because he lost interest, but because he wanted to be present—for his kids, his partner, and himself. Raised by hardworking parents who were often absent, he vowed to raise his son differently. ‘I didn’t want to leave this world without a child—and I didn’t want to raise him the way I was raised,’ he says. When asked about guest lists, Hall doesn’t shy away from ambition: Obama? Invited. Hillary Clinton playing sax? He’s already pitched it. And while he’d love to speak with Chris Brown, he’s clear: interviews must serve purpose, not spectacle. He believes in letting artists like Stevie Wonder speak truth through song and conversation—not just punchlines. To reconnect with a new generation who never saw his original show, Hall didn’t wait. He appeared everywhere—from Newsweek essays on fatherhood to multiple spots on Leno, Maher, and even filling in for Access Hollywood hosts. He wanted them to know: Arsenio’s still here, still relevant, still ready to talk. And why now? Because his 13-year-old son asked him to drop him off five blocks from the party. In that moment, Hall realized: being a dad means showing up—even when you’re tired. Even when you fall asleep holding the remote. That’s the real late-night show.

article_content: Since the 1960s, the bar for hotel room destruction has been set high—thanks largely to Keith Moon, The Who’s drummer, who celebrated his 20th birthday by stripping naked and crashing a car into a hotel pool. While today’s hotel damage can be just as costly, many argue that the era of explosive rock-star chaos is fading. Modern offenders aren’t smashing TVs or hurling furniture—they’re leaving behind cigarette ash, empty bottles, and litter, often from reality stars and manufactured pop acts rather than legendary musicians. Still, the tradition hasn’t vanished entirely. In 2015, reality TV star Scott Disick sparked outrage after allegedly trashing his room at the Hotel Jerome in Aspen, Colorado. Reports said guests complained of marijuana smoke, and the next morning, staff found cigarette butts, empty liquor bottles, and a room in disarray. Though the party spent $1,440 on drinks, the hotel added a $500 fine for violating its non-smoking policy. But Disick’s antics pale beside the legends. In 1967, Keith Moon turned a Holiday Inn in Michigan into a war zone: a food fight led to fire extinguishers being discharged in the halls, furniture was flung, and after streaking through the lobby, he stole a Lincoln Continental and drove it into the pool—then slipped on marzipan and knocked out a tooth. The band was banned for life from all Holiday Inns, and damages totaled $24,000. Other icons followed suit: Keith Richards tossed a TV from the 10th floor of the Hyatt West Hollywood in 1972. Amanda Bynes left the Ritz Carlton in 2013 with ash-covered surfaces, a ripped smoke alarm on the nightstand, and a $9,000 bill. Nirvana’s Dave Grohl and Krist Novoselic, accompanied by MTV reporter Kurt Loder, destroyed two rooms in Minnesota in 1993, smashing TVs and breaking everything they could find—totaling $19,000 in damages. Florence Welch admitted to setting her Bowery Hotel room on fire in 2012 after drinking 17 dirty martinis and forgetting a candle. Amy Winehouse and husband Blake Fielder-Civil left blood on the walls of London’s Sanderson Hotel in 2007, requiring professional cleaning. Lindsay Lohan racked up $50,000 in damages in 2012 at New York’s Union Square W Hotel—so severe, the carpet had to be replaced—and was previously banned from Shutters on the Beach after a 2007 incident. Even Johnny Depp got caught up in the chaos: in 1994, after a drunken fight with Kate Moss at New York’s Mark Hotel, he claimed an armadillo was to blame. Charges were dropped after he paid nearly $10,000 in damages. And Edie Sedgwick, Andy Warhol’s muse, repeatedly set her Chelsea Hotel room ablaze with burning candles in the mid-60s—so often, the hotel moved her to room 105 directly above the lobby for easier monitoring. Whether fueled by fame, substance abuse, or pure rebellion, these episodes reveal a dark underbelly of celebrity culture—one that leaves hotels paying the price, and sometimes, the stars paying far more.

article_content: Ahead of its anticipated $80+ million sale in New York, Edvard Munch’s iconic 1895 pastel version of 'The Scream' is currently on view in London. Created in the 1890s, there are four known versions of this haunting image — and this is the only one still held privately. The others reside in Oslo’s public museums. Simon Shaw, head of Impressionist and Modern Art at Sotheby’s, calls it the second most famous artwork globally, trailing only the Mona Lisa. Though reproduced endlessly — on mugs, posters, and even in horror films like Wes Craven’s 'Scream' — most people have never laid eyes on the real thing. Its fame has been amplified by its history: two of the three publicly held versions were stolen in the last two decades, each time recovered, yet each theft catapulted the painting into headlines worldwide. In fact, after the 1994 theft from Norway’s National Gallery, visitor numbers surged as people flocked to see the empty frame. The current owner, Petter Olsen, whose father was a close friend and neighbor of Munch, is selling the piece to finance Ramme Gaard, a new arts center in Hvitsten, Norway, opening next year to mark the 150th anniversary of Munch’s birth. 'I’ve lived with this painting my whole life,' Olsen said. 'Its energy hasn’t faded — it’s grown stronger. Now, I want others to experience it.' Sotheby’s believes this is a once-in-a-generation opportunity for a museum or collector to acquire one of art history’s most potent symbols — and demand is global.

article_content: The world’s most powerful democracy and its most absolute monarchy have long been close, if improbable, allies. Bound by shared interests — the secure flow of oil and, more recently, combating Al Qaeda — their partnership was formally established on February 14, 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt met King Abdul Aziz aboard the USS Quincy as it sailed through the Suez Canal. FDR and his advisors understood that Saudi Arabia’s vast oil reserves were critical to America’s economic future. A decade earlier, Standard Oil of California had secured exclusive rights to produce oil in the Kingdom — a foresighted move that laid the foundation for decades of cooperation. According to Thomas Lippman, an authoritative voice on U.S.-Saudi relations, FDR gifted the king a specially modified DC-3 aircraft, later fitted with a rotating throne to allow Abdul Aziz to face Mecca while airborne. In return, the king, so impressed by the meals aboard the Quincy, requested the ship’s cook — a request FDR diplomatically declined. (Slavery, which persisted in Saudi Arabia until 1962, reflected a slower evolution of human rights norms in the Kingdom.) For over six decades, the U.S.-Saudi alliance functioned effectively. As the world’s largest oil producer and holder of roughly one-fifth of global proven reserves, Saudi Arabia could influence prices by adjusting output — typically in ways that aligned with American interests. When Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, the U.S. deployed half a million troops to the Gulf to restore stability. Though the 9/11 attacks — carried out by 15 Saudis among the 19 hijackers — strained public trust, the George W. Bush administration maintained strong ties, especially after Al Qaeda began targeting Westerners and oil infrastructure within Saudi Arabia in 2003, prompting a decisive crackdown. Tensions have recently escalated under President Obama. Saudi officials, usually discreet, have openly voiced frustration: Prince Turki al-Faisal, former intelligence chief and ambassador to Washington, criticized the U.S. for blurring its ‘red lines,’ particularly regarding Syria’s use of chemical weapons. With Syria aligned with Iran — Saudi Arabia’s primary regional rival — Riyadh fears the U.S. will not confront Iran’s nuclear ambitions, especially as diplomatic engagement between Washington and Tehran has improved. Saudi leaders were also unsettled by the U.S. decision to abandon longtime ally Hosni Mubarak during the 2011 Arab Spring, raising questions about America’s commitment to its regional partners. These concerns echo those of Israel, another key U.S. ally. Prince Mohammed bin Nayef, Saudi Arabia’s powerful Interior Minister, recently visited Washington to discuss Syria — a shared priority. Both nations seek to prevent Al Qaeda’s expansion there. Saudi Arabia has since criminalized travel to Syria for combat, recognizing that over 1,200 of its citizens have joined the conflict, with 220 returning home — a source of deep concern over potential terrorist 'blowback.' Despite these strains, a senior U.S. official affirmed after Obama’s meeting with King Abdullah near Riyadh that the two nations remain 'very much aligned' on core security goals, particularly countering Al Qaeda in Syria.

article_content: NEW YORK (CNN) — During the morning rush hour on Wednesday, NYPD officers on a counter-terrorism patrol assisted in the unexpected delivery of a baby inside New York’s busy Penn Station. Caesar Penn Boothe was born at 7:20 a.m. beneath the station’s departures sign. 'Forget the ambulance — I’m having this baby right here,' recalled new mother Marie Boothe at a press conference later that day. Three members of the NYPD’s counter-terrorism unit, alongside an Amtrak police officer, stepped in to help deliver the seven-pound baby boy. As the newborn arrived, fellow commuters reacted with characteristic New York energy, shouting, 'Name him Penn — after Penn Station!' said Officer Marie Medina, one of the officers who helped. The infant, whose middle name honors his birthplace, and his mother were transported to Bellevue Hospital, where both are reported to be doing well.

article_content: In a significant development in a nearly decade-old mystery, a West Australian Supreme Court judge has named Tobias Moran — formerly known as Tobias Suckfuell — as the primary suspect in the 2005 killing of Simone Strobel, a 25-year-old German woman working as a kindergarten teacher. Strobel vanished on February 11, 2005, after spending the evening with Moran at a caravan park in Lismore, New South Wales. Her naked body was discovered a week later, concealed beneath a palm tree just 90 meters away. Forensic reports confirmed she died from suffocation, likely caused by a pillow or plastic bag. Despite extensive efforts, Australian police never charged anyone in connection with her death. In June, Moran sought a court injunction to prevent the release of a book titled 'Have You Seen Simone?' by author Virginia Peters, arguing it damaged his reputation. But Judge Kenneth Martin, presiding over the case in Western Australia, denied the request, stating there is 'reasonable suspicion' pointing to Moran as the perpetrator. The judge highlighted several troubling factors: Moran had no verifiable alibi for the hours before Strobel went missing; he failed to report her disappearance promptly; he reportedly avoided searching for her the following morning — claims he denies; and he repeatedly misled investigators by denying arguments and heavy drinking with Strobel on the night she vanished. Text messages and witness accounts suggest the couple had intense fights in the days prior, and both were intoxicated and used marijuana that night. While Judge Martin emphasized there is currently no physical or forensic evidence directly tying Moran to the murder, he concluded that the pattern of behavior and omissions leaves little room for doubt. Meanwhile, German authorities continue to offer a $15,000 reward for credible information that could solve the case.

article_content: Standing at 310 meters tall and featuring a striking 90-degree spiral twist from base to summit, the Cayan Tower in Dubai has officially opened as the world’s tallest twisted skyscraper. Designed by Skidmore Owings & Merrill — the architects behind the Burj Khalifa — this 80-story residential marvel contains 570 luxury apartments, all benefiting from panoramic views of the marina, sea, and The Palm thanks to its unique rotation and absence of interior support columns. With construction costing approximately Rs. 1578 crores, the tower has already seen 80% of its units sold, signaling strong demand among high-end buyers. Located at the entrance of Dubai Marina, the building offers residents a full suite of premium amenities including infinity pools, spas, wellness centers, gyms, and even a nursery. Though visually captivating and architecturally groundbreaking, the Cayan Tower is far from the tallest structure globally. That title still belongs to the Burj Khalifa, which rises over 828 meters — more than double the height of Cayan. Other towering giants include Canada’s CN Tower at 553 meters and Taiwan’s Taipei 101 at 501 meters. For those interested in similar twists, Sweden’s HSB Turning Torso, at 190 meters and 54 stories, remains Europe’s third-tallest residential building and the tallest in Scandinavia. On secondary markets, a single-bedroom unit in Cayan Tower is listed at around $435,000, reflecting its premium positioning. Despite not holding height records, its elegant form and engineering ingenuity make it a standout icon of modern urban living.

article_content: Moeen Ali, the England cricketer, has been prohibited by the International Cricket Council from wearing wristbands bearing the messages 'Save Gaza' and 'Free Palestine' during a Test match against India. The ban followed photos published by MailOnline showing Ali with the bands on his left wrist during play on day two of the match at the Ageas Bowl in Southampton. Match referee David Boon immediately ordered him to remove them, citing ICC regulations that forbid any display of political, religious, or racial statements on equipment or attire during international games. The ICC clarified that while players are free to voice their opinions off the field, such expressions are not permitted on the pitch. Although Ali did not request permission from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) to wear the bands, the ECB stated they do not view his actions as a violation. The ICC, however, maintains that prior written approval from a player’s national board is mandatory for any non-standard apparel — and such approval would never be given for politically charged messages. If formally ruled in breach, Ali could face a fine of up to half his match fee under ICC’s Level One sanctions. Meanwhile, England’s players will wear 'Help for Heroes' logos on their collars and observe a minute’s silence at 10:56 a.m. to honor the 100th anniversary of World War I — both initiatives having received official clearance. Notably, Ali has previously collaborated with the Ummah Welfare Trust to raise funds for civilians affected by conflict in Gaza, highlighting his long-standing community involvement beyond the cricket field.

article_content: A 10-year-old Norwegian boy who previously told police he was a dwarf who forgot his driver’s license after stealing his parents’ car has done it again. This time, he took his aunt’s Opel and drove approximately 20–25 miles from Fagernes to Tonsåsen before being stopped, according to his parents. When the parents realized their son—and his aunt’s car—were missing, they immediately contacted police. After being halted on National Highway 33, authorities discovered he had driven at least 11 miles on the E16 motorway. 'It was my sister’s car. The keys were in the ignition, so unfortunately, it was easy for him to take,' his mother told Verdens Gang. Following his previous incident, the boy had promised his parents it would never happen again—but his mother believes the temptation was simply too strong. 'He’s a boy who loves adventure and excitement—that’s all there is to it,' she added. Last week, the boy had also taken his 18-month-old sister for a ride, driving nearly seven miles before veering off a snowy road near Dokka, 65 miles north of Oslo. He was found by a snowplow driver, who reported that the boy claimed to be a dwarf and had forgotten his license at home. Police confirmed the children were unharmed and the vehicle undamaged. No charges were filed. 'We’ve spoken with them, and I’m certain they’ll be much more careful with their children and car keys in the future,' said Baard Christiansen, a spokesperson for the Vest Oppland police district.

article_content: Texas is paying four times more for its execution drugs from a new supplier — a cost that aligns with local retail rates but remains well below prices in at least one other death penalty state. According to documents obtained by The Associated Press through an open records request, the Texas Department of Criminal Justice paid $13,500 for its most recent batch of pentobarbital, at $1,500 per vial, compared to $350 per vial last year. This increase — a negligible fraction of the agency’s $3 billion annual budget — follows the refusal of its previous supplier to provide more of the sedative, citing pressure from execution opponents. Since then, Texas has secured a new source from a compounding pharmacy and successfully sued to keep the vendor’s identity confidential. Backlash from anti-death-penalty advocates has drastically reduced the number of mainstream pharmaceutical companies willing to supply lethal injection drugs. However, it remains unclear whether this pressure directly caused the price surge. Neither industry groups nor the U.S. Food and Drug Administration track these prices or can explain the spike. Several other states refuse to disclose their drug purchase details, and Texas officials have also declined to comment. 'We're confident we're complying with all state and federal laws,' said prison spokesperson Jason Clark. A survey of nearly two dozen Houston-area pharmacies found that Nembutal — the brand name for pentobarbital — retails for approximately $1,500 per vial, suggesting Texas paid a fair market price. In contrast, Missouri paid up to $8,000 per dose earlier this year. With at least ten inmates scheduled for execution in the coming months — including two in September — Texas’s current supply is expected to deplete by year-end. Officials confirm plans to purchase more, but Clark would not indicate whether costs will rise or if the same supplier will be used. The March purchase was made by the warden of the Huntsville Unit, where executions occur, and included an additional $425 for potency testing. Like many states facing drug shortages, Texas now relies on compounding pharmacies, which manufacture unapproved drugs without FDA verification of safety or efficacy. Yet Texas’s single-drug protocol has avoided the complications experienced in Ohio, Arizona, and Oklahoma, where multi-drug mixtures containing midazolam led to botched executions. Records provided to the AP are redacted to conceal the identity of Texas’s new supplier. Just a few years ago, Texas paid just $83.55 per dose for its former three-drug combination: sodium thiopental, pancuronium bromide, and potassium chloride. But Hospira Inc., the sole U.S. manufacturer of sodium thiopental, ceased production in 2010 after Italy refused to allow export unless guaranteed it wouldn’t be used in executions. Lundbeck Inc., Denmark’s sole U.S.-licensed maker of pentobarbital, later withdrew its product from the market after pressure from death penalty opponents. Texas then turned to The Woodlands Compounding Pharmacy — until the Houston-area company refused further sales in October. Its owner wrote a letter accusing state officials of placing him 'in the middle of a firestorm' of hate mail and potential lawsuits after his identity was exposed. Texas Attorney General Greg Abbott has backed the agency’s refusal to disclose the new supplier, citing a 'threat assessment' from Texas Department of Public Safety Director Steven McCraw, which warns that pharmacies supplying execution drugs face 'a substantial threat of physical harm.'

article_content: Two off-duty West Midlands Police officers, Terri Cave and Tracy Griffin, made an unexpected arrest while wearing animal onesies on their way to a fancy dress party. While walking through Coventry dressed as a monkey and a zebra, the officers heard a man allegedly shouting threatening abuse inside a Co-op supermarket. They immediately intervened—still in costume—and subdued the man after he exited the store, pinning him to the ground. The officers called for backup, and colleagues arrived in a Fiat Panda to transport the suspect to a police station. Solihull Police Station staff shared the story on Twitter, praising the officers: 'Off-duty officers dressed in zebra and monkey onesies arrested a violent man in the street — @SolihullPolice keeping you safe, whatever it takes.' 'A man threatening to kill people didn’t expect to be wrestled to the ground by our off-duty officer in a zebra onesie. We go that extra mile.' The suspect has been charged and is scheduled to appear again at Coventry Magistrates' Court next month. Superintendent Sally Bourner commended the officers for their swift and courageous action.

article_content: By Kieran Gill. Follow @@kie1410. Russia manager Fabio Capello launched a scathing critique of the referee after blaming his team’s elimination from the 2014 FIFA World Cup on a laser pointer aimed at goalkeeper Igor Akinfeev. The former England boss claimed the green beam of light from the crowd temporarily blinded Akinfeev just before Algeria’s equalizing goal, which knocked Russia out of the tournament. A furious Capello declared, 'All referees are against us,' criticizing officials for allowing the goal to stand despite what he described as clear interference. Islam Slimani’s 60th-minute equalizer came after a swinging left-foot free kick from Yacine Brahimi. Television footage showed a green laser dot moving near Akinfeev’s face moments before the kick. Russia needed a win to advance to the Round of 16 but settled for a 1-1 draw in their final Group H match, finishing the tournament with just two points and two goals scored. Capello, who previously led England at the 2010 World Cup, expressed frustration over what he saw as consistent bias against Russia — yet confirmed he would remain in his role until his contract expires in 2018. 'I will continue to work for the Russian national team, if they want me to continue,' he said. Russia had taken an early lead through Aleksandr Kokorin’s sixth-minute goal, but Algeria equalized through Slimani with 30 minutes remaining. This was Capello’s seventh World Cup match as a manager — and his only victory came in this tournament, despite earning a £6.6 million annual salary.

article_content: In less than a month, a second Republican senator has publicly endorsed same-sex marriage. Sen. Mark Kirk of Illinois, who returned to the Senate in January 2013 after recovering from a severe stroke in January 2012, stated that 'government has no place in the middle' of two people in love — regardless of gender. In a blog post, Kirk affirmed that same-sex couples deserve the right to civil marriage. Reflecting on his health journey, Kirk said, 'Our time on this Earth is limited, I know that better than most.' He added that his experience led him to return to public service with 'an open mind and greater respect for others.' Kirk has long supported LGBTQ+ rights, having voted to repeal 'Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell' and co-sponsored legislation to prohibit employment discrimination based on sexual orientation. Kirk’s endorsement follows that of Sen. Rob Portman of Ohio, who became the first Republican senator to support same-sex marriage in March 2013. Portman changed his position after his 21-year-old son, Will, came out as gay. 'It allowed me to think of this issue from a new perspective — as a dad who wants his son to have the same opportunities as his siblings,' Portman said. Portman cited his Christian faith and the Golden Rule as guiding principles behind his evolution. Meanwhile, Kirk mentioned consulting with his church in Cincinnati and former Vice President Dick Cheney, whose daughter is lesbian. Not all Republicans have followed suit. Rep. Matt Salmon of Arizona, whose son Matt Jr. is openly gay, continues to oppose same-sex marriage. 'I’m just not there,' Salmon told local media, citing longstanding social traditions and religious conviction. Despite their differences, Salmon and his son maintain a close relationship, with the younger Salmon noting, 'I love my father... I don’t pressure him to change his opinion.' Matt Salmon Jr., president of the Arizona Log Cabin Republicans, came out at age 14 and later left the LDS Church with his boyfriend due to its stance on homosexuality. Their story underscores the personal toll of religious dogma and the resilience of LGBTQ+ individuals within conservative families.

article_content: Once a regular at New York’s upscale Four Seasons, bestselling author Alexandra Penney now jokes about treating friends to Taco Bell — a darkly humorous shift reflecting her dramatic fall from wealth. After investing every dollar she’d saved since her teens with financier Bernard Madoff, she lost it all when his $50 billion Ponzi scheme collapsed in December 2008. Penney believed Madoff placed her money in ultra-safe Treasury bonds, and her confidence remained unshaken until her best friend and then her son called with the same devastating news: Madoff had been arrested. 'He’s a crook,' her son told her. For decades, Penney built her life through hard work — as a writer, editor, and artist — even helping launch the pink ribbon movement for breast cancer awareness. Her earnings allowed her to stop working and live as a full-time artist in SoHo. But with Madoff’s arrest, her world crumbled. She now faces the possibility of selling her Manhattan apartment, her beach cottage in Wainscott, and even cherished jewelry just to cover basic expenses. Though she still owns property and has a small bank balance, she admits she’s been 'Madoffed' — a term she coined for the feeling of being utterly destroyed by betrayal. Critics online mocked her for complaining, calling her a 'privileged princess,' but Penney insists she never inherited money or took alimony. Every asset she owns, she earned herself. Meanwhile, federal prosecutors revealed Madoff had prepared nearly 100 checks totaling $173 million right before his arrest — likely an effort to hide assets from victims. Madoff, now 70, remains under house arrest in his Manhattan penthouse, sparking outrage from Penney and others. 'Repulsive is too soft,' she says. 'He’s loathsome. This isn’t human behavior — it’s sociopathy.' Penney believes the real villain isn’t just Madoff, but the broken financial system that let him operate unchecked for years. Like the soufflé she was baking when she got the call — everything rose beautifully… then suddenly collapsed. Now, she’s picking up her pen again, determined to write her way back to stability.

article_content: It was supposed to be a festive cruise to experience the delights of Amsterdam’s Christmas markets. But after four days at sea, the closest passengers got to the Netherlands was a view from the ship’s deck. Holidaymakers were forced to return empty-handed to Southampton last night after spending four days circling the English Channel due to severe weather. Around 2,100 passengers aboard the Queen Elizabeth were furious at the decision to turn back—a move that sparked what some described as a 'mutiny' among frustrated travelers. They stormed the reception desk, clapping and chanting, 'We want the captain!' demanding answers. Matters worsened when Cunard, the operator of the Queen Elizabeth, announced passengers would receive only $75 (approximately £48) in onboard spending credit as compensation for their £400 tickets. Passenger Charmaine Lynch, 50, from Aldershot, had booked the cruise to celebrate her parents’ 55th wedding anniversary. Her father had been unwell, and she saw the trip as a meaningful pre-Christmas gift. 'It was my parents’ first trip with Cunard,' she told MailOnline. 'I explained everything to them. Don’t I look stupid now?' Alongside the missed destination, Lynch and others endured a persistent diesel odor in their cabins. 'It was not Cunard’s finest hour,' she said. 'I’ve taken other cruises with them—this wasn’t their usual standard.' She noted that while the Marco Polo had successfully reached port, the Queen Elizabeth received only one daily update from the captain, followed by 24-hour silences. The compensation offer came late—and passengers later learned the onboard shops closed at 7 p.m., rendering the credit useless for non-drinkers. Steve Gordon, 42, from Stratford-upon-Avon, a loyal Cunard customer, said the diesel smell permeated the ship and disrupted meals. 'We had to grab our food and leave because it was so crowded. And when we couldn’t dock, updates came from crew—not the captain.' He added that staff seemed unprepared for Cunard’s typical clientele, assuming the voyage would attract 'booze cruisers' instead of experienced travelers. 'They didn’t turn on the bells and whistles,' he said. 'We got gold badges upon boarding—but I’d have preferred robes, slippers, and proper pillows for my mother.' Many passengers reported minimal entertainment beyond a single oversubscribed pub quiz. Sophie Humphrey, 30, and her mother Eve, 64, paid £389 each and called the experience 'outrageous.' Even before the weather issue, passengers complained of a strong diesel smell near the front decks, making casinos and shops unpleasant. Cunard responded by stating all onboard facilities remained open and that two alternative ports were considered but rejected due to similar weather conditions. They framed the £48 credit as a 'gesture of goodwill.'

article_content: Polluted environments, especially those with poor air quality, can lead to respiratory conditions such as emphysema, lung cancer, and heart disease. In areas of India like Delhi-NCR, Mumbai, and even Pune—where air pollution remains persistent—it is critical to take actionable steps to combat it. Long-term exposure has also been linked to damage in the kidneys, liver, brain, nervous system, and other vital organs. Follow these evidence-informed measures, recommended by Dr. Mickey Mehta, a holistic health expert: * Regular exercise and yoga asanas can help prevent many pollution-related ailments. Dr. Mehta notes that high-intensity activities like jumping jacks and spot jogging improve heart rate and lung capacity. Practicing yoga asanas with controlled breathing is equally beneficial. * Cover your nasal passages when stepping outdoors in polluted or crowded areas. * Practice Jalaneti (nasal irrigation) and Kapalbhati pranayama to clear pollutants from the nasal passages. Anulom-Vilom (alternate nostril breathing) is also highly recommended. * Most importantly, rest. Shavasana—the corpse pose—allows the body to enter deep relaxation, reducing stress and enabling the immune system to function optimally. 'The body naturally combats infections more effectively when at rest, and immunity improves,' says Dr. Mehta. * Proper nutrition is essential to fuel the body’s detoxification processes. As Shivani Bajwa, founder of YogaSutra Holistic Living, explains, the ability to neutralize airborne and plastic-derived toxins varies by individual. * Boost your antioxidant levels by incorporating: curcumin from turmeric, sulforaphane from cruciferous vegetables, quercetin from onions and green tea, giloy, stinging nettle root, and oregano oil. * Dr. Mehta suggests these safe home remedies—if you have no known allergies:   - Add 1/4 teaspoon pippali and 1/2 teaspoon crushed bay leaf to a cup of green tea to soothe your respiratory system.   - Mix 1/4 cup fresh onion juice with 1 teaspoon honey and a pinch of black pepper, and consume daily for relief.   - Boil half a teaspoon each of fresh ginger and licorice root (mulethi) in tea for immediate comfort. * Reduce inflammation caused by vitamin C deficiency by increasing intake of citrus fruits, bell peppers, and leafy greens. * Improve lung capacity to help flush out toxins before they enter the bloodstream. Dr. Bajwa recommends adding Vitamin E (specifically the tocotrienol form) for individuals with breathing difficulties. * Intermittent fasting for 14–15 hours, once or twice weekly, may help stabilize blood sugar levels disrupted by chronic inflammation and infection. * Avoid synthetic products—including hair dyes, GMO foods, and chemical skin treatments—that contribute to endocrine disruption. Bajwa warns these substances may elevate estrogen levels, leading to digestive issues and menstrual irregularities.

article_content: In a world dominated by scrolling and notifications, a small team in Glasgow is bringing back the quiet pleasure of holding a real newspaper — but with a modern twist. Meet PaperLater: a service that lets you pick your favorite articles from blogs, journals, and news sites, then turns them into a custom-printed newspaper delivered right to your doorstep. Whether it’s a deep-dive interview, a medical research paper, or a long-form essay, you can save them with a simple click of a browser button. Once you’ve collected enough, PaperLater arranges everything neatly into an 8- to 24-page paper, adds a personalized cover showing the total word count and number of pieces, prints it on classic newsprint, and mails it out. Launched earlier this year by the Newspaper Club, the service was born from a simple observation: not everything reads well on a screen. Founder Tom Taylor says many people — even younger ones who’ve never bought a paper — still crave the rhythm of turning pages. It’s not meant for breaking news; the few-day wait is part of the charm. Since starting with just 40–50 testers in January, the company now prints over 100 issues every week. Right now, it’s only available in the UK, costing £4.99 per edition — a small price, perhaps, for a tangible slice of the digital world.

article_content: The U.S. government’s demand for information on Google users reached a new high in the first half of 2013, according to Google’s latest transparency report. The tech giant received 10,918 requests from U.S. authorities targeting 21,683 user accounts — the highest number ever recorded in a single six-month period. The United States remains the world’s leading source of such requests, with an 83% compliance rate — meaning Google provided user data in the vast majority of cases. India, Germany, and France followed, each submitting between 2,000 and 3,000 requests. For the first time, Google broke down U.S. legal requests by type: subpoenas, warrants, wiretap orders, PEN register orders, and emergency disclosures. Subpoenas were the most common, followed by warrants. Only seven wiretap requests were made. Since Google began tracking government data requests in 2009, the total volume has doubled. This marks the company’s eighth transparency report since it began public disclosures in 2010. Google has set the standard for tech industry transparency, inspiring rivals like Facebook, Twitter, Yahoo, and Apple to release similar reports. These companies are also urging the U.S. government to permit greater disclosure of requests made under the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA). Google continues to voice frustration over U.S. restrictions on what it can reveal about national security inquiries. 'We believe it's your right to know what kinds of requests and how many each government is making of us and other companies,' said Google Legal Director Richard Salgado in a blog post.

article_content: After a turbulent three-year spell at West Ham, Ravel Morrison’s contract with the club has been officially terminated by mutual consent. The 22-year-old midfielder, who has signed a pre-contract agreement with Serie A side Lazio, is now a free agent. However, under FIFA rules prohibiting players from registering with more than two clubs in a single season, Morrison cannot make his debut for Lazio—or any other team—until next season. His last appearance for West Ham came in a 3-1 home defeat to Southampton on August 31, and he made just two competitive outings under manager Sam Allardyce this campaign. Persistent disciplinary concerns led to loan spells at Birmingham City, Queens Park Rangers, and Cardiff City—the latter terminated early in December. Over his time at Upton Park, Morrison played 24 matches and netted five goals since joining in January 2012. Once touted as a generational talent by Manchester United’s academy and admired by Sir Alex Ferguson, Morrison left Old Trafford in 2012 after a contract dispute. He recently posted images on Instagram from Rome, wearing a Lazio jersey with the caption ‘Ravel 4,’ confirming his move. Although several Premier League clubs expressed interest, he chose to pursue a fresh beginning in Italy, where he completed a medical and finalized his transfer. Across his senior career, Morrison has amassed 81 appearances and scored 14 goals, including an FA Youth Cup win with Manchester United in 2011. With his future now focused on Lazio, he aims to reignite his career on the European stage.

article_content: CNN — Brazilian World Cup hero Ronaldo has announced he will retire from professional football at the end of 2011. The 33-year-old striker, who played a pivotal role in Brazil’s 1994 and 2002 World Cup victories — scoring twice in the 2002 final against Germany — currently plays for Corinthians in his native Brazil. In a statement posted on the club’s official website, www.corinthians.com, Ronaldo confirmed he will honor the remaining two years of his contract before hanging up his boots. 'I renewed for two more years, and those will be the last,' he said after morning training on Monday. Ronaldo boasts an illustrious international career with Brazil, netting 62 goals in 97 appearances and setting a World Cup record with his 15th goal during the 2006 tournament, when Brazil exited in the quarterfinals. Despite his age and a history of serious injuries, he still harbors hopes of being selected for the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, though he acknowledges the challenge of convincing coach Dunga to include him. 'It’s still something that could happen for me,' he said. Currently focused on the Copa Libertadores, Ronaldo has remained sharp, scoring 12 goals in 20 appearances to help Corinthians win the Paulista Championship. 'I am determined. I want to give my best, have fun, and I hope to finish by winning the Libertadores,' he added. When he retires, Ronaldo will be remembered as one of the greatest footballers of all time. His career goal-scoring rate approached one goal per game across top European clubs including PSV Eindhoven, Barcelona, Real Madrid, Inter Milan, and AC Milan. A three-time FIFA World Player of the Year, Ronaldo began his career with Cruzeiro in Brazil. After a severe knee injury while at AC Milan nearly ended his career, he briefly trained with Flamengo before joining Corinthians — where he plans to serve as an ambassador at Parque São Jorge after retirement.

article_content: Khizri Kurazov, a Russian corporal assigned to Unit 3737 of the Russian Guard, suffered severe injuries in Ukraine after a mine accidentally detonated due to improper handling by fellow soldiers. Although he was wounded in a war zone, Russian military policy denies him the $30,000 lump-sum payment meant for combat-injured troops because the harm came from within his own unit—not from Ukrainian forces. Medical documentation from March 14 confirmed the injury’s origin, and an internal probe on May 25 ruled it a result of negligence, not frontline combat. Kurazov, a contract soldier, applied for the compensation Russia has provided since early 2022, but his claim was rejected first by the Nalchik Garrison court in June and later upheld by the Southern District Military Court in Rostov-on-Don on September 8. The judges agreed that eligibility requires direct engagement with enemy forces, though they affirmed Kurazov could pursue other forms of aid. He contended that any Russian soldier hurt in Ukraine, regardless of cause, deserves support—but the courts held firm. His case mirrors that of Aziz Magomedov, another soldier denied payment after receiving initial treatment at a civilian hospital, as reported by Radio Free Liberty. The Russian Defense Ministry has yet to respond to inquiries.

article_content: By Bianca London. PUBLISHED: 10:05 EST, 19 March 2013. | UPDATED: 10:06 EST, 19 March 2013. The phrase 'I'm eating for two' has burdened many pregnant women with excess weight to lose after childbirth. Although official guidelines recommend gaining no more than two stone during pregnancy, it's easy to overindulge during those nine months. Recent statistics show that up to 15% of mothers are obese during pregnancy—jeopardizing not only their own health but also that of their unborn children. Hazel Frewin certainly embraced 'eating for two'—gaining a staggering 8st 5lbs during her pregnancy, which rendered her clinically obese. After giving birth, she shed nearly half her body weight through disciplined diet and exercise—including pole dancing. At 25, from Poole, Dorset, Hazel weighed 19st (approximately 266 lbs) at the time of her daughter Ivy’s birth, having gone from a size 12 to a maternity size 24. Ivy weighed a substantial 10lb 3oz. Overwhelmed with guilt, Hazel blamed herself for her baby’s size. After a two-year journey, Hazel has returned to a size 12 and now weighs 10st 10lb (approximately 150 lbs). Her transformation included adopting a healthier diet and incorporating pole dancing into her routine—even installing a pole at home for practice. Hazel said: 'I hope my story stops other pregnant women from making the same mistake. When I was pregnant, I happily indulged every craving because I was 'eating for two.' I ignored how much I was gaining—but as soon as my baby was born, reality hit.' She added: 'Not only was I still huge after delivery, but Ivy was much larger than expected, which meant I couldn't have the birth I wanted and required emergency surgery.' During her first pregnancy, Hazel had sailed through without issue. But after miscarrying her second baby in early 2010, she turned to food for comfort. 'I was so crushed I didn't care about my diet or myself. I ate whatever I wanted, whenever I wanted—and told myself it was okay because I’d be pregnant again soon.' Within months, she gained two stone. When she became pregnant again, her joy overshadowed concerns about weight. 'I was so happy and relieved—I didn’t care about the scale. All I cared about was my baby.' Her cravings were intense: chocolate bars, biscuits, cakes, milkshakes. 'Nobody batted an eyelid. People smiled and told me to enjoy it.' At seven months, she developed Symphysis Pubis Dysfunction (SPD)—a painful condition linked to excessive weight gain—that left her nearly bedridden. She ate more to cope. By April 2011, she weighed 19st at 5ft 4in. She was denied a water birth because she was too large for the pool. After a six-hour labor, Ivy was born—so large that midwives gasped. 'She looked like a three-month-old baby,' Hazel recalled. Once home, Hazel weighed 18st 2lb. 'I felt sickened, ashamed, and plain fat,' she said. Too embarrassed to seek help, she resolved to lose weight alone. In August 2011, she joined a slimming club and adopted a structured eating plan. 'It was hard after months of constant eating, but the group kept me accountable. I filled up on salads and vegetables.' Today, Hazel is fit, confident, and healthy. Her daily meals now include: breakfast of Muller Light yogurt and melon; lunch of feta cheese salad with light dressing; dinner of roasted vegetables, Quorn, and boiled potatoes; snacks of fruit and yogurt; and drinks of water and herbal tea. 'The weight took months to gain—and almost two years to lose. 'Eating for two' ruined what should have been the happiest time with my newborn—and I’ve spent the last two years paying for it.'

article_content: A fraudster couple who used £1.1 million stolen from a hospital to fund their decadent lifestyle were jailed yesterday. Anne and Andrew Baker spent the money on landscaping their garden and installing cascading waterfalls and fountains at their Grade II-listed 'dream home' in Cornwall. The couple also purchased a luxury villa in Bodrum, Turkey, using funds Anne Baker embezzled from her position as a manager in the radiology department of Princess Grace Hospital in Marylebone, West London. Andrew and Anne Baker were sentenced to a total of 10 years in prison for a 13-year fraud that netted them £1.14 million from hospital funds. Anne Baker, 61, orchestrated a 'breathtaking' scheme over nearly three decades, inventing a fictional 'Dr. Baker' and submitting 131 fraudulent invoices for radiology consultancy services, all approved under her maiden name, Anne Fitzpatrick. She concealed the theft for 13 years—from 1999 to 2012—until an internal audit exposed the nonexistent consultant. The couple spent £88,882 on renovations at Manderley, their historic 2.5-acre estate, and £94,000 on the Turkish villa. They hid £85,000 in two Turkish bank accounts and £25,000 in a gun cupboard at their 16th-century home. They also owned two Jaguars and an Aston Martin and marketed Manderley as a premium wedding venue featuring a 30-foot koi carp lake, an exotic bird aviary, and a pitch-and-putt golf course. Andrew Baker, 65, was convicted of two counts of money laundering. Though he claimed ignorance, the court found his assertion that the money came from a flat sale and a £132,000 retirement bonus 'patently untrue.' Anne Baker admitted to false accounting and money laundering and has since been declared bankrupt. The private healthcare company that operated the hospital has initiated legal action to recover the stolen funds. Anne was sentenced to four years; Andrew received six years, reflecting his decision to plead not guilty and proceed to trial.

article_content: In a bold move to shake up British takeaway culture, acclaimed French chef Bruno Loubet has introduced what’s being called Britain’s first Michelin-starred delivery service. No longer do you need to book a table at a fancy restaurant to enjoy refined French cooking—now, dishes like duck confit, tarragon chicken fricassie, and caramelised fennel gratin can be ordered online and delivered right to your door. Loubet, who once held a Michelin star as head chef at London’s Four Seasons Inn on the Park, now runs Bistro Bruno Loubet at The Zetter Hotel in Clerkenwell. He’s teamed up with Housebites, a local delivery platform serving London and Brighton, to bring his elevated cuisine to everyday diners. To ensure quality, he personally trained 35 chefs to replicate his recipes exactly in a central kitchen. The menu blends rustic charm with precision: slow-roasted pork belly with aromatic mustard salsa (£11.95), a rich gratin of squash, courgette, and garlic confit topped with béarnaise (£9.95), and duck confit glazed in honey and wholegrain mustard, served with beetroot marmalade and sherry vinegar sauce (£12.95). Even dessert gets the gourmet treatment—French toast soaked in cider vinegar and crowned with sticky toffee apple, all for £5.95. Loubet says the goal isn’t just to sell food—it’s to change perceptions. 'For too long, French cooking has been locked away in expensive restaurants,' he explains. 'But it doesn’t have to be. It’s simple, deeply satisfying, and full of soul. We’re bringing that energy home.' With this service, he hopes to dethrone greasy takeaways and prove that good food doesn’t need a white tablecloth to be extraordinary.

article_content: Imagine running an optical fibre to any point on Earth—or even into space. That’s the vision of Professor Howard Milchberg, a physicist at the University of Maryland, who believes air waveguides could make it possible. These temporary, laser-created channels in the atmosphere could guide light over vast distances without signal loss, enabling breakthroughs in long-range communication, atmospheric monitoring, and remote sensing. Traditional optical fibres rely on glass cores and cladding to trap light through total internal reflection. But they’re limited by physical installation and power capacity. Air waveguides solve this by using ultra-short, high-power laser pulses to generate filaments. As these filaments race through the air, they heat it, creating narrow trails of low-density air—effectively forming a 'pipe' with a lower refractive index than the surrounding air. This low-density channel acts like the cladding of a fibre optic cable, keeping light focused and intense within the central core. Though each filament lasts only a trillionth of a second, the resulting air channel persists for a few milliseconds—a lifetime in laser terms. In lab tests, researchers fired four filaments in a square formation to create a stable, hollow waveguide. They then directed a laser spark through it, successfully transmitting a signal 1 metre away with 50% more strength than an unguided beam. While this may sound modest, the implications grow exponentially over longer distances. At 100 times the current test range, the signal enhancement could be transformative. The team aims to extend the waveguide’s reach to 50 metres, paving the way for applications like atmospheric chemistry analysis near nuclear reactors, high-resolution Lidar mapping, and potentially, interplanetary laser communication to Mars. As Professor Milchberg puts it: 'It’s like you could unreel a physical optical fibre at the speed of light, place it next to something you want to measure remotely, and have the signal come right back.'

article_content: BEIJING, China (CNN) — A U.S. surveillance ship, the USNS Impeccable, violated Chinese and international laws during patrols more than 100 nautical miles (approximately 185 kilometers) off the Chinese coast over the weekend, according to China’s state-run media. The Pentagon released photos showing two Chinese trawlers forcing the Impeccable to make an emergency stop. China has lodged serious representations with the United States after the USNS Impeccable conducted activities in China’s exclusive economic zone in the South China Sea,” said Ma Zhaoxu, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Ministry. “We demand that the United States immediately cease such activities and take effective measures to prevent similar incidents.” This comes after the Pentagon stated Monday that Chinese vessels harassed the U.S. ship on Sunday, marking the latest in a series of ‘increasingly aggressive’ encounters. The Pentagon said five Chinese vessels shadowed and maneuvered dangerously close to the Impeccable in what appeared to be a coordinated effort to disrupt its routine operations in international waters. According to the Pentagon, Chinese crew members aboard two vessels came within 50 feet of the Impeccable, waved Chinese flags, and ordered the ship to leave. When their intentions remained unclear, the Impeccable deployed its fire hoses defensively. In response, Chinese crew members removed their clothing down to their underwear and closed to within 25 feet. After the Impeccable peacefully signaled its intent to depart, two Chinese vessels positioned themselves directly ahead, forcing the U.S. ship to execute an emergency ‘all stop’ to avoid collision. The Chinese vessels also dropped pieces of wood into the water directly in front of the Impeccable’s path. A Pentagon spokesperson called the incident ‘one of the most aggressive actions we’ve seen in some time,’ adding that Chinese crew members used poles to attempt to snag the Impeccable’s submerged acoustic equipment. The U.S. Embassy in Beijing formally protested the incident to the Chinese government. The Impeccable, a 281.5-foot oceanographic vessel, is unarmed and crewed by 20 civilian mariners, five technicians, and up to 20 Navy personnel. It operates at 3 knots while towing its surveillance array, gathering underwater acoustic data. The Chinese vessels involved included a naval intelligence ship, a maritime fisheries patrol vessel, a state oceanographic patrol vessel, and two small Chinese-flagged trawlers. The Pentagon cited three prior incidents of alleged harassment, the first occurring last Wednesday.

article_content: A 14-year-old boy from Mississippi, Blake Thompson, along with his alleged romantic partner—25-year-old police officer Jasper Pittman—and two other men, Greg Fortenberry, 26, and LeJerrious Perkins, 17, have been arrested in connection with the murder of Blake’s father, Kenneth Thompson, 53. According to the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, the suspects lured Kenneth Thompson to a location in Pike County on Sunday, where they slashed his throat, killing him. Blake, who had recently run away from home, allegedly enlisted Pittman’s help to bury the body in a shallow grave on Pittman’s property in McComb and burn Kenneth’s pickup truck. Police have charged Pittman with sexual battery, alleging he sexually penetrated the minor. Authorities confirm that Blake had been staying at Pittman’s residence with Fortenberry and Perkins. Family members, including Blake’s aunt Lillian Mallard, described Kenneth Thompson as a devoted, hardworking father who had been striving to keep his son out of trouble since the death of his wife five years earlier. Kenneth, who worked full-time at a local Wal-Mart distribution center and cared for his grandchildren daily, was reportedly searching for Blake when he was killed. A family member spotted Blake and two others in the Wal-Mart parking lot and alerted police. The burned truck was later found on land owned by one of Pittman’s relatives. Pittman, who had served as a police officer for only two weeks in Brookhaven and 11 months in McComb, was terminated following his arrest. All four suspects face multiple charges, including murder, conspiracy to commit murder, arson, and conspiracy to commit arson. Blake was charged as an adult. Pittman additionally faces charges of accessory after the fact and sexual battery.
