article_content: Clutching a razor-sharp bayonet, British infantryman Rifleman Stuart Gray peered over the edge of a trench — not into the horrors of the Western Front, but into a meticulously preserved replica buried beneath the heathland of Gosport, Hampshire. A century after World War I began, this site, spanning the equivalent of 17 football pitches, has emerged as the UK’s best-preserved example of a full-scale WWI training battlefield. Hidden for decades under gorse and bracken, the complex features two opposing trench systems, supply lines, dugouts, and a wide No Man’s Land — all designed to simulate the brutal reality of trench warfare. Here, tens of thousands of soldiers from Britain, Canada, and the United States trained under grueling conditions: dodging live fire, donning gas masks, sprinting through zig-zag trenches, and enduring sleep deprivation and poor rations. The site was rediscovered in 2013 by Rob Harper, a conservation officer with Gosport Borough Council, who noticed unusual linear patterns in a 1950s aerial photograph. His investigation revealed an astonishingly intact network of trenches, untouched since the war’s end. For Gray — a veteran of Afghanistan — standing in these trenches offered a sobering glimpse into the physical and psychological trials faced by his predecessors. 'It’s difficult walking up and down these trenches today,' he said. 'To do it in a war? That’s something else. Going over the top? Pretty scary. I have so much respect for those men.' TV historian Dan Snow called the discovery 'unprecedented' in the UK. 'This wasn’t just basic drilling,' he noted. 'They were preparing men to break through one of history’s deadliest military stalemates — with real weapons, real noise, real fear.' Wayne Cocroft of English Heritage added that while Tudor castles and Victorian railroads are well-recorded, the built heritage of WWI on British soil has largely vanished — until now. The site is now central to the Home Front Legacy 1914-18 project — a collaboration between English Heritage and the Council for British Archaeology — aimed at mapping and preserving forgotten wartime sites across the UK: drill halls, prisoner-of-war camps, gun emplacements, and more. Their goal: connect national expertise with community memory to honor those who trained, worked, and waited at home — so others could fight abroad.

article_content: The U.S. men’s soccer team has decided to cancel its upcoming friendly against Egypt in Cairo, citing growing political unrest in the country. Originally set for February 9, the match was meant to be a showdown between the Americans and Egypt, Africa’s most decorated national team. U.S. Soccer President Sunil Gulati said both sides agreed the decision was necessary for safety reasons. 'We were really looking forward to this game,' he said, 'but the situation on the ground made it clear that proceeding wasn’t responsible.' He thanked the Egyptian Football Association and the U.S. State Department for their collaboration during the review process. Meanwhile, the U.S. squad will shift focus to two high-profile matches in March — hosting World Cup champions Argentina on the 26th in New Jersey, followed by Paraguay in Nashville three days later. These games are part of their buildup to the CONCACAF Gold Cup this June, which will bring together 12 teams from across North and Central America and the Caribbean. In Egypt, protests against longtime President Hosni Mubarak have intensified over the past week, with citizens demanding political reform after 30 years of rule. In response, the U.S. has deployed additional armed Marine security forces to bolster protection at its embassy in Cairo.

article_content: In Longmont, Colorado, Sue Frederick helps people uncover their dream careers—not with resumes or job boards, but with intuition, numerology, and vivid mental images. A former journalist and magazine editor, Frederick says she’s had psychic sensitivities since childhood, though she kept them private until her mid-40s, when she made a bold switch: trading newsrooms for soul-searching sessions. Today, she guides thousands of clients—mostly people feeling stuck or recently laid off—through one-hour phone calls priced at $250. To begin, clients share their birthdate. Frederick reduces the numbers to a single digit, which she says reveals their core life energy and purpose. Then, she meditates and claims to see clear visuals: people doing work that lights them up, whether it’s painting, coding, teaching, or running a bakery. She insists these aren’t random guesses, but glimpses of the path already within them. 'You already have everything you need,' she tells them. 'It’s not about becoming someone else—it’s about remembering who you truly are.' Frederick challenges the idea that you must choose between financial stability and joy. 'You don’t have to live on rice and yoga mats to be fulfilled,' she says. Instead, she argues that when you align your work with your deepest self, abundance follows—even if that means starting a podcast from your garage or selling handmade candles online. She ties these awakenings to nine-year cycles, suggesting that periods of job loss or discontent aren’t failures, but cosmic nudges toward reinvention. Her home, filled with Ganesh statues beside soccer cleats and smoothie blenders, reflects her blend of spirituality and everyday life. With her book, 'I See Your Dream Job,' and seminars selling out months ahead, Frederick isn’t just preaching transformation—she’s living it. And she believes this moment, even amid economic uncertainty, is the perfect time for anyone ready to stop surviving—and start thriving.

article_content: Scientists have found that traditional oral stories passed down by Australian Aboriginal peoples may be among the oldest accurate historical records in human history. These narratives, preserved across hundreds of generations, describe dramatic environmental changes that occurred at the end of the last ice age—approximately 10,000 years ago. Many Aboriginal groups across Australia recount remarkably consistent tales of coastal landscapes now submerged beneath the sea. For instance, stories from northeastern Queensland describe how the Great Barrier Reef once formed part of the mainland, while Port Phillip Bay in Victoria was once fertile hunting ground for kangaroos and opossums. The Yidindji and Goonganji peoples recall that Fitzroy Island was once known as 'gabar'—a lower arm extending from the mainland—and that nearby Green Island was once four times its current size. They also remember a place called 'mudaga,' named after pencil cedar trees that once grew between Fitzroy Island and King Beach. On Kangaroo Island, the Ngarrindjeri people tell of an ancestral hero, Ngurunderi, who chased his wives inland and raised the sea in anger, drowning them and turning them into the rocky outcrops visible today. Geological evidence suggests this event corresponds to a time when sea levels were roughly 30 meters lower than today—placing the origin of the story between 9,800 and 10,650 years ago. Stories from the Tiwi Islands speak of an elder woman whose passage triggered a flood that separated Melville and Bathurst Islands from the mainland—possibly dating back 7,500 to 8,900 years. In Western Australia, Aboriginal accounts describe how fires split the land, allowing the sea to flood Rottnest, Carnac, and Garden Islands—events estimated to have occurred 7,500 to 8,900 years ago. Dr. Nick Reid, a linguist at the University of New England, and Professor Patrick Nunn, a geographer at the University of the Sunshine Coast, analyzed 18 distinct Aboriginal stories and found striking alignment with known paleogeographical data. Crucially, none of the stories describe receding seas exposing land—only rising waters submerging former terrain. The geographic dispersion of these accounts, their local specificity, and their shared core details make it highly unlikely they stem from a single invented source. These findings challenge long-held anthropological assumptions that oral traditions cannot reliably persist beyond 1,000 years. Instead, they suggest that Indigenous knowledge systems, maintained with extraordinary care and precision, may preserve environmental memory for millennia. Similar patterns may exist elsewhere: oral histories among the Klamath people of Oregon are estimated to be 7,700 years old, and researchers speculate that comparable traditions may endure in Indigenous communities across India and beyond.

article_content: Managing Ebola isn’t just about fear—it’s about discipline. While it doesn’t spread through the air like SARS or MERS, Ebola is deadlier because it passes through direct contact with blood, sweat, or other bodily fluids. The 2003 SARS outbreak in Toronto, where 224 people fell ill and 38 died, was a wake-up call. That crisis didn’t just vanish—it reshaped how hospitals prepare. Today, every hospital screens incoming patients for recent travel, arms staff with proper protective gear, and trains them relentlessly on how to wear and remove it safely. Hand hygiene isn’t optional anymore; it’s non-negotiable. Whether it’s soap and water or alcohol-based sanitizer, clean hands are the first and last line of defense. Lessons from West Africa, where teams now use a ‘buddy system’ to double-check PPE use, are being brought home. Governments responded after SARS by funding better isolation units, updating hospital accreditation rules, and mandating clear emergency plans. Communication became a priority too—making sure patients, staff, and communities all know what’s happening and why. Months before any Ebola case arrived, Canadian hospitals started working with public health officials to build these safeguards. We don’t wish for an outbreak—but thanks to SARS, we’re not caught off guard anymore.

article_content: SAN FRANCISCO — Over the past few days, President Joe Biden and other global leaders have met with Silicon Valley’s top executives in San Francisco, centering their discussions on artificial intelligence — a technology poised to redefine the world, for better or worse. Despite the concentration of intellectual power gathered for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, no definitive answer emerged to the critical question: Will AI propel humanity to unprecedented heights, or trigger a dystopian collapse? ‘The world is at an inflection point — this is not hyperbole,’ Biden declared Thursday at a CEO summit held alongside APEC. ‘The decisions we make today will shape the trajectory of the world for decades.’ Unsurprisingly, most tech CEOs present expressed strong confidence in AI’s capacity to boost worker productivity and elevate global living standards. None were more enthusiastic than Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, whose company has invested over $10 billion in OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT. Nadella compared AI’s potential impact to that of the personal computer in the 1980s, the internet in the 1990s, and smartphones in the 2000s. ‘We finally have a way to interact with computing using natural language — a technology that understands us, not the other way around,’ Nadella said. ‘As our interactions grow more intuitive, computers will increasingly perceive our intent and make sense of the world around us.’ Google CEO Sundar Pichai, whose company is embedding AI deeply into its search platform, echoed this optimism. ‘We must work hard to harness it,’ he said. ‘But that’s true of every major technological shift — the Industrial Revolution, the digital age. We can learn from history.’ Investors have shared this confidence: Microsoft and Alphabet Inc., Google’s parent company, have each seen their stock prices rise more than 50% this year, driven largely by AI momentum. Together, these gains have generated over $1.6 trillion in new shareholder wealth. Yet perspectives beyond Silicon Valley remain cautious. ‘Everyone knows how to spell AI, but few know what to do with it,’ said Condoleezza Rice, director of Stanford’s Hoover Institution. ‘The benefits are clear — but so are the dangers of misuse.’ Robert Moritz, global chair of PwC, warned of widespread job displacement. ‘Companies have historically retrained workers after technological disruptions,’ he noted. ‘If we fail to do so again, we risk social unrest we simply cannot afford.’ San Francisco, hosting APEC, is banking on AI-driven investment and job growth — particularly from startups like OpenAI and Anthropic — to revitalize its economy after the pandemic-induced exodus of remote workers. ‘We’re in the spring of another innovation boom,’ said Mayor London Breed, highlighting that eight of the world’s largest AI firms are headquartered in the city. Amid these hopes, Elon Musk — with an estimated net worth of $240 billion — founded xAI this summer, citing existential risks from unchecked AI development. He had been scheduled to speak at the CEO summit with Salesforce’s Marc Benioff but canceled due to an undisclosed conflict. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called AI ‘the greatest leap forward of any technological revolution so far’ — but stressed the urgent need for safeguards. ‘I truly believe the world will rise to the occasion,’ he said. ‘Everyone wants to do the right thing.’

article_content: Nancy Wilson, an author and advocate of Christian parenting, is married to Douglas Wilson, pastor of Christ Church in Moscow, Idaho. In a video, she details her method of disciplining her 3-4-year-old daughter, Rachel, after the child responded with indifference — 'Is it time to go?' — when Wilson arrived to pick her up from a neighbor’s house. Wilson states she later administered a spanking, explaining to the child that the expected response upon her arrival should be, 'Hi, Mom!' The next time Rachel visited the neighbor, Wilson reviewed the expectation, and upon returning, the child greeted her enthusiastically: 'Yes! Mom is here! Yeah, yeah!' Wilson frames this as successful behavioral training. However, this approach contradicts decades of child development research, which consistently links corporal punishment to increased aggression, antisocial behavior, physical harm, anxiety, depression, and weakened parent-child trust. Experts warn that children disciplined through fear may learn compliance through coercion, not respect or emotional security. The video, shared on social media, has drawn widespread criticism for normalizing physical punishment as a tool for teaching basic social etiquette.

article_content: In May 2013, an 18-year-old girl from Cathedral City, California, named Jackie Rosas, took action after seeing a distressing post on Tumblr from a stranger — a 16-year-old who wrote she intended to die by suicide. With only the girl’s first name and a link to her blog, Rosas contacted local police, initiating an urgent, cross-country investigation. Armed with little more than a name and a clue that the girl was a color guard, Cathedral City Police Officer Kelly Nava enlisted the help of school resource officer Heather Olsen and Assistant Principal Karen Dimick. Despite initial dead ends, Dimick discovered a Twitter profile linked to a marching band in Union Township, New Jersey. This breakthrough led officers to the girl’s address. At approximately 1:30 a.m., local police in New Jersey arrived at the home and found the teen unconscious after consuming a large quantity of prescription pills. She was rushed to a hospital and placed on a psychiatric hold. Rosas, who had followed the girl’s Tumblr page for nearly a year and witnessed ongoing cyberbullying, said she knew the post was genuine. 'I kind of cried,' she told reporters. 'I was happy to know that I saved someone’s life. It happened at random — and it’s an amazing feeling knowing you can help someone thousands of miles away.' Officer Olsen reflected on the gravity of the moment: 'Life is so precious. It is worth every effort to save.' The collaborative effort between a compassionate stranger, school staff, and law enforcement ultimately prevented a tragedy.

article_content: Abigail Hernandez, a 15-year-old from New Hampshire, has been safely reunited with her family after disappearing nine months ago. She vanished on October 9, 2013, from her home in North Conway. Her mother, Zenya Hernandez, said in a statement released by the New Hampshire Attorney General's Office: 'We are the happiest people on earth.' Authorities have not disclosed details about the circumstances of her disappearance, as the investigation remains ongoing. Shortly after vanishing, Abigail mailed a letter to her family, postmarked October 23 and received on November 6. Law enforcement withheld its contents to prevent copycat letters that could hinder the investigation. In December, Zenya Hernandez published an emotional open letter, pleading with Abigail to come home for Christmas. She included a hand-drawn Christmas tree and wrote: 'I thank God every day that you are alive! I miss hearing your voice and your sense of humor. Please let me know what I can do to help you. Please come home for Christmas.' She also posted online: 'I will ALWAYS love you. I will ALWAYS have hope. I will NEVER stop looking. Love, MOM.' Police initially believed Abigail returned home after school, but later confirmed she never arrived. Her last known location was near Cranmore Mountain, about two miles from home, where her cellphone last transmitted a signal at 6:30 p.m.—four hours after she was last seen leaving Kennett High School. Authorities released images of a necklace and purse she carried that day, hoping someone might recognize them. They emphasized that Abigail had no income and likely relied on someone else for support. FBI investigator Kieran Ramsey expressed concern that while Abigail may have left voluntarily, she is now being manipulated or controlled—comparing her potential situation to victims of the Cleveland kidnappings. The FBI offered a $20,000 reward for information leading to her safe return. Abigail celebrated her 15th birthday on October 12, 2013, while still missing.

article_content: Last night, Ian Katz, the newly appointed editor of BBC’s Newsnight, publicly acknowledged a major misstep after accidentally posting a disrespectful tweet about Labour MP Rachel Reeves. The message, which he believed was a private direct message, instead went out to his 26,000 followers, calling Reeves 'boring snoring' and mocking her appearance on the show. The comment sparked immediate outrage across political circles and social media. In response, Katz issued several apologies — first online, then in a rare on-air admission during the broadcast, where '#fail' appeared next to his Twitter handle in the closing credits. Labour officials were furious, condemning the remark as damaging to the BBC’s reputation for impartiality. They demanded a full written apology, stressing that such comments from a senior editor erode trust in the programme. Though Katz insisted the tweet was never meant for public view and that Newsnight remains fair and balanced, Labour refused to accept his explanation without formal redress. Reeves herself responded with dry sarcasm, simply replying 'thanks...', while fellow Labour figures mocked the show as dull and questioned Katz’s credibility given his newspaper background. The controversy has also revived scrutiny over Katz’s lack of television experience, especially following the turbulent departure of his predecessor amid the Savile scandal.

article_content: From the grim-faced Edwardian woman in her patterned dress to the unsmiling visage of photographer Robert Cornelius, the world’s oldest selfies are a surprisingly joyless bunch. But while modern selfies are often taken for fun, for the pioneering posers of the 1800s, photographic self-portraits were revolutionary. Now Mashable.com has rounded up some of the best—and the results are surprisingly impressive. Stunning: This image, dating from 1900, shows a female photographer with her Box Brownie. Alongside the woman standing beside her Kodak Box Brownie, there are group shots and even one taken outdoors, apparently in the Alps. Other images include a 1930s effort of a beautifully dressed woman posing with what looks like a trophy, and a wonderful close-up of a tweed-suited gentleman taken in 1938. Like the modern selfie trend, which emerged with the rise of social media and the iPhone, the vintage version was also born from technical innovation. Photography began in the 1790s with a basic model created by Britain’s Thomas Wedgwood, and by 1826, French inventor Joseph Nicéphore Niépce had developed a device resembling modern cameras. In 1838, human beings appeared on film for the first time—a milestone swiftly followed by the first selfie, taken by American photographer Robert Cornelius in 1839. But the era of the selfie didn’t truly begin until 1900, when Kodak’s revolutionary Box Brownie camera hit the market. Priced at just $1, the cardboard Box Brownie captured two-inch photos on 117mm roll film and sold in the millions. It was cheap, easy to use, and helped introduce the world to the concept of the snapshot. As the image of the Edwardian woman, her Box Brownie poised at waist height, demonstrates, it also helped popularize the selfie. Vintage classic: A Fox Photos staff photographer captures his own image in a mirror, circa 1948. Launched in February 1900, the Kodak Box Brownie was the first mass-produced camera. Easy to use and, at just a dollar each, affordable to buy, it revolutionized photography—which until then had been accessible only to a small, wealthy elite. Made from cardboard and equipped with a simple meniscus lens, it took tiny two-inch square photos at the push of a button. Unlike modern cameras, its viewfinder sat atop the body, forcing users to hold the device at waist height and look down. Later models included the Bakelite Brownie 127, of which millions were sold between 1952 and 1967. There was also a slightly more expensive variant, the Beau Brownie, which featured a more advanced doublet lens and was smaller than standard models. Although the Box Brownie is no longer in production, many historical examples still exist—and, if properly cared for, can still produce wonderful photos today.

article_content: On October 6, 2013, Argentine President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner was ordered to take one month of rest after doctors discovered a chronic subdural hematoma — a slow accumulation of blood between her brain and skull — resulting from a head injury sustained on August 12. Although a CAT scan conducted shortly after the August incident showed no abnormalities and she exhibited no symptoms at the time, new headaches during a routine cardiac evaluation prompted further neurological testing. A statement issued by her physicians, signed by doctors from the Fundación Favaloro, confirmed the diagnosis of a 'chronic subdural collection' and mandated complete rest to prevent complications. The condition, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health, rarely resolves on its own and often requires surgery involving small skull drills to drain accumulated fluid and relieve pressure on the brain. President Fernández’s spokesman, Alfredo Scoccimarro, did not clarify whether she would govern remotely from the presidential residence or formally transfer authority to Vice President Amado Boudou, who was returning from Brazil. Her withdrawal from public life comes at a critical moment: just weeks before the October 27 midterm elections, where her ruling Front for Victory party seeks to retain control of Congress. This follows previous health challenges, including a 2012 thyroidectomy performed out of concern for cancer — later ruled unnecessary — and ongoing management of chronic hypertension.

article_content: A compelling story of a young woman determined to contribute to Australia’s war effort is among many being explored in research on the impact of war on Australian women. In 1915, 16-year-old Maud Butler from Kurri Kurri in the Hunter Valley coalfields caused a stir when she cut her hair, dressed in a soldier’s uniform, and stowed away on the Suevic troopship bound for Egypt. According to ABC News, historian Professor Victoria Haskins is researching Maud’s remarkable journey. She boarded the Suevic in Sydney on 23 December 1915, hoping to reach Egypt where her brother was serving. Two days later, at sea, a suspicious officer noticed her non-regulation boots and requested a medical examination — during which Maud confessed she was female. Maud had assembled her uniform piece by piece: a tunic and breeches purchased from a soldier, putties from George Street, and a cap from Bathurst Street — but she could not find regulation tan boots. 'I had to chance it,' she told reporters from the Farmer and Settler. She disembarked in Melbourne on Christmas Day, 1915, and gave an interview to local newspapers, explaining she had a 'terrible desire to help in some way.' She had previously tried to join the Red Cross in Sydney but was turned away. Professor Haskins, who has received a grant to study the experiences of Australian women during WWI, says: 'I’m reconstructing personal stories like Maud’s to reveal what life was like for women from diverse backgrounds during the war.'

article_content: Grant Harrold, a former butler to Prince Charles, has reached a confidential out-of-court settlement with the Royal Household after alleging he was unfairly dismissed and subjected to bullying. Harrold, who served the Prince and the Duchess of Cornwall at Highgrove from 2004, claimed he was forced out after refusing a transfer to Clarence House in London. In legal documents filed last year, the 34-year-old described being ostracized by senior staff, threatened, and labeled a 'pariah'—despite an exemplary work record. His doctor later diagnosed him with Phobic Anxiety Depersonalisation Syndrome, triggered by anxiety around urban environments, which reportedly led an unnamed royal staffer to deem him 'too dangerous' to interact with the royal family. Harrold was also allegedly compared to Raoul Moat, the convicted killer whose 2008 spree shocked the UK. The Royal Household initially maintained his role was redundant and offered a relocation package, which he declined. However, the Household has now confirmed the matter was settled amicably before reaching tribunal, expressing regret for the distress caused. Harrold, who continues to live in a cottage on the Highgrove estate, emphasized his enduring respect for Prince Charles and the Duchess. Since leaving royal service, he founded Nicholas Veitch, a business offering fine dining events, etiquette training, and butler instruction. Inspired by royal documentaries like 'Elizabeth R' and his early work in a Scottish country house, Harrold rose through the ranks after being recommended by his brother, a footman for the Queen. He recalls memorable moments, including dancing with the Queen at Balmoral and nearly running over one of her corgis—a moment she simply smiled at. Demand for his expertise has surged since his departure.

article_content: Lance Armstrong’s final Tour de France unravelled dramatically on Stage 8, as twin crashes and relentless misfortune dashed his dream of an unprecedented eighth win. The stage, claimed by Luxembourg’s Andy Schleck, propelled Australia’s Cadel Evans into the yellow jersey with a narrow 20-second lead over Schleck. Defending champion Alberto Contador, despite his Astana team forcing a punishing pace on the final climbs, finished over a minute behind. At 38, Armstrong crashed twice — once shortly after the start and again at high speed approaching the Col de la Ramaz — finishing more than eleven minutes down, his right arm heavily bandaged. 'My Tour is over,' he told AFP, but added he’d keep racing to support his teammates. His Radioshack squad, already reeling from a key puncture on Stage 3, now look to veteran teammate Levi Leipheimer, who secured an impressive eighth-place finish. Schleck’s victory — his first of the season — came after outsprinting Spain’s Samuel Sanchez on the final meters, establishing him as Contador’s most credible threat. Evans and Contador both joined the main chase group, 10 seconds behind Schleck, while Britain’s Bradley Wiggins lost 1 minute and 45 seconds after fading in the final kilometers. Schleck’s resilience was bolstered by his brother Frank’s earlier crash and the support of teammate Fabian Cancellara, who kept him in contention through the tough early stages.

article_content: In May 2012, 22-year-old Sam Fretwell from Eakring, Nottinghamshire, was involved in a severe 50mph collision on the A614 while wearing a seatbelt. Another vehicle pulled out from a side junction, striking his car with tremendous force. The impact drove his face into the steering wheel, causing 42 facial fractures, a crushed nose that shifted two inches downward, shattered eye sockets, and a severed ear. He also suffered a broken sternum and a punctured lung. Rushed by air ambulance to Nottingham University Hospital, Fretwell underwent a 13-hour reconstructive surgery. Surgeons replaced his eye sockets with wire mesh, inserted titanium plates from his jaw to his cheekbones, and successfully reattached his ear. A tracheostomy was performed while he was awake to secure his airway. For four months, his jaw was wired shut due to three breaks in his upper jaw and palate. He lost vision in one eye but survived thanks to immediate aid from three skilled bystanders: a retired traffic police officer, a former navy officer, and a general practitioner. Fretwell recalls waking up in the air ambulance with only the seven-minute estimated time of arrival etched in his memory. 'If we’d gone by road, it would’ve taken another hour — it saved my life,' he said. Psychologically, returning to the scene of the crash was harrowing. Months later, while driving cautiously on the same road, a car pulled out at the exact junction where he’d crashed. He stopped in time but had to pull over, overwhelmed by flashbacks. Despite ongoing challenges—including impaired short-term memory from brain trauma—he made a remarkable recovery within a year. He has since opened his own business buying and selling vintage cars, a lifelong passion. 'I love driving and being around cars,' he said. 'I nearly died in one, but that won’t stop me living fully.'

article_content: According to Hotels.com’s annual Destination Romance Report, London has been named the UK’s most romantic destination, securing 18% of the public vote. This marks a shift from last year, when the Lake District held the top spot; this year, it placed second with 15%. Meanwhile, Hull has been voted the UK’s least romantic destination, receiving 19% of the vote — a sharp rise from third place last year. Slough, which topped the least romantic list in 2014, has now fallen out of the top 10 entirely. Interestingly, London also appears in the bottom 10, tied for third place with Blackpool at 7%, reflecting sharply divided public opinion about the capital’s romantic appeal. Other notable entries in the most romantic top 10 include Cornwall (7%), the Cotswolds and Edinburgh (tied at 6%), Stratford-upon-Avon (5%), and new entrants York, Devon, Bristol, and Cardiff (all between 2–4%). In the least romantic rankings, Birmingham remains in second place with 11%, while Leicester, Glasgow, and Coventry tie for fifth place at 4%. Newcomers Swansea, Liverpool, and Sheffield also join the bottom tier with 3% each. Caroline Annand of Hotels.com commented: 'With numerous new cities now featuring in both our lists, it is clear that those who previously held the top spot are working hard to prove they can be romantic too. Last year’s number one least romantic city, Slough, has been able to avoid the top ten list altogether this year — other locations need to show that romance can be found in the most unlikely of places as well.'

article_content: Dr. Lam Hoe Yeoh, a 62-year-old NHS consultant and hearing specialist, appeared at Croydon Crown Court in south London, where he faces multiple charges of voyeurism. Over a three-year period, Yeoh secretly filmed more than 1,000 individuals—including patients, colleagues, friends, and children as young as three—using hidden cameras installed in hospital bathrooms, his home, and on trains. The devices, disguised as memory sticks, pens, and watches, were placed in locations such as St Anthony’s Hospital in Surrey, the Portland Hospital in London, and his £750,000 detached home in Banstead. He was apprehended after a camera fell from a toilet at St Anthony’s Hospital and was discovered by a colleague. Police later found footage of Yeoh installing the devices. Investigators recovered 17 digital storage devices containing thousands of hours of video. Many recordings were meticulously labeled with victims’ names, descriptions, and dates. Yeoh compiled edited videos that merged footage of patient consultations with intimate bathroom scenes. One colleague was filmed over 300 times. Police have identified 32 victims; over 1,000 remain unknown. Among the footage were images of a girl believed to be three years old. Yeoh admitted to seven counts of voyeurism, six counts of making indecent images of a child, and one count of possessing extreme pornography. He claimed a familial link to actress Michelle Yeoh, but her spokesperson confirmed no relationship. Victims described profound trauma after being forced to review their own violating footage. Several recounted feeling violated, disgusted, and unsafe in workplaces they once trusted. Yeoh’s defense argued he was an obsessive collector who never viewed most of the material. He expressed regret, asking, 'Will I go to jail? I was so stupid—don’t tell my family.' He is scheduled for sentencing, facing a significant prison term. The case has been described by prosecutors as the most extensive case of organized voyeurism ever investigated by the Metropolitan Police.

article_content: Captain Francesco Schettino abandoned the cruise ship Costa Concordia after it ran aground in January 2012, while hundreds of passengers were still onboard, according to testimony and recorded phone calls presented in court in Grossetto, Italy, on Monday. Gregorio Di Falco of the Livorno Port Authority, who repeatedly ordered Schettino to return to the ship, told the court he initiated rescue operations on his own after distressed passengers called emergency services. Di Falco said he did not wait for a formal distress signal from Schettino, whose reports about the number of people still aboard were inconsistent. In audio recordings played in court, Schettino initially claimed from a lifeboat that only about a dozen people remained on the vessel — contradicting Coast Guard estimates of hundreds. He later revised his estimate to between 200 and 300 people still onboard. Schettino now faces charges of manslaughter, causing a maritime disaster, and abandoning ship with passengers still aboard. He denies any wrongdoing. The Costa Concordia capsized after striking submerged rocks off the coast of Giglio Island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, resulting in the deaths of 32 of the 4,200 people on board. Schettino’s trial is expected to last several more weeks.

article_content: On April 1, 2013, 25-year-old Tara Lewman of Batavia, Iowa, made a fatal decision: she drove her 2004 Dodge Caravan around lowered crossing gates at a railroad intersection, ignoring warning signals. Her action led to a catastrophic collision with a westbound Burlington Northern Santa Fe freight train. Two of her three children—four-year-old Erika and five-year-old Kallie—were killed instantly. Tara and her one-year-old son, Jordan, survived and were airlifted to the University of Iowa Hospitals and Clinics; their conditions remained undisclosed. According to Iowa State Patrol Sgt. Scott Bright, Lewman’s view was blocked by a stationary eastbound train, preventing her from seeing the oncoming freight train. Witness Verdae Blom, who works near the tracks, described hearing a loud crash and seeing dust rise before finding the minivan crushed into a ditch, resembling a 'tangled mess.' Emergency responders and railroad workers attempted CPR on the children, but were unable to save them. The children, known to their grandmother as Erica and Callie, were described by family and neighbors as joyful and full of life. Their school, the Cardinal Community School District in Eldon, expressed deep sorrow, with parents sharing how their own children struggled to comprehend the loss. 'He asked if they were coming back,' said one mother. Tara’s uncle, Bert Lewman, called her a 'real good mom' who would do anything for her children, adding, 'She knew better,' reflecting the community’s mix of grief and regret. Batavia, a town of about 500 residents, has experienced two other train-vehicle collisions since 1975, including a 1991 incident where a driver also bypassed crossing gates with fatal results. A 1990 derailment in the same town injured over 85 people and caused $1.8 million in damage—equivalent to more than $3 million today. Officials stress that the crossing lacks sufficient safeguards for its location and traffic volume. Trains pass through Batavia at approximately 60 mph, unlike larger cities where speeds are reduced. Sgt. Bright urged the public: 'The best thing to do is to wait—and never assume a train isn’t coming.'

article_content: NASCAR driver Kurt Busch testified that he was naked and sobbing on the floor of his motorhome after watching the film 'Seven Years in Tibet' — a moment he described as deeply spiritual — when his ex-girlfriend, Patricia Driscoll, unexpectedly entered with her young son. Busch, appearing in court during a hearing for a protective order filed by Driscoll, admitted to grabbing her face and asking her to leave, but strongly denied her allegations that he smashed her head into a wall three times and choked her in September. Driscoll, who works as a narcotics and homeland security consultant and runs a charity for wounded veterans, claims she fears for her safety and says she waited six weeks to report the incident because she was in shock. During testimony, Busch’s personal assistant, Michael Doncheff, stated that Driscoll had made several extraordinary claims in the past — including that she was a trained assassin, owned Washington D.C., and had been forcibly detained at the Mexican border while helping round up undocumented immigrants. Doncheff also noted that Driscoll appeared physically injured the weekend before the Dover incident, though she attributed the injury to a violent encounter at the border — a claim unverified by authorities. Busch’s legal team argues that Driscoll is motivated by revenge after their breakup and has fabricated the assault allegations to damage his career. Police in Dover are still investigating the September 26 incident, but no arrests have been made. Busch’s attorney confirmed that cross-examination will resume on January 12, where Busch will further detail his account.

CCTV footage captured the moment a masked man, wearing a hooded maroon jacket and a scarf over his face, entered the store carrying a concealed firearm. Without warning, he pulled out a sawn-off shotgun and struck the cashier directly in the eye with the barrel, causing her to collapse in pain. Despite his efforts to break into the cash register, the assailant failed to steal anything and fled the scene empty-handed. The victim, who was alone in the store at the time, was rushed to hospital where she received treatment for significant swelling and bruising around her left eye. Warwickshire Police have since released the disturbing video in hopes that members of the public can help identify the suspect. Authorities describe him as a slim white male in his early twenties, standing between 5 feet 8 inches and 5 feet 10 inches tall, dressed in dark trousers and wearing a dark glove on his left hand. Anyone with information is urged to contact Detective Constable Gareth Unett or report anonymously through Crimestoppers.

article_content: A public forum in St. Louis aimed at discussing a new civilian oversight board for the police devolved into chaos late Wednesday, as tensions boiled over between community members and Jeff Roorda, head of the city’s police union. Roorda, who was wearing a blue wristband that read 'I am Darren Wilson,' drew sharp backlash from attendees — many of whom had been involved in protests following the 2014 killing of Michael Brown by Wilson, a white officer who was not charged. As the meeting, chaired by Alderman Terry Kennedy, progressed peacefully for an hour, the atmosphere shifted when Roorda stood to demand order. Alderman Antonio French, the bill’s sponsor, later accused Roorda of deliberately provoking the crowd by displaying the wristband toward front-row protesters. Witnesses reported Roorda pushing through the aisle, causing a woman to fall, while others described a chaotic scene of shoving and raised voices. Police officers intervened to shield Roorda, and some attendees moved to protect others. Though no arrests were made and no one required ambulance transport, the meeting ended abruptly. Roorda insisted he was simply exercising his right to free speech, comparing his wristband to the protests in Ferguson. French countered that such symbolism, in that setting, was inflammatory, not expressive. Bishop Derrick Robinson, a local pastor and activist, said the clash became physical, with punches thrown. Both sides remain entrenched: Roorda sees himself as a target of mob aggression; French and many residents see his actions as a deliberate affront to healing. The city now faces renewed calls for accountability — and deeper reflection on how to bridge its enduring divides.

article_content: Forget paracetamol or honey and lemon — according to a new survey, the best remedy for feeling unwell might be listening to music. Nearly 90% of respondents agreed that a good tune can lift spirits during illness or tough times, and more than 80% said music has personally helped them feel better when sick or down. Queen’s 'Bohemian Rhapsody' emerged as the nation’s favorite song for combating illness or depression. The 1975 epic, written by Freddie Mercury for Queen’s landmark album 'Night at the Opera', features a dramatic blend of ballad, opera, and hard rock — and was voted top choice by 29% of British men. Among women, Abba’s 'Dancing Queen' took the lead at 28%, while only 16% of men selected it. Pharrell Williams’ 2013 hit 'Happy' tied with classical music for third place. 'Happy' was especially popular among 18–34-year-olds (30%), while those over 65 favored classical music (39%) and 'Dancing Queen' (31%). The ComRes poll, conducted among 1,000 UK adults, coincided with BBC Radio 2’s Faith in the World Week, themed around the healing power of music. Other beloved tracks include The Beatles’ 'Let it Be', Bob Marley’s 'Three Little Birds', and Robbie Williams’ 'Angels'. Michael Jackson’s 'Billie Jean', Elvis Presley’s 'The Wonder of You', and Frank Sinatra’s 'My Way' also ranked highly. Nearly 70% of participants said they prefer music over speech when unwell, with only 36% favoring spoken content. Research from the University of Kent adds depth: people experiencing sadness often choose emotionally rich, 'beautiful' music — even melancholic tunes by Johnny Cash or Leonard Cohen — because these songs evoke meaningful memories and help counteract low moods.

article_content: On May 25, 2013, tens of thousands of demonstrators marched through central Paris to protest France’s recent legalization of same-sex marriage. The demonstration, organized by the group 'La Manif Pour Tous', gathered at the historic Esplanade des Invalides, where protesters waved pink, blue, and white flags — symbols of their campaign for traditional family values. As night fell, violence erupted when several hundred individuals, many affiliated with far-right groups, clashed with police. Protesters threw bottles, attacked journalists, and attempted to breach barriers. In response, riot police deployed tear gas and pepper spray, making approximately 100 arrests. Among those detained were members of the militant group GUD and individuals wearing Guy Fawkes masks to conceal their identities. Police estimated 150,000 attendees, though organizers claimed over a million. The protest was not only about marriage equality but also reflected growing public discontent with President Francois Hollande’s administration, which faces criticism over high unemployment (exceeding 10%) and economic stagnation. Protesters hung banners on the headquarters of the ruling Socialist Party demanding Hollande’s resignation. The movement, originally backed by the Roman Catholic Church, has since broadened to include opposition politicians and nationalist activists. Some UMP party leaders, including Jean-Francois Cope, participated, encouraging youth to join their ranks as a 'new generation' of conservatives. Others, like former Prime Ministers Francois Fillon and Alain Juppe, declined to attend, arguing that change should be pursued through parliamentary channels. The tension intensified after far-right writer Dominique Venner, linked to a nationalist faction, committed suicide inside Notre Dame Cathedral on May 21, 2013. He left a note condemning same-sex marriage and calling for 'spectacular' resistance to defend French identity. Hollande’s government condemned the act, emphasizing that the marriage law had already been ratified by Parliament and upheld by the Constitutional Council. Despite the unrest, polls showed that over 50% of French citizens supported the law, and more than 70% believed the protests should end. France’s first legal same-sex wedding was scheduled for May 29, 2013, in Montpellier, a city known for its vibrant LGBTQ+ community. Protesters hope their mobilization will stall future legislation on adoption, assisted reproduction, and surrogacy for same-sex couples.

article_content: A rare signed copy of Adolf Hitler’s autobiography, Mein Kampf, has surfaced for sale. Dated March 5, 1945, the copy was signed by Hitler in his Berlin bunker as Allied forces closed in on the capital. It is believed to be the final autographed copy he produced before his suicide on April 30, 1945. Hitler reportedly gave the book to a senior staff member — possibly as a parting gift — in a symbolic act meant to preserve his ideology beyond his death. The signature, once bold and confident, had deteriorated into a faint, shaky scrawl, reflecting his declining mental state and awareness of impending defeat. Mein Kampf, first published in two volumes in 1925 and 1926 after Hitler’s imprisonment following the failed 1923 Munich Putsch, lays out his extremist worldview: virulent antisemitism, hatred of communism, and the belief that Germany must conquer 'Lebensraum' (living space) in Eastern Europe at the expense of Slavic peoples. It also rejects parliamentary democracy, blaming it for Germany’s post-WWI struggles. This particular copy is from a limited 1939 edition issued to commemorate Hitler’s 50th birthday. Beneath his signature is the handwritten date: March 5, 1945. On or around that date, Allied forces captured Cologne, signaling the collapse of Nazi defenses on multiple fronts. At the time, Hitler had retreated permanently to the Führerbunker beneath the Reich Chancellery. With Soviet forces advancing from the east and Western Allies from the west, he clung to delusional hopes of a miraculous military turnaround. Twelve days later, he and Eva Braun died by suicide — he by gunshot, she by cyanide. The book was acquired decades ago by a British man from an American collector and is now being auctioned by Mullocks with a pre-sale estimate of £5,000. Richard Westwood-Brooks of Mullocks noted, 'Material from Hitler’s final weeks is exceptionally rare. This book is a chilling testament to the futility and decay of his regime.' Although Mein Kampf is not illegal in Germany, official publishing remains restricted to prevent the resurgence of Nazi propaganda.

article_content: Former Vice President Dick Cheney praised the Obama administration for carrying out a targeted drone strike that killed Anwar al-Awlaki, an American-born cleric and top al-Qaeda recruiter operating in Yemen. He called the operation justified and effective. Yet Cheney also urged the administration to retract its earlier criticisms of George W. Bush’s counterterrorism tactics — especially the use of enhanced interrogation techniques — arguing that approving lethal drone strikes against U.S. citizens without trial undermines previous moral objections. The strike, conducted with CIA support, also eliminated Samir Khan, an American of Pakistani descent who authored al-Qaeda’s online magazine, Inspire, along with two other individuals. Liz Cheney, Dick’s daughter, went further, accusing President Obama of betraying American values and claiming he owes the public an apology. While Republicans viewed the strike as necessary and consistent with security priorities, Democrats like former Congresswoman Jane Harman cautioned that expanding drone warfare without clear legal oversight could damage America’s credibility and fuel extremism. She emphasized the need for transparent legal standards and adherence to democratic principles. Retired CIA Director Michael Hayden dismissed concerns over civilian casualties as exaggerated, insisting drones remain the most precise and indispensable tool in combating al-Qaeda. The central tension remains: can the U.S. legally and ethically kill its own citizens overseas — and does doing so ultimately strengthen or weaken the fight against terrorism?

article_content: Twelve people were arrested on Friday during an 'Occupy' demonstration at the U.S. Supreme Court, where protesters dressed as justices and sang songs by the Motown group The Supremes, according to court officials. One individual was arrested inside the building, while the other 11 were taken into custody on the courthouse steps and plaza. More than 200 demonstrators gathered around the court to mark the second anniversary of the Supreme Court’s 2010 ruling in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which lifted restrictions on corporate spending in federal elections. The ruling permitted organizations to raise and spend unlimited funds on political campaigns, as long as they did not coordinate directly with candidates or contribute funds to their campaigns. This decision paved the way for the rise of Super PACs—entities that can accept unlimited donations from corporations, unions, and individuals. Protests were also planned at federal courthouses in more than 50 cities nationwide, including Akron, Ohio; Gainesville, Florida; and Honolulu, Hawaii. The one-day event, titled 'Occupy the Courts,' was organized by the grassroots group Move to Amend and drew inspiration from the Occupy Wall Street movement. According to the Occupy the Courts website, 'Move to Amend volunteers across the USA will lead the charge against the judiciary, which created—and continues to expand—corporate personhood rights.' The Occupy Wall Street movement, which began in New York City in September 2011, has since grown into a global call to address economic inequality. CNN’s Bill Mears, Stacey Samuel, and Michael Martinez contributed to this report.

article_content: More than 100 protesters were arrested outside the White House on Monday after refusing to disperse, according to the U.S. Park Service. All 114 individuals were later released pending court dates. The demonstrators — mostly residents of Appalachian coal-mining states including West Virginia, Virginia, Kentucky, and Tennessee — had obtained permits to gather in front of the White House. However, some violated conditions of their permit, prompting the arrests. The protest marked the culmination of a three-day event called 'Appalachia Rising,' which began with a regional conference titled 'Voices from the Mountains.' On Monday, hundreds assembled at Freedom Plaza before marching to the White House, where 114 participants staged a sit-in. Climate scientist James Hansen, arrested during the action, stated: 'The science is clear — mountaintop removal destroys historic mountain ranges, poisons water supplies, and pollutes the air with coal and rock dust. It provides only a small fraction of our energy and can and should be abolished. The time for half-measures and yielding to polluting industries must end.' Mickey McCoy, former mayor of Inez, Kentucky, added: 'I’ve talked, begged, debated, written letters, published op-eds, and lobbied at every level to stop mountaintop removal. Being arrested? That’s a small price to pay for being heard. My home and my people are paying the real price — they’re dying.' Mountaintop removal is a form of surface mining used primarily in the Appalachian region, involving the removal of mountain peaks to access coal seams. This practice has led to widespread environmental degradation, affecting streams, wildlife, and plant ecosystems.

article_content: A review of the police handling of Nicola Bulley’s disappearance is set to be published later this morning. Ms. Bulley, 45, went missing in St Michael’s-on-Wyre, Lancashire, in January while walking her dog. Her body was found 23 days later, just over a mile from where she was last seen. Lancashire Police faced criticism for disclosing that she had been struggling with menopause and alcohol-related issues. The College of Policing review, commissioned by Lancashire’s Police and Crime Commissioner, Andrew Snowden, is scheduled for release at 10:00 GMT. It will examine the investigation and search operations, communication strategies, public engagement, and the release of personal information. A coroner later determined that Ms. Bulley died accidentally after falling into the River Wyre. Police and specialist diving teams conducted an extensive search across land, sea, and the river. On 27 January, Ms. Bulley dropped her two daughters — aged six and nine — off at school before embarking on her regular dog walk beside the river. Her phone, still connected to a Microsoft Teams call for her job as a mortgage adviser, was found on a bench on a steep riverside bank, alongside her dog’s lead and harness.

article_content: Following the tragic death of footballer Piermario Morosini during a Serie B match, Italian club Udinese has vowed to ensure the lifelong care of his severely disabled sister, Maria Carla. Morosini, who was 25 at the time of his death, lost his parents and brother in his teens, leaving Maria Carla as his only surviving close relative — cared for in a residential facility in Bergamo and supported by an elderly aunt. In a heartfelt statement, Udinese declared it their duty to never leave her alone after fate took her entire family. To secure her future, the club has established a dedicated donation fund, accessible through a publicly listed bank account, to be managed by Maria Carla’s legal guardian. Donations are being encouraged from other football clubs across Italy. Morosini collapsed during the first half of Livorno’s match against Pescara on Saturday due to suspected cardiac arrest. Despite immediate medical intervention, he could not be revived. In mourning, all Serie B matches were postponed, and tributes including moments of silence were held globally. A former Italy U-21 international, Morosini joined Udinese in 2005, making only five appearances before being loaned to multiple clubs, including Livorno since January. Udinese captain Antonio di Natale described him as 'an exceptional lad, so full of life,' emphasizing his unwavering commitment to the team despite personal hardships. Livorno confirmed Monday they have permanently retired the No. 25 jersey worn by Morosini at the time of his passing.

article_content: OnePlus has long been known for delivering some of the fastest charging speeds in the smartphone industry — both wired and wireless. However, with the OnePlus 11, the company chose to remove wireless charging to achieve a slimmer profile. Now, according to recent leaks, the upcoming OnePlus 12 is expected to bring back 50W wireless charging, mirroring the capability of the OnePlus 10 Pro. Leakers Digital Chat Station and Max Jambor both reported this development on Monday, aligning with earlier speculation from July. The OnePlus 12 is also anticipated to support 100W wired charging. When questioned about the absence of wireless charging in the OnePlus 11, OnePlus explained the decision was driven by design goals: removing the charging coil allowed for a thinner device. A similar rationale likely applied to the foldable OnePlus Open, which prioritized slimness for pocket-friendly folding. As a result, the OnePlus 12 is expected to be slightly thicker than the 8.53mm-thick OnePlus 11 due to the reintroduction of the wireless charging coil. Renderings suggest the overall design remains largely unchanged from its predecessor. Beyond charging, leaks indicate the OnePlus 12 will feature a 5,400mAh battery (up from 5,000mAh), a 64MP telephoto lens with 3X optical zoom (improving on the 11’s 32MP with 2X zoom), a 6.7-inch 120Hz display, up to 16GB of RAM, and the Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor. It will launch with OxygenOS 14, a software layer built on ColorOS but retaining OnePlus-specific UI customizations. In terms of wireless charging speed, the OnePlus 12 will outpace flagship offerings from Samsung (15W), Apple (15W), and Google (23W), matching the 50W speed of the Xiaomi 13 Ultra. The device is slated for a December 2023 release in China and a January 2024 global rollout. While the OnePlus 11 received high praise, expectations for the 12 extend beyond just restoring wireless charging — users hope for broader improvements, particularly in software performance. Although OxygenOS is transitioning toward ColorOS, OnePlus has signaled confidence in its continued evolution, leaving room for optimism.

article_content: On Tuesday, authorities in Winder, Georgia, began investigating whether a concrete-encased body found in a backyard belonged to Sean Dugas, a 30-year-old former crime reporter for the Pensacola News Journal who went missing on August 27. Twin brothers William and Christopher Cormier, both 31, have been arrested on charges of concealing a death. Police say the brothers arrived at their father’s home in Winder three weeks ago from Florida. According to Winder Police Chief Dennis Dorsey, the brothers told their father they had been caring for Dugas’ dog—but later admitted to killing it. The dog was buried in the backyard of the rented property. During a search of the yard, officers uncovered a human body inside a plastic storage container sealed with concrete, buried approximately two feet underground. Authorities believe the burial occurred around the time the brothers arrived, and the concrete may have been purchased at a nearby Home Depot. Pensacola Police Captain David Alexander confirmed that Dugas’ girlfriend reported him missing on September 13 after finding his home empty except for a television. A male roommate was also unaccounted for. Managing Editor Ginny Graybiel of the Pensacola News Journal described Dugas as a 'very gentle, good-hearted soul' who worked at the paper from 2005 to 2010, starting as a clerk before becoming a respected police and entertainment reporter. article_content: Most people assume emails vanish into thin air the moment they hit ‘send.’ But in reality, every message undertakes a long, winding journey across thousands of miles of physical cables and servers. A new tool called Email Miles reveals this hidden path. Developed by Jonah Brucker-Cohen, a 39-year-old design lecturer from New York, Email Miles is a free plugin for email platforms like Apple Mail and Google Gmail. Once installed, it tracks the geographic locations of every server an email passes through — from sender to recipient — using GPS coordinates and internet routing data. Each time an email hops from one server to another, the plugin logs the new location, building a trail of geotags. It then calculates the total distance traveled — not as the crow flies, but by summing the direct segments between each server stop. One striking example: an email sent from New York to Dakar, Senegal, covered 12,115 miles — far beyond the direct 4,700-mile distance. Why? Because it first traveled west to Chicago (790 miles), then further west to Mountain View, California (2,163 miles), then east to Dallas (1,699 miles), across the Atlantic to London (4,745 miles), and finally south to Dakar (2,718 miles). This detour isn't a glitch — it's standard. Email traffic follows complex global networks managed by different telecom providers, each controlling their own cable segments. Routing decisions are based on cost, bandwidth, and international agreements, not geography. Brucker-Cohen says the goal is to make the invisible infrastructure of digital communication visible. 'Information feels weightless, but it moves through real places,' he explains. 'Email Miles helps people feel the distance — literally.' To expand access, Brucker-Cohen launched a crowdfunding campaign on FundAnything to make the plugin freely available to everyone.

article_content:
A failed terrorist attack in a central Stockholm district crowded with Christmas shoppers could have been catastrophic, Swedish authorities said late Saturday. Police are investigating whether two explosions in Stockholm, an email threat sent shortly before the attacks, and the death of a man apparently killed in one of the blasts are connected. "Most worrying attempt at a terrorist attack in a crowded part of central Stockholm," Swedish Foreign Minister Carl Bildt said in a Twitter post on Saturday. "Failed — but could have been truly catastrophic."
 A Swedish news agency and police received an email threat targeting the Swedish people 10 minutes before the explosions, which killed one person and injured two others. "We have not taken any decision to increase the terror threat level," said Swedish Security Police spokesman Mikael Gunnarsson. "Apart from the email, we had no other indications or warnings that this would happen."
 The email referenced Swedish troop presence in Afghanistan and Lars Vilks, a cartoonist who depicted the Prophet Muhammad with a dog’s body. The message included audio files in Swedish and Arabic. The sender condemned Sweden’s silence on its role in Afghanistan and support for Vilks, stating: "Now your children, daughters, and sisters will die like our brothers, sisters, and children are dying."
 "Our actions will speak for themselves," the voice in the recording said. "As long as you don’t end your war against Islam and the humiliation of the Prophet, and your stupid support for Lars Vilks the pig."
 Terrorism expert Magnus Ranstorp told CNN he believed the attacker did not act alone. "This was not something where he just woke up and thought he would blow himself up," said Ranstorp, a professor at the Swedish Military Academy and former terrorism studies professor at the University of St. Andrews. The first explosion occurred at the intersection of Drottninggatan and Olof Palmes Gata, involving a car that detonated multiple times, likely due to pressurized gas cylinders. Two people sustained minor injuries and were hospitalized. A second explosion occurred approximately five minutes later at Drottninggatan and Bryggargatan. An unidentified man was found dead at the scene. A bag was discovered nearby. Bomb technicians used a robot to retrieve the bag for examination. The cause of the second explosion remains under investigation. Video footage from TV4 showed flames erupting from the vehicle, which was parked among other cars. The email ended with a call to action for "all Mujahideen in Europe and Sweden": "Now is the time to strike, don’t wait any longer. Step up with whatever you have — even if it’s a knife. I know you have more than a knife. Fear no one. Fear no prison. Fear no death."
 It remains unclear whether the sender belonged to any specific organization. He claimed to have traveled to the Middle East for jihad, not work, and asked his family for forgiveness for deceiving them.

article_content: (CNN) — What’s happening in Ferguson? Nine days have passed since Michael Brown was killed, yet his family remains without basic information from investigators. Eyewitnesses and cell phone videos captured the moments after his death — when his body lay uncovered in the street for five hours — but officials have released no autopsy reports, witness statements, or grand jury indictments. Something is deeply wrong here. Imagine needing to perform an autopsy on your own son while his body rests in a funeral home, simply to understand how he died before burial. The Ferguson Police Department was previously cited in a 2013 Missouri Attorney General report for racial profiling. How can anyone believe they are capable of impartially investigating one of their own? The FBI should have been involved from day one. While the National Guard deploys to Ferguson, local law enforcement must exercise common sense: step aside. State Highway Patrol Captain Ron Johnson has emerged as a vital, calming presence in the community — we now need the same level of integrity on the prosecutorial side. The Missouri Attorney General should immediately appoint a special prosecutor, working jointly with the U.S. Department of Justice. The community demands it. The first — and very preliminary — autopsy results have now been released. Dr. Michael M. Baden, a renowned forensic pathologist hired by Brown’s family, found that Michael was shot at least six times, including twice in the head. (Let that sink in: the family had to hire a private pathologist to get answers.) At least one bullet entered and exited multiple times, shattering Brown’s right eye, passing through his face, exiting his jawbone, and re-entering near his collarbone. The final shot, which struck the top of his head, was fatal. With five decades of experience — and over 20,000 autopsies — Baden delivered his findings with calm authority. He noted that the state medical examiner, a trusted colleague, would likely reach similar conclusions. But Baden lacked access to Brown’s clothing, X-rays, toxicology reports, or witness statements — raising questions about why these materials were withheld. He estimated the shots were fired from between one and thirty feet away. Wounds on Brown’s arms could indicate he raised his hands or made a defensive motion. From my perspective, six bullets fired into an unarmed teenager in broad daylight constitute excessive force. But even this detail moves us only slightly closer to the truth. Eyewitness accounts vary wildly — and such testimony is notoriously unreliable, often contradicted by physical evidence. One witness, Piaget Crenshaw, told CNN it appeared the officer attempted to pull Brown into the vehicle, then chased him until Brown turned around and was shot. Others claim Brown was shot in the back. The case now hinges on two conflicting testimonies: those of Dorian Johnson and Officer Darren Wilson. Johnson, who was walking with Brown, recounted to MSNBC that Wilson initially ordered them to use the sidewalk. When they complied, Wilson reversed his patrol car and nearly hit them. Johnson claims Wilson then opened his door, slammed it into Brown, grabbed him by the neck, and shot him once. After both fled, Wilson fired a second shot into Brown’s back. Brown then turned, raised his hands, and pleaded, ‘I don’t have a gun. Stop shooting!’ According to Johnson, Wilson then advanced and fired multiple more shots until Brown collapsed into a fetal position. Meanwhile, an anonymous caller identifying herself as ‘Josie’ told a St. Louis radio station she knew Wilson’s side: Wilson says he saw Brown and Johnson walking in the street, noticed they matched the description of suspects in a recent robbery, and asked them to move. When he stepped out, Brown shoved him back into the car twice, punched him in the face, and wrestled for his gun. Wilson says the weapon discharged during the struggle. Brown and his friend ran. Wilson pursued, ordered them to stop, and when they turned, Brown charged him. Wilson fired in self-defense, landing the fatal shot in the forehead. Brown fell two or three feet in front of him. A source with direct knowledge of the investigation told CNN this account is accurate. Where testimonies conflict, an autopsy can provide clarity — revealing distance, positioning, and whether Brown ever touched Wilson’s weapon. One question Baden could definitively answer: Did Michael Brown suffer? His mother asked. Baden replied: ‘The head wound rendered him unconscious immediately. In my professional opinion, he did not suffer.’ I urge local authorities to recuse themselves and transfer the investigation to an independent special prosecutor. And please — hurry. Complete the remaining autopsies, the investigation, and the grand jury proceedings. Ferguson and Michael Brown’s family don’t need speculation. They need answers. Until then, there will only be more heartbreak, chaos, and uncertainty.

article_content: Perhaps Ibrox was simply saving its energy for Monday’s annual general meeting. At the close of another tumultuous week in the club’s recent, chaotic history, there was scarcely any reaction from supporters as they watched yet another low-key home victory. There was no show of support for Ally McCoist, despite his manager enduring another week of emotional strain—moving closer to severing ties with the club and learning that former colleague Mark Hateley had been working behind his back. Rangers striker Fraser Aird put his side ahead after 10 minutes against Livingston. Aird celebrated with his teammates after scoring. Rangers lineup: Simonsen, Foster, McGregor, McCulloch, Wallace, Aird, Black (Shiels 81'), Law, Smith (Templeton 73'), Miller (Boyd 73'), Clark. Subs not used: Mohsni, Daly, Robinson, Faure. Goals: Aird 10', Mensing (o.g.) 74'. Livingston lineup: Jamieson, Fordyce, Kyle Jacobs (Praprotnik 82'), Mensing, Gallacher, Rutherford, Keaghan Jacobs, Mullen (McKenna 83'), O'Brien, Glen (Hippolyte 74'), White. Subs not used: Sives, Ogleby, Beaumont, Grant. Referee: William Collum. Attendance: 28,053. There was barely a ripple of protest directed at the boardroom that has been undermining their club hero. And there was, of course, little to celebrate: a strike from Fraser Aird and a Simon Mensing own goal secured a routine Championship win. Sadly, it is apathy and resignation that now greet the realization that McCoist’s time at Rangers is running out. Even anger seems scarce where match days once offered a platform for protest. A quiet acquiescence now suggests McCoist won’t lead the team much further. The only vocal demand from fans for who should be removed from power came from a small group at the foot of the Broomloan Road Stand, chanting anti-boardroom slogans targeting Sandy and James Easdale: 'You greedy b*******, get out of our club!' It was claimed that 28,053 were present—but chairman David Somers, as he did two weeks ago, may need to revise this number to reflect the shrinking crowd. McCoist, who remained visibly engaged in his technical area throughout the match, suggested it could take time before disaffected fans return in previous numbers after enduring repeated disappointments from Rangers’ leadership. McCoist said: 'I’m not sure attendances are a worry. Obviously, when we play at home, I’d rather see 50,000 than 15,000, 20,000, or 25,000—that goes without saying. But I understand, 100 percent, the feelings of the vast majority of fans over the last three years. I’ve felt unbelievably sorry for them. I believe the club will win them back. But in the short term? I don’t know.' Livingston captain Simon Mensing scored a late own goal to make it 2-0. On what may be his final home match in charge, McCoist selected a frontline of Nicky Clark and Kenny Miller, with Jon Daly joining Kris Boyd on the bench. The players, perhaps still shell-shocked by the leak of McCoist’s potential resignation, were sluggish in their last outing at Queen of the South—and they survived an early scare here before seizing a 10th-minute lead. For Mark Burchill’s caretaker reign to begin in spectacular fashion, he would have needed Danny Mullen’s shot to find the net—but Steve Simonsen made a brilliant left-handed save, diving to push it away. Rangers struggled to create clear chances against the Championship’s bottom side and were happy to take a 1-0 lead into halftime. From an inadequately cleared Stevie Smith corner, the ball fell to Aird, who fired a precise shot into the bottom-right corner of Darren Jamieson’s net. Ian Black rattled the side netting, but Livingston’s defense never looked truly under pressure. In their earlier meeting this season, Lewis Macleod’s overhead kick decided the game—but with Macleod injured, there was no such spark today. With little support from the stands, Livingston defended resolutely. Had Jordan White converted a close-range header, the spotlight might have shifted back onto McCoist’s squad. McCoist spent long stretches of the second half in deep conversation with assistant Kenny McDowall, searching for a breakthrough. But even those discussions couldn’t inspire Nicky Law to convert a 12-yard chance after Aird’s cutback—he failed to hit the target. With 17 minutes left, McCoist introduced David Templeton and Kris Boyd to inject flair. But it wasn’t magic—it was a mix-up—that broke the deadlock. Aird’s cross was misjudged by Mensing, who inadvertently headed it past Jamieson as the keeper rushed out. Substitute Dean Shiels denied Keaghan Jacobs a late consolation, and Rangers’ relief was palpable—even if the atmosphere remained numb. Half-time advertising promoted second-half season tickets for £125. It will take more than a discounted price tag—preferably without Sports Direct branding—to lure even the most loyal fans back to Ibrox.

article_content: In recent weeks, global attention has focused on match-fixing scandals — from Europol’s announcement of over 680 suspicious football matches to China’s lifetime bans of 33 players and officials. Yet one critical question remains underexplored: How, exactly, do you fix a football match? Unlike cricket, which has natural pauses, football is a fluid, continuous team sport — seemingly resistant to manipulation. But investigators say hundreds of games have been successfully corrupted. So how is it done? There are three main methods. First, the corrupt referee: for decades, some officials have been swayed by bribes — including, as documented in 'The Fix: Soccer & Organized Crime,' sexual favors offered by clubs to influence match outcomes. While referees can influence games through dubious penalties or red cards, their ability to control results is inherently limited. Second, a small group of players — typically four or five — can be coerced into deliberately underperforming. To outsiders, it appears as normal play: everyone runs, shouts, and reacts. But while six players compete earnestly, five are playing to lose. This subtle sabotage is nearly impossible to detect without insider knowledge. The most insidious and effective method involves club owners. Some owners strategically plan which matches to lose at the start of a season — betting against their own team to profit financially. In extreme cases, they intimidate players directly: threatening to withhold salaries unless the team loses. As revealed in FIFPro’s 'Black Book of Football,' such coercion is alarmingly common. Players across Europe have reported being told, 'Lose today, or you won’t get paid.' While corruption is far worse in parts of Asia — where entire leagues in China and South Korea have been shut down for investigations — Europe is not immune. Without decisive action, the integrity of football as a global sport hangs in the balance.

article_content: Leicester Tigers have secured third place in the Aviva Premiership and will face Northampton Saints away in the semi-finals next weekend, following a thrilling 31-27 bonus-point victory over leaders Saracens at Welford Road. The match featured a dramatic 21-minute spell around halftime during which six tries were scored, Saracens winger Michael Tagicakibau was sin-binned, and flanker Justin Melck was sent off for what appeared to be eye-gouging. Leicester overturned an early 8-3 deficit to lead 10-8 at half-time, thanks to a penalty try, followed by touchdowns from Manu Tuilagi, Blaine Scully, and Graham Kitchener — securing the crucial bonus point. Saracens responded with tries from Ben Spencer (twice), a penalty try, and Jack Wilson. Spencer’s late try earned them a losing bonus point. Both teams were significantly weakened: Saracens rested most of their top 30 players ahead of the Heineken Cup final and a possible Premiership decider. Leicester also suffered key injuries, including to Owen Williams, David Mele, Boris Stankovich, and Geoff Parling. Stankovich exited within a minute of kickoff after a ruck injury, replaced by Marcos Ayerza. Tom Croft made a highly anticipated return for Leicester after undergoing knee surgery in Round 1. Meanwhile, Maro Itoje made his Premiership debut for Saracens. After the break, Leicester extended their lead to 17-8 in quick succession as Tagicakibau received a yellow card for a dangerous tip tackle, and Melck was shown a red card for apparent eye-gouging. Tuilagi, Scully, and Kitchener all scored tries in a nine-minute span. Saracens replied with a penalty try and a try from Jack Wilson. With four minutes remaining, Spencer intercepted a pass and sprinted 70 yards to score, but Leicester held on for the win.

article_content: A bull being transported to slaughter escaped and triggered a six-mile chase through Chengdu, China. It leapt from the back of a truck and ran wild through the city, injuring four people along the way. The animal, weighing approximately 400kg, rampaged along busy roads, terrifying bystanders and disrupting traffic. Its owner, Zhou, along with his wife and assistants, pursued the bull on foot for more than six miles before calling police for assistance. Eight officers responded to the scene, and a passing private vehicle also joined the effort, striking the bull multiple times without stopping it. At one point, a police officer fired four shots at the animal. Eventually, an SUV rammed the bull, pinning it against a tree. The bull was left severely injured on a pedestrian crossing. It remains unclear whether it survived. Among the injured were an elderly man, a young child, and a police officer — all of whom were taken to hospital. Eyewitness photos show the bull airborne after being struck by a vehicle and lying motionless on the road afterward. One bystander attempted to stop the bull with a baseball bat before the SUV intervention.
