When Scott Warner swallowed a handful of pills and washed them down with vodka, all he could think about was the way his son looked back at him and smiled before boarding a plane to Iraq. Heath Warner was 19, an Army private, when a bomb killed him in al-Anbar Province on November 22, 2006. 'From the moment those men in uniforms arrived at our door, each day, the pain only got worse,' recalled Scott Warner. 'I was crawling up the walls. People out in the real world would ask me, "Why aren't you over this? He's been gone for years. Why aren't you better by now?" All I wanted to do was end my life. I know I'm not alone. I've talked to other parents, other family members. We are hurting—and someone must do something.'",
      "If you need help, contact the Veterans Crisis Line at 1-800-273-8255, press 1.",
      "Though the military tracks suicides among service members, suicides among their family members—spouses, siblings, and parents—go uncounted. But CNN learned Wednesday that the Pentagon’s Defense Suicide Prevention Office has sent a report to Congress detailing, for the first time, a proposal to track these deaths.",
      "The report came partly in response to cries for help from groups like the National Military Family Association, whose members know firsthand about these suicides and have struggled to draw attention to the issue.",
      "In interviews with CNN, military family members who have attempted or considered suicide say the cumulative trauma of 12 years of war—America’s longest conflicts—and unprecedented multiple deployments of their loved ones have left them exhausted and desperate. Some have attempted suicide while caring for injured service members. Others, like Scott Warner, have been pushed to the edge by the loss of a loved one in war.",
      "Warner has slowly emerged from the darkness that engulfed him before his suicide attempt in 2010. When he heard about the Defense Department’s report, he felt hope. 'If they do this, it would validate that families are traumatized,' Warner said. 'This is a lonely journey that parents, siblings, and spouses are walking. I know—I’ve talked to them. I don’t care how long it takes—we all want this.'",
      "The report, obtained by CNN on Wednesday, states that the Defense Department currently lacks the ability to investigate, monitor, or receive notifications of military family member deaths. It outlines how such a system could be implemented and estimates the cost: $681,600 in the first year and $502,200 annually thereafter.",
      "The Pentagon would need 18 to 24 months to analyze data purchased from the CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics, which tracks deaths across the U.S. population. That data—names and locations of deaths—could then be cross-referenced with the Defense Department’s records of family members enrolled in the ID card program, which grants access to health benefits and base services like commissaries.",
      "However, the report acknowledges limitations: some family members opt out of the ID program, and parents of service members often are not enrolled. If a relative not in the program dies by suicide, they may not be counted.",
      "Spokespersons for the House and Senate Armed Services Committees told CNN they are still reviewing the 20-page report. '$600,000 is very little money to spend on something this important,' said Kristina Kaufmann, a longtime military wife who has advocated for tracking family suicides since 2006. 'A couple years ago, people told me I was being histrionic—that military spouses weren’t killing themselves. But we have the anecdotes. What we don’t have—and I’m glad we’re finally trying to get—is the actual data.'",
      "Kaufmann personally knew military wives who died by suicide, including Faye Vick, who in 2006 killed herself and her two young children in a car. Monique Lingenfelter, the wife of a Special Operations sergeant at Fort Bragg, barricaded herself in her home and shot herself in 2009.",
      "Karen Ruedisueli, who works for the National Military Family Association, said the nonprofit, serving 250,000 military relatives, has heard increasing reports of family members dying by suicide. 'We have a large network of volunteers across the country who come to us with these accounts—and we have no way to track them,' she said. 'We’re encouraged that DOD has come up with some kind of methodology.'",
      "Four years ago, Deborah Mullen, wife of then-Joint Chiefs Chairman Admiral Mike Mullen, raised the issue at a Defense Department conference. She asked if the Army tracked family member suicides. She was told there were nine in 2009. When she asked how many had attempted suicide, she was stunned: 'There were too many to track.'",
      "'If that number is that large just in the Army, we really don’t have an idea of the scope of the problem,' she said. 'It’s our responsibility. These are our family members. We have got to find a way to track them.'",
      "An annual survey by Blue Star Families, the largest military family advocacy group, found that among 5,100 military family members surveyed in 2012, 9% of spouses reported considering suicide. Nearly a quarter of those said they hadn’t sought help—even if they had, it’s unclear whether support systems were equipped to respond.",
      "The DSPO report also noted that military branches lack standardized procedures for tracking suicide. The Army is the only branch that attempts to track military family member suicides.",
      "'I think we understand the bureaucracy,' Scott Warner said. 'I know this will be difficult—it’s government. But what else can we believe other than that they will try?' Sharing experiences can help.
